The torque is
$$\tau(t) = \frac{d L(t)}{d t}$$
Therefore
$$\tau(t) = M A^2 \omega^2 \begin{pmatrix} \sin 2 \theta \sin \omega t \\ - \sin 2 \theta \cos \omega t \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form τ(t) = [τ_x(t), τ_y(t), τ_z(t)] with components along e_1', e_2', e_3', and your response should be written with M, A, θ, ω, t.

subquestions.subproblem: Calculate the kinetic energy of the dumbbell.
subquestions.solution:
The rotational kinetic energy is
$$T = \frac{1}{2} I_{zz} \omega^2$$
With
$$I_{zz} = 2 M A^2 \sin^2 \theta$$
Therefore
$$T = M A^2 \omega^2 \sin^2 \theta$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form T = ..., and your response should be written with M, A, θ, ω.

grading_standard.formula: $$I(0) = \begin{pmatrix} 2 M A^2 \cos^2 \theta & 0 & - M A^2 \sin 2 \theta \\ 0 & 2 M A^2 & 0 \\ - M A^2 \sin 2 \theta & 0 & 2 M A^2 \sin^2 \theta \end{pmatrix}$$

context: A thin square plate with side length a and mass m rotates at a constant angular frequency ω about a fixed axis through the center. The axis is the z'-axis of an inertial laboratory frame (x', y', z') and is tilted by an angle θ with respect to the normal to the plate. Attach a body-fixed frame (x, y, z) to the plate with origin at the center o, the x- and y-axes along the sides of the square, and the z-axis along the normal to the plate. The unit vectors of these frames are e_x, e_y, e_z and e_{x'}, e_{y'}, e_{z'}, respectively. The axes e_x, e_z, and e_{z'} are coplanar. Let t denote time. Let J denote the angular momentum vector and M denote the torque vector. Use I_{xx}, I_{yy}, and I_{zz} for the principal moments of inertia about the x-, y-, and z-axes, respectively. The angular frequency ω has units \unit{rad/s}, the mass m has units \unit{kg}, and the length a has units \unit{m}. Express vector answers in both the body-fixed frame and the laboratory frame where asked.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the principal moments of inertia.
subquestions.solution:
By symmetry, the principal axes about o are the x-, y-, and z-axes of the plate. The corresponding principal moments of inertia are
$$I_{xx}=\frac{1}{12} m a^2$$
$$I_{yy}=\frac{1}{12} m a^2$$
$$I_{zz}=\frac{1}{6} m a^2$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given as three equations: I_xx = ..., I_yy = ..., I_zz = ..., expressed in terms of m and a only. Use the symbols I_xx, I_yy, I_zz, m, a.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the angular momentum J in the laboratory system.
subquestions.solution:
Resolve the angular velocity vector in the body-fixed frame
$$\omega_x=\omega \sin \theta$$
$$\omega_y=0$$
$$\omega_z=\omega \cos \theta$$
The angular momentum components in the body-fixed frame are
$$J_x=I_{xx}\omega \sin \theta$$
$$J_y=0$$
$$J_z=I_{zz}\omega \cos \theta$$
Substituting the principal moments gives
$$J_x=\frac{1}{12} m a^2 \omega \sin \theta$$
$$J_y=0$$
$$J_z=\frac{1}{6} m a^2 \omega \cos \theta$$
Choose the laboratory frame so that its y'-axis coincides with the body y-axis at t=0. The unit vectors are related by
$$e_x=\cos \theta \cos \omega t \, e_{x'}+\cos \theta \sin \omega t \, e_{y'}+\sin \theta \, e_{z'}$$
$$e_y=-\sin \omega t \, e_{x'}+\cos \omega t \, e_{y'}$$
$$e_z=-\sin \theta \cos \omega t \, e_{x'}-\sin \theta \sin \omega t \, e_{y'}+\cos \theta \, e_{z'}$$
Express J in the body basis
$$J=J_x e_x+J_y e_y+J_z e_z$$
The laboratory-frame components are
$$J_{x'}=-\frac{1}{12} m a^2 \omega \sin \theta \cos \theta \cos \omega t$$
$$J_{y'}=-\frac{1}{12} m a^2 \omega \sin \theta \cos \theta \sin \omega t$$
$$J_{z'}=\frac{1}{12} m a^2 \omega \left(1+\cos^2 \theta\right)$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given as the laboratory-frame vector J = J_{x'} e_{x'} + J_{y'} e_{y'} + J_{z'} e_{z'}, with J_{x'}, J_{y'}, and J_{z'} expressed in terms of m, a, ω, θ, and t only. Use the unit vectors e_{x'}, e_{y'}, e_{z'} and the symbols J, J_{x'}, J_{y'}, J_{z'}, m, a, ω, θ, t.

subquestions.subproblem: Calculate the torque on the axis. (UC, Berkeley)
subquestions.solution:
The torque equals the time derivative of the angular momentum in the laboratory frame
$$M=\left(\frac{dJ}{dt}\right)_{lab}$$
The transport theorem gives
$$\left(\frac{dJ}{dt}\right)_{lab}=\left(\frac{dJ}{dt}\right)_{rot}+\omega \times J$$
For steady rotation in the body frame
$$\left(\frac{dJ}{dt}\right)_{rot}=0$$
Hence
$$M=\omega \times J$$
Use the body-frame components
$$\omega=(\omega \sin \theta,0,\omega \cos \theta)$$
$$J=(I_{xx}\omega \sin \theta,0,I_{zz}\omega \cos \theta)$$
Therefore
$$M=-(I_{zz}-I_{xx})\omega^2 \sin \theta \cos \theta \, e_y$$
With the principal moments
$$I_{zz}-I_{xx}=\frac{1}{12} m a^2$$
So
$$M=-\frac{1}{12} m a^2 \omega^2 \sin \theta \cos \theta \, e_y$$
Express e_y in the laboratory frame
$$e_y=-\sin \omega t \, e_{x'}+\cos \omega t \, e_{y'}$$
Thus
$$M=-\frac{1}{12} m a^2 \omega^2 \sin \theta \cos \theta \left(-\sin \omega t \, e_{x'}+\cos \omega t \, e_{y'}\right)$$
Equivalently, this result is obtained by differentiating J in the laboratory frame
$$M=\frac{dJ}{dt}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be provided in both frames: (i) in the body-fixed frame as M = ... e_y, expressed in terms of m, a, ω, and θ only; and (ii) in the laboratory frame as M = M_{x'} e_{x'} + M_{y'} e_{y'}, with M_{x'} and M_{y'} expressed in terms of m, a, ω, θ, and t only. Use the symbols M, M_{x'}, M_{y'}, m, a, ω, θ, t and the unit vectors e_y, e_{x'}, e_{y'}.

grading_standard.formula: $$M=-\frac{1}{12} m a^2 \omega^2 \sin \theta \cos \theta \left(-\sin \omega t \, e_{x'}+\cos \omega t \, e_{y'}\right)$$

context: A thin flat rectangular plate of mass M and sides a by 2a rotates with constant angular velocity ω about a rigid axle through two diagonal corners A and B, as shown in Fig. 1.138. The axle is supported at A and B by bearings that can exert forces only on the axle. Ignore gravitational and frictional forces. Let O be the center of mass. Use a body-fixed right-handed frame Oxyz with y normal to the plate, z along the long side 2a, and x along the short side a. Let e_x, e_y, e_z be the unit vectors of Oxyz. The axis of rotation z′ lies in the plane of the plate through A and B, and α is the angle between z and z′, with sin α = 1/√5 and cos α = 2/√5. Let O x′ y′ z′ be obtained by rotating Oxyz about the y-axis so that z′ coincides with the axle AB, with y′ = y and x′ completing the right-handed triad. Denote by N_A and N_B the forces exerted by the bearings on the axle at A and B, respectively, and by N_{Ax′}, N_{Ay′}, N_{Bx′}, N_{By′} their components in O x′ y′ z′. Let d = (1/2) AB = (√5/2) a be the half-distance between the bearings measured along the axle. Finally, let O x″ y″ z″ be an inertial frame with z″ = z′ and with x″ coinciding with x′ at t = 0. Find the forces exerted by the two bearings as functions of time, expressed in components along x″ and y″.
solution:
The principal moments of inertia about Oxyz are
$$
I_{xx}=\frac{M a^2}{12}
$$
$$
I_{yy}=\frac{5 M a^2}{12}
$$
$$
I_{zz}=\frac{4 M a^2}{12}
$$
The angular velocity components in Oxyz are
$$
\omega_x=\omega\sin\alpha
$$
$$
\omega_y=0
$$
$$
\omega_z=\omega\cos\alpha
$$
The angular momentum components are
$$
L_x=I_{xx}\omega\sin\alpha
$$
$$
L_y=0
$$
$$
L_z=I_{zz}\omega\cos\alpha
$$
The angular momentum vector is
$$
L=L_x e_x+L_z e_z
$$
The torque required to maintain steady rotation about the space-fixed axis is
$$
\tau=\omega\times L
$$
Hence
$$
\tau=\omega^2\sin\alpha\cos\alpha\left(I_{xx}-I_{zz}\right)e_y
$$
Using the geometry of the diagonal, we have
$$
\sin\alpha=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}
$$
$$
\cos\alpha=\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}
$$
Also
$$
I_{xx}-I_{zz}=-\frac{M a^2}{4}
$$
Therefore
$$
\tau=-\frac{M a^2\omega^2}{10}e_y
$$
In the rotating frame O x′ y′ z′, force balance at the center of mass gives
$$
N_{Ax′}+N_{Bx′}=0
$$
$$
N_{Ay′}+N_{By′}=0
$$
Taking torques about O about the y′-axis gives
$$
N_{Bx′}d-N_{Ax′}d=-\frac{M a^2\omega^2}{10}
$$
Similarly
$$
N_{Ay′}d-N_{By′}d=0
$$
The half-distance between the bearings is
$$
d=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}a
$$
Solving for the bearing force components in O x′ y′ z′ yields
$$
N_{Ay′}=0
$$
$$
N_{By′}=0
$$
$$
N_{Ax′}=\frac{M a^2\omega^2}{20 d}
$$
$$
N_{Bx′}=-\frac{M a^2\omega^2}{20 d}
$$
Substituting d gives
$$
N_{Ax′}=\frac{M a\omega^2}{10\sqrt{5}}
$$
$$
N_{Bx′}=-\frac{M a\omega^2}{10\sqrt{5}}
$$
These components are constant in the rotating frame O x′ y′ z′. In the inertial frame O x″ y″ z″ with x″ aligned with x′ at t=0, they rotate with angular velocity ω, so
$$
N_{Ax″}(t)=\frac{M a\omega^2}{10\sqrt{5}}\cos\omega t
$$
$$
N_{Ay″}(t)=-\frac{M a\omega^2}{10\sqrt{5}}\sin\omega t
$$
$$
N_{Bx″}(t)=-\frac{M a\omega^2}{10\sqrt{5}}\cos\omega t
$$
$$
N_{By″}(t)=\frac{M a\omega^2}{10\sqrt{5}}\sin\omega t
$$
Thus, the time-dependent bearing forces in the inertial frame are fully specified by these component functions.
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given as the four time-dependent component functions N_Ax″(t) = ..., N_Ay″(t) = ..., N_Bx″(t) = ..., and N_By″(t) = ..., representing the bearing forces expressed along the x″ and y″ axes of the inertial frame. Each expression must be written solely in terms of the variables M, a, ω, and t, and no other symbols or variables should appear.

context: A thin ring of mass M and radius R is pivoted at point P on a frictionless horizontal table, as shown in Fig. 1.140. A bug of mass m runs along the ring with constant speed v relative to the ring. The bug starts from the pivot P while the ring is initially at rest. When the bug reaches the diametrically opposite point on the ring (point x), find its speed relative to the table. Use the following notation: I is the moment of inertia of the ring about P; ω is the angular velocity of the ring about P at the instant the bug reaches point x; J is the angular momentum of the ring about P; v_table is the speed of the bug relative to the table at point x
solution:
The moment of inertia of the ring with respect to the pivot P is

$$
I = M R^2 + M R^2
$$

$$
I = 2 M R^2
$$

At point x, define the bug's speed relative to the table as

$$
v_{table} = v - 2 R \omega
$$

The angular momentum of the ring about P is

$$
J = 2 M R^2 \omega
$$

Initially the total angular momentum of the ring and bug about P is zero. Conservation of angular momentum gives

$$
2 M R^2 \omega - 2 m R ( v - 2 R \omega ) = 0
$$

Solving for the angular velocity yields

$$
\omega = \frac{m v}{R ( M + 2 m )}
$$

Substituting into the expression for v_{table} gives

$$
v_{table} = v - 2 R \omega
$$

$$
v_{table} = \frac{M v}{M + 2 m}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of v_table = ..., and your response should be written only with M, m, and v.

grading_standard.formula:
$$
2 M R^2 \omega - 2 m R ( v - 2 R \omega ) = 0
$$

context: A rigid cone of height h and base radius R is constrained to rotate about its vertical symmetry axis. A thin, straight groove is cut along the cone surface from the apex to the base (along a generatrix). The cone is set rotating with initial angular velocity ω_0 about its axis. A small point-like bead of mass m is released at the apex into the frictionless groove and is permitted to slide downward under gravity. Assume the bead always remains in the groove during the motion. The moment of inertia of the cone about its axis is I_0. The gravitational acceleration is g, directed downward. When the bead reaches the base, let ω denote the cone's angular velocity at that instant. Let v_{\parallel} be the bead's velocity component along the groove and v_{\perp} the component perpendicular to the groove (azimuthal, due to the cone's rotation). Let i and j be unit vectors perpendicular and parallel to the groove, respectively. Define the bead's laboratory-frame velocity vector at the base as v_{\text{vec}} = v_{\perp} i + v_{\parallel} j, and define the speed magnitude as v_{\text{mag}} so that v_{\text{mag}}^2 = v_{\parallel}^2 + v_{\perp}^2.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the angular velocity of the cone when the bead reaches the bottom?
subquestions.solution: As the total angular momentum of the system is conserved, the angular velocity ω of the cone when the bead reaches the bottom satisfies the relation $$I_0 ω_0 = (I_0 + m R^2) ω$$ Hence $$ω = \frac{I_0 ω_0}{I_0 + m R^2}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of ω = ..., and your response should be written with I_0, ω_0, m, R.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the speed of the bead in the laboratory just as it leaves the cone.
subquestions.solution: By energy conservation, the bead's speed magnitude v_{\text{mag}} when it reaches the bottom satisfies $$\frac{1}{2} I_0 ω_0^2 + m g h = \frac{1}{2} m v_{\text{mag}}^2 + \frac{1}{2} I_0 ω^2$$ with the decomposition $$v_{\text{mag}}^2 = v_{\parallel}^2 + v_{\perp}^2$$ and the kinematic relation at the base $$v_{\perp}^2 = R^2 ω^2$$ Thus $$\frac{1}{2} m v_{\parallel}^2 = \frac{1}{2} I_0 ω_0^2 + m g h - \frac{1}{2} I_0 ω^2 - \frac{1}{2} m R^2 ω^2$$ giving $$v_{\parallel}^2 = \frac{I_0}{m} ω_0^2 - \frac{I_0 + m R^2}{m} ω^2 + 2 g h$$ Substituting the result for ω from part (a) yields $$v_{\parallel}^2 = \frac{I_0 ω_0^2 R^2}{I_0 + m R^2} + 2 g h$$ Therefore, at the bottom the bead’s velocity components and vector are $$v_{\perp} = R ω$$ $$v_{\perp} = \frac{I_0 ω_0 R}{I_0 + m R^2}$$ $$v_{\parallel} = \sqrt{\frac{I_0 ω_0^2 R^2}{I_0 + m R^2} + 2 g h}$$ $$v_{\text{vec}} = v_{\perp} i + v_{\parallel} j$$ and the speed is $$v_{\text{mag}} = \sqrt{\frac{I_0^2 ω_0^2 R^2}{(I_0 + m R^2)^2} + \frac{I_0 ω_0^2 R^2}{I_0 + m R^2} + 2 g h}$$ This speed could have been obtained directly by substituting the expression for ω in the energy equation
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of v_{\text{mag}} = ..., and your response should be written with I_0, ω_0, m, R, g, h.

grading_standard.formula: $$v_{\parallel}^2 = \frac{I_0}{m} ω_0^2 - \frac{I_0 + m R^2}{m} ω^2 + 2 g h$$
$$v_{\parallel}^2 = \frac{I_0 ω_0^2 R^2}{I_0 + m R^2} + 2 g h$$
$$v_{\parallel} = \sqrt{\frac{I_0 ω_0^2 R^2}{I_0 + m R^2} + 2 g h}$$

context: A thin uniform disc of radius a and mass m rotates freely on a frictionless bearing with uniform angular velocity of magnitude ω about a fixed vertical axis z′ passing through its center O. The axis z′ is inclined at angle α to the symmetry axis of the disc. Introduce a body-fixed orthonormal frame Oxyz with origin at O, the z-axis along the disc’s normal, the x-axis in the plane spanned by z and z′, and the y-axis completing a right-handed triad. Let e_x, e_y, e_z be the unit vectors along x, y, z, respectively. Let Ω denote the angular velocity vector, with magnitude ω and components in the body frame specified by Ω = ω sin α e_x + ω cos α e_z. Let I_x, I_y, I_z denote the principal moments of inertia of the disc about the x, y, z axes, respectively. Let L denote the angular momentum of the disc about O. Let M denote the torque exerted by the axis on the disc, defined by M = (dL/dt)_{fixed}, where (d/dt)_{fixed} is the time derivative in the inertial frame and (d/dt)_{rot} is the time derivative in the rotating body frame Oxyz. Let F denote the net force exerted by the axis on the disc. Determine the magnitude and direction of M and F.
solution:
In the body-fixed frame Oxyz the principal moments of inertia of a thin uniform disc are

$$
I_x = \frac{1}{4} m a^2
$$

$$
I_y = \frac{1}{4} m a^2
$$

$$
I_z = \frac{1}{2} m a^2
$$

The angular velocity vector in the body frame is

$$
\Omega = \omega \sin \alpha e_x + \omega \cos \alpha e_z
$$

The angular momentum about O is

$$
L = \frac{1}{4} m a^2 \omega \sin \alpha e_x + \frac{1}{2} m a^2 \omega \cos \alpha e_z
$$

The transport theorem gives

$$
\frac{dL}{dt}_{fixed} = \frac{dL}{dt}_{rot} + \Omega \times L
$$

For this steady motion in the body frame

$$
\frac{dL}{dt}_{rot} = 0
$$

The torque exerted by the axis on the disc is

$$
M = \frac{dL}{dt}_{fixed}
$$

$$
M = \Omega \times L
$$

Evaluating the cross product gives

$$
M = - \frac{1}{4} m a^2 \omega \sin \alpha \cos \alpha e_y
$$

The torque lies in the plane of the disc and is perpendicular to the plane formed by the disc normal z and the axis of rotation z′; it rotates with the disc. Since the center of mass of the disc is stationary, the net force on the disc is

$$
F = 0
$$
final_answer_instructions: Provide explicit symbolic expressions for both the torque vector M and the net force vector F in the body-fixed basis. Your final answer should be given in the form M = (M_x) e_x + (M_y) e_y + (M_z) e_z and F = (F_x) e_x + (F_y) e_y + (F_z) e_z, written only in terms of m, a, ω, α, and the unit vectors e_x, e_y, e_z.

grading_standard.formula: $$L = \frac{1}{4} m a^2 \omega \sin \alpha e_x + \frac{1}{2} m a^2 \omega \cos \alpha e_z$$

context: A pendulum consists of a uniform rigid rod of length L and mass M, and a bug of mass M/3 that can crawl along the rod. The rod is pivoted at one end and swings in a vertical plane. Let theta(t) be the small angle from the vertical, with initial value theta_0 at t=0, where theta_0 << 1 \unit{rad}. The bug is initially at the pivot, so l(0)=0, and the system is released from rest. For t>0 the bug crawls slowly outward along the rod toward the free end with constant speed V, where V=dot l and l(t) in [0,L]. Let g be the gravitational acceleration. Define omega(l) as the instantaneous small-oscillation angular frequency when the bug is at distance l. Let E(l) be the energy of oscillation and E_0=E(0). Let T and U denote the kinetic and potential energies of the oscillation, respectively. Let theta_max be the oscillation amplitude at the instant l=L. Overbars denote averages over one oscillation period. A dot denotes a time derivative. Let I be the moment of inertia of the rod-plus-bug system about the pivot. Let f be the force exerted by the rod on the bug along the rod direction. Let W be the work done by f on the surroundings for an outward displacement dl. Let K be the integration constant that appears when integrating the energy balance.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the frequency $\omega$ of the swing of the pendulum when the bug has crawled a distance $l$ along the rod.
subquestions.solution: The moment of inertia about the pivot is $$I=\frac{1}{3} M \big( L^2+l^2 \big)$$ The equation of motion is $$\frac{d}{dt} \big( I \dot\theta \big)=- M g \frac{L}{2} \sin\theta-\frac{M}{3} g l \sin\theta$$ Expanding the time derivative gives $$\frac{1}{3} M \big( L^2+l^2 \big) \ddot\theta+\frac{2}{3} M l \dot l \dot\theta=- M g \bigg( \frac{L}{2}+\frac{l}{3} \bigg) \sin\theta$$ For small oscillations, $$\sin\theta\approx\theta$$ Hence $$\ddot\theta+\frac{2 l \dot l}{L^2+l^2} \dot\theta+\frac{g \big( 2 l+3 L \big)}{2 \big( L^2+l^2 \big)} \theta=0$$ Under the slow-crawl condition in which the change in l during one period is negligible, $$V\ll l \omega$$ the second term can be neglected, yielding $$\ddot\theta+\frac{g \big( 2 l+3 L \big)}{2 \big( L^2+l^2 \big)} \theta=0$$ Therefore, $$\omega=\sqrt{\frac{g \big( 2 l+3 L \big)}{2 \big( L^2+l^2 \big)}}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \omega = ..., and your response should be written with g, L, l.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the amplitude of the swing of the pendulum when the bug has crawled to the bottom end of the rod $\left( l=L \right)$ ：
subquestions.solution: The bug’s motion along the rod satisfies $$\frac{M}{3} \big( \ddot l-l \dot\theta^2 \big)=\frac{M}{3} g \cos\theta-f$$ For constant crawl speed, $$\ddot l=0$$ For small oscillations, $$\cos\theta\approx 1-\frac{\theta^2}{2}$$ Hence $$f=\frac{M g}{3}-\frac{M g}{6} \theta^2+\frac{M l}{3} \dot\theta^2$$ The work increment is $$dW=- f \ dl$$ Substituting for f gives $$dW=-\frac{M g}{3} dl+\frac{M}{3} \bigg( \frac{g \theta^2}{2}-l \dot\theta^2 \bigg) dl$$ The change in the oscillation energy is $$dE=\frac{M}{3} \bigg( \frac{g \theta^2}{2}-l \dot\theta^2 \bigg) dl$$ Under the slow-crawl condition, $$V\ll l \omega$$ we can average over one period at fixed l to obtain $$dE=\frac{M}{3} \bigg( \frac{g \overline{\theta^2}}{2}-l \overline{\dot\theta^2} \bigg) dl$$ The time-averaged kinetic energy is $$\overline{T}=\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{M}{3} \big( L^2+l^2 \big) \overline{\dot\theta^2}$$ and $$\overline{T}=\frac{E}{2}$$ The time-averaged potential energy is $$\overline{U}=\frac{M g L}{2} \big( 1-\overline{\cos\theta} \big)+\frac{M g l}{3} \big( 1-\overline{\cos\theta} \big)$$ Using the small-angle average, $$\overline{U}=\frac{M g}{2} \bigg( \frac{L}{2}+\frac{l}{3} \bigg) \overline{\theta^2}$$ and $$\overline{U}=\frac{E}{2}$$ Therefore, $$\overline{\dot\theta^2}=\frac{3 E}{M \big( L^2+l^2 \big)}$$ and $$\overline{\theta^2}=\frac{6 E}{M g \big( 3 L+2 l \big)}$$ Substituting into the averaged energy balance yields $$\frac{dE}{E}=\bigg( \frac{1}{3 L+2 l}-\frac{l}{L^2+l^2} \bigg) dl$$ Integration gives $$\ln E=\frac{1}{2} \ln \bigg( \frac{3 L+2 l}{L^2+l^2} \bigg)+K$$ The initial condition at l=0 gives $$\ln E_0=\frac{1}{2} \ln \bigg( \frac{3}{L} \bigg)+K$$ Hence $$\ln \frac{E}{E_0}=\frac{1}{2} \ln \bigg( \frac{ \big( 3 L+2 l \big) L}{3 \big( L^2+l^2 \big)} \bigg)$$ At l=L, $$\ln \frac{E}{E_0}=\frac{1}{2} \ln \frac{5}{6}$$ so $$E=\sqrt{\frac{5}{6}} E_0$$ The amplitude at l=L occurs when the kinetic energy vanishes, so E equals the potential energy at the turning point, giving $$\frac{1}{2} M g \bigg( \frac{L}{2}+\frac{L}{3} \bigg) \theta_{\max}^2=E$$ Initially at l=0, $$\frac{1}{2} M g \frac{L}{2} \theta_0^2=E_0$$ Using E=\sqrt{5/6} E_0 yields $$\theta_{\max}=\bigg( \frac{3}{10} \bigg)^{\frac{1}{4}} \theta_0$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \theta_{\max} = ..., and your response should be written with \theta_0.

subquestions.subproblem: How slowly must the bug crawl in order that your answers for part a and b be valid? (Wisconsin)
subquestions.solution: The radial speed of the bug must be much smaller than the characteristic tangential speed so that l is quasi-constant over each period $$V\ll l \omega$$ This is the validity condition for the results above
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form V ≪ l ω, and your response should be written with V, l, ω.

grading_standard.formula: $$\frac{1}{3} M \big( L^2+l^2 \big) \ddot\theta+\frac{2}{3} M l \dot l \dot\theta=- M g \bigg( \frac{L}{2}+\frac{l}{3} \bigg) \sin\theta$$

context: A uniform solid bowling ball is projected along a horizontal alley with initial center-of-mass speed v_0 at t=0 so that it initially slides without rolling. The ball has mass m and radius R. The coefficient of static friction with the floor is mu_s and the coefficient of kinetic (sliding) friction is mu_d. Let g be the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration. Ignore air resistance. While the ball is sliding, let f denote the magnitude of the kinetic friction force, a the linear acceleration of the center of mass, alpha the angular acceleration about the center, I the moment of inertia about the center, and t the time at which the ball first transitions to rolling without slipping. Let v_roll denote the linear speed at that instant. Compute v_roll in terms of v_0. Use I = \frac{2}{5} m R^2 for a uniform solid sphere and the rolling-without-slipping condition v = R omega at the transition, with omega = alpha t.
solution:
While the ball slides without rolling, the kinetic friction has magnitude
$$
f = \mu_d m g
$$
This produces a constant linear acceleration of the center of mass
$$
a = - \frac{f}{m}
$$
Hence
$$
a = - \mu_d g
$$
The friction also produces a torque about the center, giving the angular acceleration via
$$
f R = \frac{2}{5} m R^2 \alpha
$$
Thus
$$
\alpha = \frac{5 f}{2 m R}
$$
At time t when rolling without slipping begins, the no-slip condition requires
$$
R \alpha t = v_0 + a t
$$
Solving for t gives
$$
t = \frac{v_0}{R \alpha - a}
$$
Using the above expressions for a and alpha yields
$$
t = \frac{2 m v_0}{7 f}
$$
Substituting f = \mu_d m g gives
$$
t = \frac{2 v_0}{7 \mu_d g}
$$
The linear speed at the onset of rolling without slipping is
$$
v_{\text{roll}} = v_0 + a t
$$
Equivalently
$$
v_{\text{roll}} = v_0 - \mu_d g t
$$
Therefore
$$
v_{\text{roll}} = \frac{5}{7} v_0
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of v_roll = ..., and your response should be written using only v_0.

context: A uniform coin of mass m and radius R is initially spinning about its axis of symmetry with angular frequency ω. At time t=0 it is gently set down on a horizontal surface. The coefficient of sliding friction between the coin and the surface is μ, and g is the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration. Choose coordinates as in Fig. 1.149 with the x-axis in the plane of the surface. Let x_c(t) be the x-coordinate of the center of mass and θ(t) the rotation angle about the symmetry axis, with θ increasing in the sense of the initial spin so that ω>0. The coin’s moment of inertia about its symmetry axis is I=1/2 m R^2. During slipping, kinetic friction of magnitude μ m g acts along the negative x direction. Let t_s be the time when slipping ceases and pure rolling begins. Define v_f as the x-component of the center-of-mass velocity at t=t_s. Find v_f, expressed as v_f=...
solution:
Before the coin stops slipping, the translational equation of motion is
$$
 m \frac{d^2 x_c}{dt^2}=-\mu m g
$$
The rotational equation of motion about the symmetry axis is
$$
I \frac{d^2 \theta}{dt^2}=-\mu m g R
$$
The moment of inertia about the symmetry axis is
$$
I=\frac{1}{2} m R^2
$$
With initial conditions
$$
\frac{dx_c}{dt}(0)=0
$$
$$
\frac{d\theta}{dt}(0)=\omega
$$
integration gives
$$
\frac{dx_c}{dt}=-\mu g t
$$
$$
\frac{d\theta}{dt}=\omega-\frac{2 \mu g t}{R}
$$
At the onset of rolling without slipping, the no-slip condition at the contact point is
$$
\frac{dx_c}{dt}=-R \frac{d\theta}{dt}
$$
Let this occur at time t=t_s, then
$$
-\mu g t_s=-\omega R+2 \mu g t_s
$$
Solving for t_s yields
$$
 t_s=\frac{\omega R}{3 \mu g}
$$
The final center-of-mass velocity is
$$
 v_f=\frac{dx_c}{dt}(t_s)
$$
$$
 v_f=-\mu g t_s
$$
$$
 v_f=-\frac{1}{3} \omega R
$$
Thus the coin rolls away along the negative x direction with speed equal to \frac{1}{3} \omega R
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of v_f = ..., and your response should be written with ω and R only.

context: A uniform solid wheel (disk) of mass M and radius R moves on a horizontal surface. Its center of mass is projected to the right with initial linear velocity V_0, and it has an initial angular velocity about its axle of magnitude ω_0 such that this initial spin tends to produce rolling opposite to the translational motion. Let x(t) be the horizontal coordinate of the center of mass and θ(t) the rotation angle. Define the positive x direction to the right and define positive angular velocity to be clockwise. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the wheel and the surface is μ, assumed constant, and g denotes the magnitude of the acceleration due to gravity. The wheel’s moment of inertia about its axle is (1/2) M R^2. Pure rolling (no slipping) begins when the linear speed of the center of mass equals R times the angular speed.

subquestions.subproblem: How long is it till the sliding ceases? Let T denote the time at which slipping stops (the onset of pure rolling).
subquestions.solution:
Equations of motion for translation and rotation are
$$M \frac{d^2 x}{dt^2} = - \mu M g$$
$$\frac{1}{2} M R^2 \frac{d^2 \theta}{dt^2} = \mu M g R$$
Initial conditions at t = 0 are
$$\frac{dx}{dt}(0) = V_0$$
$$\frac{d\theta}{dt}(0) = - \omega_0$$
Integrating gives
$$\frac{dx}{dt} = V_0 - \mu g t$$
$$\frac{d\theta}{dt} = - \omega_0 + \frac{2 \mu g t}{R}$$
The no-slip condition at t = T is
$$\frac{dx}{dt} = R \frac{d\theta}{dt}$$
Evaluating at t = T yields
$$V_0 - \mu g T = - R \omega_0 + 2 \mu g T$$
Solving for T gives
$$T = \frac{V_0 + R \omega_0}{3 \mu g}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of T = ..., and your response should be written with V_0, R, ω_0, μ, g.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the velocity of the center of mass of the wheel at the time when the slipping stops? (Columbia)
subquestions.solution:
At t = T the center-of-mass speed is
$$\frac{dx}{dt}(T) = V_0 - \mu g T$$
Substituting T from part (a) gives
$$\frac{dx}{dt}(T) = \frac{1}{3} (2 V_0 - R \omega_0)$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of (dx/dt)(T) = ..., and your response should be written with V_0, R, ω_0.

context: A thin hollow cylinder of radius R and mass M slides across a frictionless floor with initial forward speed V_0 along a fixed straight line. The cylinder initially spins backward relative to the forward direction. Let V(t) be the signed linear velocity along the line of motion, where V>0 denotes the initial forward direction, and let ω(t) be the signed angular velocity about the cylinder’s axis, where ω>0 corresponds to the sense that would produce forward rolling. The cylinder then passes onto a rough horizontal segment and continues along the same line. During slipping, a kinetic friction force of magnitude f(t) acts at the contact point opposite the direction of slipping. Let t=0 be the instant the cylinder enters the rough segment, and let t_0 be the instant when pure rolling without slipping begins. The moment of inertia about the symmetry axis is I = M R^2 for a thin hollow cylinder. The initial conditions are V(0) = V_0 and ω(0) = -ω_0 with ω_0 = 2 V_0 / R. Define the final signed linear velocity and angular velocity at the onset of rolling as V_f = V(t_0) and ω_f = ω(t_0). Find V_f. Report the final answer as V_f, where a negative value indicates motion opposite to the initial direction.
solution:
Assume the cylinder enters the rough area at t=0 and reaches pure rolling at t=t_0. For 0<t<t_0 the equations of motion are

$$-f = M \frac{dV}{dt}$$

$$f R = I \frac{d\omega}{dt}$$

with

$$I = M R^2$$

Integrating from t=0 to t=t_0 gives

$$M (V_f - V_0) = - \int_0^{t_0} f dt$$

$$I (\omega_f - (-\omega_0)) = R \int_0^{t_0} f dt$$

Eliminating the impulse of friction yields

$$I (\omega_f + \omega_0) = M R (V_0 - V_f)$$

At t=t_0 the rolling constraint holds

$$V_f = \omega_f R$$

From the given initial spin

$$\omega_0 R = 2 V_0$$

Solving for V_f gives

$$V_f = - \frac{1}{2} V_0$$

Therefore, the cylinder eventually moves backward with speed \frac{1}{2} V_0, i.e., its final signed linear velocity is V_f as above
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of V_f = ..., and your response should be written with V_0 only.

context: Calculate the minimum coefficient of static friction mu_min necessary to keep a thin circular ring (hoop) from sliding as it rolls without slipping down a plane inclined at an angle theta with respect to the horizontal. Let the ring have mass m and radius R. Let x(t) be the coordinate of the ring’s center measured along the incline, and varphi(t) be the ring’s rotation angle about its symmetry axis. Let g be the magnitude of gravitational acceleration with units \unit{m/s^2}. Let f be the magnitude of the static friction force acting along the plane, and N be the normal reaction of the plane. The ring’s moment of inertia about its symmetry axis is I = m R^2. Let mu be the coefficient of static friction between the ring and the plane.
solution:
Equations of motion along the incline and for rotation are

$$
m \frac{d^2 x}{dt^2} = m g \sin \theta - f
$$

$$
I \frac{d^2 \varphi}{dt^2} = f R
$$

Using the hoop moment of inertia

$$
I = m R^2
$$

the equations combine to

$$
\frac{d^2 x}{dt^2} + R \frac{d^2 \varphi}{dt^2} = g \sin \theta
$$

The no-slip condition is

$$
R \frac{d \varphi}{dt} = \frac{d x}{dt}
$$

which implies

$$
R \frac{d^2 \varphi}{dt^2} = \frac{d^2 x}{dt^2}
$$

Hence

$$
\frac{d^2 x}{dt^2} = \frac{1}{2} g \sin \theta
$$

The friction force is

$$
f = m g \sin \theta - m \frac{d^2 x}{dt^2}
$$

so

$$
f = \frac{1}{2} m g \sin \theta
$$

The normal reaction is

$$
N = m g \cos \theta
$$

For no slipping we require

$$
f < \mu N
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{1}{2} m g \sin \theta < \mu m g \cos \theta
$$

so

$$
\frac{1}{2} \tan \theta < \mu
$$

Therefore the minimum coefficient of static friction is

$$
\mu_{min} = \frac{1}{2} \tan \theta
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form mu_min = [expression in terms of theta only]. Use only the variable theta; you may include numerical constants. Do not include any other variables, parameters, or units.

context: A solid uniform cylinder of mass m and radius R is placed on a plane inclined at angle \theta relative to the horizontal, as shown in Fig. 1.154. Let g denote the magnitude of the acceleration due to gravity. Let a be the linear acceleration of the cylinder’s center of mass along the incline. The coefficient of static friction between the cylinder and the plane is \mu. Define \theta_c as the critical angle below which the cylinder rolls without slipping. Let f denote the static friction force along the plane, N the normal force exerted by the plane on the cylinder, and \alpha the angular acceleration about the cylinder’s central axis. Assume the positive direction is down the incline.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the angle \theta_c?
subquestions.solution:
For rolling without slipping, the kinematic and friction conditions are
$$a=R\alpha$$
$$f<\mu N$$
The normal force is
$$N=m g \cos \theta$$
From the equations of motion for a uniform solid cylinder rolling without slipping, the friction is
$$f=\frac{1}{3} m g \sin \theta$$
The no-slip requirement implies
$$\mu m g \cos \theta>\frac{1}{3} m g \sin \theta$$
which is equivalent to
$$3\mu>\tan \theta$$
Define \theta_c by
$$\tan \theta_c=3\mu$$
Thus, the critical angle is
$$\theta_c=\arctan(3\mu)$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \theta_c = ..., and your response should be written only in terms of \mu.

subquestions.subproblem: For \theta<\theta_c, what is the acceleration a?
subquestions.solution:
For \theta<\theta_c, the cylinder rolls without slipping, so using the result for f above,
$$a=g\sin \theta-\frac{f}{m}$$
$$a=\frac{2}{3} g \sin \theta$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of a = ..., and your response should be written only in terms of g and \theta.

context: A wheel of radius r, mass m, and moment of inertia I equal to m R squared is pulled along a horizontal surface by application of a horizontal force F to a rope unwinding from an axle of radius b, as shown in Fig. 1.155. You may assume there is a frictional force between the wheel and the surface such that the wheel rolls without slipping. In the expression I = m R squared, the quantity R is a constant with dimensions of length (the radius of gyration). Use x(t) for the horizontal position of the wheel’s center and theta(t) for its rotation angle about the center. Take the positive x-direction to the right and positive theta as counterclockwise. Let f denote the static friction force at the contact point, defined positive when it opposes the forward motion of the wheel. The no-slip rolling constraint relates the translational and rotational motions.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the linear acceleration of the wheel?
subquestions.solution:
The equations of motion of the wheel are (Fig. 1.155)
$$m \ddot{x} = F - f$$
$$I \ddot{\theta} = F b + f r$$
The constraint for no sliding is
$$\dot{x} = r \dot{\theta}$$
$$\ddot{x} = r \ddot{\theta}$$
Using I = m R^2 and eliminating \ddot{\theta} gives
$$\frac{m R^2}{r} \ddot{x} = F b + (F - m \ddot{x}) r$$
Solving for \ddot{x} yields the linear acceleration
$$\ddot{x} = \frac{F (b + r) r}{m (R^2 + r^2)}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \ddot{x} = ... , and your response should be written using only the variables F, b, r, m, R.

subquestions.subproblem: Calculate the frictional force that acts on the wheel
subquestions.solution:
The frictional force is
$$f = F - m \ddot{x}$$
Substituting the result for \ddot{x} from part (a) gives
$$f = F \left(1 - \frac{(b + r) r}{R^2 + r^2}\right)$$
which simplifies to
$$f = \frac{F (R^2 - b r)}{R^2 + r^2}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of f = ... , and your response should be written using only the variables F, R, b, r.

context:
A flat uniform disc lies on a frictionless horizontal table. The disc has mass m = 9/5\unit{kg} and radius r = 1/5\unit{m}. A string wound around the cylindrical rim of the disc exerts a horizontal force f = 3\unit{N} directed toward the north (see Fig. 1.156). Use a for the magnitude of the acceleration of the center of mass and specify its direction. Use alpha for the angular acceleration about the center of mass and specify its sense. Use I for the moment of inertia of the disc about its center, defined by
$$
I = \frac{m r^2}{2}
$$
Find the magnitude and direction of a and alpha. Determine whether the relation
$$
a = r \alpha
$$
holds, and explain.
solution:
The translational equation of motion is
$$
f = m a
$$
Thus
$$
a = \frac{f}{m}
$$
Numerically
$$
a = 1.7\unit{m/s^2}
$$
The rotational equation of motion about the center is
$$
f r = I \alpha
$$
With the disc’s moment of inertia
$$
I = \frac{m r^2}{2}
$$
we obtain
$$
\alpha = \frac{f r}{I}
$$
Hence
$$
\alpha = \frac{2 f}{m r}
$$
Numerically
$$
\alpha = 17\unit{rad/s^2}
$$
The direction of a is north, the same as the applied force. The sense of \alpha is that of the torque produced by the string about the disc’s center. Regarding the proposed relation,
$$
a \neq r \alpha
$$
This is because the disc is not rolling without slipping; lying on a frictionless horizontal surface, there is no kinematic constraint linking a and \alpha, even though both arise from the same applied force.
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the magnitudes of a and alpha as numerical values with units, and also state their direction/sense. Report them in the following format: a = [number] m/s^2, direction: [north/south/east/west]; alpha = [number] rad/s^2, sense: [clockwise/counterclockwise]. Additionally, include the sentence: "The relation a = r alpha holds." or "The relation a = r alpha does not hold." followed by a brief one-sentence explanation.

context: A wheel of radius $R$ and moment of inertia $I$ about a fixed, frictionless axle through point $O$ has a light, flexible cord wrapped around its rim. The cord supports a body of mass $M$ that descends vertically without slipping, as shown in Fig. 1.157. Let $F$ be the tension in the cord, $x$ the downward displacement of the body, $\theta$ the rotation angle of the wheel (positive in the direction of descent), and $g$ the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration. Find the tension $F$ in the cord during the motion.
solution:
Using rotational dynamics of the wheel about the axle
$$
I \ddot{\theta} = F R
$$
Using translation of the mass
$$
M \ddot{x} = M g - F
$$
Using the no-slip kinematic constraint
$$
\ddot{x} = R \ddot{\theta}
$$
Solving these equations for the cord tension yields
$$
F = \frac{M g I}{I + M R^{2}}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form F = ..., and your response should be written using only the symbols M, g, I, and R.

context: Two uniform solid discs in a vertical plane have masses M_1 and M_2 and radii R_1 and R_2, respectively. A light inextensible thread is wound about their circumferences and connects them as shown in Fig. 1.158. Disc 1 rotates about a fixed frictionless horizontal axle through its center. Assume the thread does not slip on either disc. Define x(t) as the vertical distance of the center of mass of disc 2 from the center of disc 1, measured positive downward. Define theta_1(t) and theta_2(t) as the rotation angles of discs 1 and 2, respectively, increasing in the sense that pulls the thread downward on disc 2. Let F be the tension in the thread, g the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration, and I_1 and I_2 the moments of inertia of discs 1 and 2 about their centers. For uniform discs, I_1 = (1/2) M_1 R_1^2 and I_2 = (1/2) M_2 R_2^2. Set up the equations needed to determine the acceleration d^2 x/dt^2 of the center of mass of disc 2 as it falls freely
source: You need not solve the equations.
solution:
Let F be the tension in the thread, x(t) the vertical distance of the center of mass of disc 2 from that of disc 1, and theta_1(t), theta_2(t) the rotation angles of the discs, as defined in the context. Taking downward as positive for x, the equations of motion and the no-slip kinematic constraint are

$$
M_2 \frac{d^2 x}{dt^2} = M_2 g - F
$$

$$
I_1 \frac{d^2 \theta_1}{dt^2} = F R_1
$$

$$
I_2 \frac{d^2 \theta_2}{dt^2} = F R_2
$$

with the moments of inertia for uniform discs

$$
I_1 = \frac{1}{2} M_1 R_1^2
$$

$$
I_2 = \frac{1}{2} M_2 R_2^2
$$

and the no-slip constraint

$$
\frac{dx}{dt} = R_1 \frac{d\theta_1}{dt} + R_2 \frac{d\theta_2}{dt}
$$

$$
\frac{d^2 x}{dt^2} = R_1 \frac{d^2 \theta_1}{dt^2} + R_2 \frac{d^2 \theta_2}{dt^2}
$$

From these equations, the unknowns \frac{d^2 \theta_1}{dt^2}, \frac{d^2 \theta_2}{dt^2}, \frac{d^2 x}{dt^2}, and F can be determined
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be a set of four equations sufficient to determine d^2x/dt^2: (1) the translational force balance for disc 2, (2) the rotational equation for disc 1, (3) the rotational equation for disc 2, and (4) the no-slip acceleration constraint relating d^2x/dt^2, d^2theta_1/dt^2, and d^2theta_2/dt^2. Write all equations using only the symbols x(t), theta_1(t), theta_2(t), F, g, M_2, R_1, R_2, I_1, I_2, and their time derivatives (do not introduce additional variables or substitute for I_1 or I_2).

context: A yo-yo is modeled as two identical solid disks of radius R and thickness t, separated by a distance t, connected by a solid cylindrical shaft (spool) of radius r and length t. The yo-yo has uniform volumetric mass density ρ, total mass M, and moment of inertia I about its central axis. A massless string is wound around the shaft and the yo-yo descends vertically under gravity with acceleration g. Let x be the downward displacement of the center of mass, θ the angular displacement as the string unwinds, and F the tension in the string. Assume the string unwinds without slipping so that x = r θ and hence ddot{x} = r ddot{θ}. Find the tension F in the string during the descent.
solution:
Let the uniform mass density be ρ. The total mass M and the moment of inertia I about the central axis are

$$
M = 2 
\pi t \rho R^2 + \pi t \rho r^2
$$

$$
I = 2 \cdot \frac{1}{2} \pi t \rho R^4 + \frac{1}{2} \pi t \rho r^4
$$

Thus

$$
I = \frac{1}{2} M \frac{2 R^4 + r^4}{2 R^2 + r^2}
$$

The equations of motion are

$$
M \ddot{x} = M g - F
$$

$$
I \ddot{\theta} = F r
$$

The no-slip kinematic constraint is

$$
\ddot{x} = r \ddot{\theta}
$$

Eliminating \ddot{x} and \ddot{\theta} gives

$$
F = \frac{I M g}{I + M r^2}
$$

Substituting I in terms of M, R, and r yields

$$
F = \frac{(2 R^4 + r^4) M g}{2 R^4 + 4 R^2 r^2 + 3 r^4}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form F = ..., and your response should be written using only the variables M, R, r, and g.

context: A homogeneous solid sphere of mass M and radius R, with moment of inertia about its center I = \frac{2}{5} M R^2, rests on the horizontal platform of a truck. The truck starts from rest and moves with constant horizontal acceleration A relative to the ground. The sphere rolls without slipping on the platform. Use two coordinate frames: an inertial ground frame O'x'y' and a truck-attached frame Oxy. The x and x' axes are horizontal and parallel. Let x be the x-coordinate of the sphere's center of mass in the truck frame Oxy, and x' its x-coordinate in the ground frame O'x'y'. Let \xi be the truck platform's x-displacement relative to the ground, so that x' = x + \xi and \ddot \xi = A. Let f be the static friction force acting on the sphere along the x direction at the contact with the platform. Let \theta be the rotation angle of the sphere about its center. Rolling without slipping in the truck frame gives \dot x = - R \dot \theta, with dots denoting time derivatives. Find the acceleration of the sphere's center of mass relative to the truck, i.e., find \ddot x.
solution:
From the kinematics of the two frames
$$
x' = x + \xi
$$
Hence for accelerations
$$
\ddot x' = \ddot x + \ddot \xi
$$
With the truck's constant acceleration
$$
\ddot \xi = A
$$
The only horizontal external force on the sphere is the static friction f, so in the inertial ground frame
$$
f = M \ddot x'
$$
Substituting the acceleration relation gives
$$
f = M \ddot x + M A
$$
Equivalently
$$
M \ddot x = f - M A
$$
Taking torques about the center of mass
$$
I \ddot \theta = f R
$$
The rolling-without-slipping constraint yields
$$
\dot x = - R \dot \theta
$$
and therefore
$$
\ddot x = - R \ddot \theta
$$
Eliminating \ddot \theta using the torque equation gives
$$
\ddot x = - \frac{f R^2}{I}
$$
Combining with the translational equation
$$
M \ddot x = f - M A
$$
leads to
$$
- M \frac{f R^2}{I} = f - M A
$$
which can be written as
$$
f \Big( 1 + \frac{M R^2}{I} \Big) = M A
$$
Using I = \frac{2}{5} M R^2 yields
$$
f = \frac{2}{7} M A
$$
Finally, the center-of-mass acceleration relative to the truck is
$$
\ddot x = \frac{f - M A}{M}
$$
so
$$
\ddot x = - \frac{5}{7} A
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \ddot x = ... , expressed solely in terms of A (the truck's constant horizontal acceleration) and numerical constants.

context: Referring to Fig. 1.160, find the minimum initial height h, measured vertically above the topmost point of a vertical loop of radius R, that will permit a solid spherical ball of radius r and mass m, rolling without slipping, to maintain constant contact with the rail throughout the loop. The moment of inertia of the solid sphere about its center is I = 2/5 m r^2. Let g denote the acceleration due to gravity. Let v and ω denote, respectively, the speed of the sphere’s center of mass and its angular velocity about its center when the sphere reaches the top of the loop. Let T denote the total kinetic energy of the sphere at the top of the loop.
solution:
By conservation of mechanical energy, the decrease in gravitational potential energy from the initial position to the loop top equals the kinetic energy T at the loop top

$$
m g h = T
$$

The kinetic energy is the sum of translational and rotational parts

$$
T = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 + \frac{1}{2} I \omega^2
$$

The moment of inertia of the solid sphere is

$$
I = \frac{2}{5} m r^2
$$

The no-slip rolling condition gives

$$
v = \omega r
$$

Substituting I and v = \omega r into T

$$
T = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 + \frac{1}{2} \frac{2}{5} m r^2 \frac{v^2}{r^2}
$$

Thus

$$
T = \frac{7}{10} m v^2
$$

At the top of the loop, constant contact at the limiting case requires the normal force to vanish, so gravity alone supplies the centripetal force

$$
\frac{m v^2}{R} = m g
$$

Hence

$$
v^2 = R g
$$

Therefore

$$
T = \frac{7}{10} m R g
$$

Using energy conservation

$$
m g h = \frac{7}{10} m R g
$$

Solving for h

$$
h = \frac{7}{10} R
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form h = ..., and your response should be written with R only.

context:
A solid homogeneous sphere of mass m, radius a, and moment of inertia about its center I is initially at rest at the top of a fixed cylinder of radius b. The sphere rolls without slipping on the outer surface of the cylinder until it loses contact. The distance from the cylinder center to the sphere center is a+b. Let g be the gravitational acceleration and t be time. Let θ be the angular position of the sphere's center measured from the top of the cylinder, with θ=0 at the top and θ increasing in the direction of motion. Let \varphi be the rotation angle of the sphere about its center. Let N be the normal force exerted by the cylinder on the sphere, and f be the tangential friction force. Assume static friction is sufficient to prevent slipping before the sphere loses contact. The rolling-without-slipping constraint holds until separation. Define θ_{max} as the angle at which the sphere leaves the cylinder. Let v denote the speed of the sphere's center. Define unit vectors e_r (radially outward from the cylinder center to the sphere center) and e_t (tangent to the cylinder in the direction of increasing θ). Let v_r and v_t be the components of the center-of-mass velocity along e_r and e_t, respectively. The sphere's moment of inertia is
$$
I=\frac{2}{5} m a^2
$$

subquestions.subproblem: Determine the angle θ_{max} at which the sphere leaves the cylinder.
subquestions.solution:
The tangential equation of motion of the sphere's center is
$$
m(a+b) \ddot{\theta}=m g \sin \theta - f
$$
The radial equation of motion of the sphere's center is
$$
m(a+b) \dot{\theta}^2=m g \cos \theta - N
$$
The rotational equation about the sphere's center is
$$
\frac{2}{5} m a^2 \ddot{\varphi}=f a
$$
The rolling-without-slipping angular-acceleration constraint is
$$
(a+b) \ddot{\theta}=a \ddot{\varphi}
$$
Eliminating \ddot{\varphi} gives
$$
f=\frac{2}{5} m (a+b) \ddot{\theta}
$$
Substituting into the tangential equation yields
$$
\ddot{\theta}=\frac{5 g \sin \theta}{7(a+b)}
$$
With initial conditions
$$
t=0
$$
$$
\theta=0
$$
$$
\dot{\theta}=0
$$
and using
$$
\ddot{\theta}=\frac{1}{2} \frac{d \dot{\theta}^2}{d \theta}
$$
integration gives
$$
\dot{\theta}^2=\frac{10 g (1-\cos \theta)}{7(a+b)}
$$
Substituting into the radial equation gives
$$
N=m g \cos \theta - m(a+b) \dot{\theta}^2
$$
Therefore
$$
N=m g \left( \frac{17}{7} \cos \theta - \frac{10}{7} \right)
$$
The sphere leaves the cylinder when
$$
N=0
$$
Thus
$$
\cos \theta_{max}=\frac{10}{17}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express θ_max as an exact numerical value without rounding, in the form 'θ_max = ...'.

subquestions.subproblem: What are the components of the velocity of the sphere's center at the instant it leaves thecylinder? (Wisconsin)
subquestions.solution:
At the instant of loss of contact the speed is
$$
v=(a+b) \dot{\theta}
$$
Using the result at \theta=\theta_{max} gives
$$
v=\sqrt{\frac{10}{17} g (a+b)}
$$
The velocity is tangent to the cylinder, so the radial and tangential components are
$$
v_r=0
$$
$$
v_t=v
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should provide the components along e_r and e_t in the forms 'v_r = ...' and 'v_t = ...', written solely with a, b, and g.

context: In Fig. 1.163, two identical uniform solid spheres (each of mass M and radius R) move on a horizontal plane. Ball 1 initially rolls without slipping toward ball 2, which is initially at rest. Let V be the initial center-of-mass speed of ball 1. The collision is instantaneous and perfectly elastic. During the collision interval, frictional forces are negligible so the impulsive interaction is along the line through the centers. Let I be the moment of inertia of each sphere about its center, with I = (2/5) M R^2. Let V_1 and V_2 denote the translational speeds of balls 1 and 2, respectively, and let omega_1 and omega_2 denote their angular velocities, all taken just before the collision. A single prime (') denotes quantities immediately after the collision. A double prime ('') denotes quantities long after the collision when each ball is again rolling without slipping. The positive directions for linear and angular variables are as shown in Fig. 1.164.

subquestions.subproblem: The velocity of each ball a long enough time after the collision when each ball is again rolling without slipping.
subquestions.solution:
Before the collision
$$V_1 = V$$
$$V_2 = 0$$
$$\omega_1 = \frac{V}{R}$$
$$\omega_2 = 0$$
During the collision, friction is negligible and the interaction force passes through the centers, so angular momentum about each center is conserved
$$\omega_1^{\prime} = \omega_1$$
$$\omega_2^{\prime} = 0$$
Because the collision is perfectly elastic and central between equal masses, the translational velocities exchange
$$V_1^{\prime} = 0$$
$$V_2^{\prime} = V$$
Long after the collision, each ball rolls without slipping. Consider angular momentum about the instantaneous point of contact with the plane for each ball. For ball 1
$$M R V_1^{\prime} + I \omega_1^{\prime} = M R V_1^{\prime\prime} + I \omega_1^{\prime\prime}$$
Using \(V_1^{\prime} = 0\), \(\omega_1^{\prime} = V/R\), and the rolling condition \(\omega_1^{\prime\prime} = V_1^{\prime\prime}/R\)
$$\frac{I V}{R} = \left( M R + \frac{I}{R} \right) V_1^{\prime\prime}$$
$$V_1^{\prime\prime} = \frac{V}{\frac{M R^2}{I} + 1}$$
With \(I = \frac{2}{5} M R^2\)
$$V_1^{\prime\prime} = \frac{2}{7} V$$
For ball 2
$$M R V_2^{\prime} + I \omega_2^{\prime} = M R V_2^{\prime\prime} + I \omega_2^{\prime\prime}$$
Using \(V_2^{\prime} = V\), \(\omega_2^{\prime} = 0\), and \(\omega_2^{\prime\prime} = V_2^{\prime\prime}/R\)
$$M R V = \left( M R + \frac{I}{R} \right) V_2^{\prime\prime}$$
$$V_2^{\prime\prime} = \frac{V}{1 + \frac{I}{M R^2}}$$
With \(I = \frac{2}{5} M R^2\)
$$V_2^{\prime\prime} = \frac{5}{7} V$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form V_1'' = ... and V_2'' = ..., and your response should be written using only the variable V (no additional variables or numerical approximations).

subquestions.subproblem: The fraction of the initial energy transformed by the frictional forces to thermal energy. The moment of inertia of a sphere of mass M, radius R about its center is (2/5) M R^2 (CUSPEA).
subquestions.solution:
Let W_i be the initial total kinetic energy and W_f be the final total kinetic energy after both balls again roll without slipping. Initially
$$W_i = \frac{1}{2} M V_1^2 + \frac{1}{2} I \omega_1^2$$
$$W_i = \frac{1}{2} \left( M V^2 + \frac{2}{5} M R^2 \cdot \frac{V^2}{R^2} \right)$$
$$W_i = \frac{1}{2} M V^2 \cdot \frac{7}{5}$$
Finally, using \(\omega_1^{\prime\prime} = V_1^{\prime\prime}/R\) and \(\omega_2^{\prime\prime} = V_2^{\prime\prime}/R\)
$$W_f = \frac{1}{2} M \left( V_1^{\prime\prime 2} + V_2^{\prime\prime 2} \right) + \frac{1}{2} I \left( \omega_1^{\prime\prime 2} + \omega_2^{\prime\prime 2} \right)$$
$$W_f = \frac{1}{2} M \left[ V_1^{\prime\prime 2} + V_2^{\prime\prime 2} + \frac{2}{5} \left( V_1^{\prime\prime 2} + V_2^{\prime\prime 2} \right) \right]$$
$$W_f = \frac{1}{2} M V^2 \cdot \frac{7}{5} \cdot \frac{29}{49}$$
Hence the loss of energy is
$$W_i - W_f = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{7}{5} M V^2 \cdot \frac{20}{49}$$
The fractional loss of the initial energy to thermal energy is
$$\eta = \frac{W_i - W_f}{W_i}$$
$$\eta = \frac{20}{49}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be in the form η = ... as a numerical value. Provide either the exact fraction or a decimal rounded to 3 significant figures. Here, η denotes the fraction of the initial kinetic energy transformed into thermal energy.

grading_standard.formula: $$M R V_1^{\prime} + I \omega_1^{\prime} = M R V_1^{\prime\prime} + I \omega_1^{\prime\prime}$$
$$M R V_2^{\prime} + I \omega_2^{\prime} = M R V_2^{\prime\prime} + I \omega_2^{\prime\prime}$$

context: A small homogeneous sphere of mass m and radius r rolls without sliding on the outer surface of a larger stationary sphere of radius R, as shown in Fig. 1.165. The origin is at the center of the large sphere with the z-axis vertical. The polar angle of the small sphere is θ, measured from the top of the large sphere. The small sphere starts from rest at θ = 0. Let g be the gravitational acceleration. Let t denote time. Let v(θ) denote the speed of the center of the small sphere as a function of θ. Let N be the normal reaction on the small sphere and f the tangential friction force. Let μ be the coefficient of friction. Let θ_c be the angle at which the small sphere loses contact with the large sphere, defined by N = 0. Let θ_s be the angle at which the small sphere first starts to slide. Let φ be the rotation angle of the small sphere about its center. Let ω be the angular speed of the small sphere about its center, related to v during rolling without slipping by ω = v/r. Let I be the moment of inertia of the small sphere about its center; for a solid homogeneous sphere I = (2/5) m r^2. The distance from the large-sphere center to the small-sphere center is R + r.

subquestions.subproblem: Calculate the velocity of the center of the small sphere as a function of θ
subquestions.solution:
Using energy conservation between θ = 0 and a general θ during pure rolling
$$m g (R + r) (1 - \cos \theta) = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 + \frac{1}{2} I \omega^2$$
For a solid homogeneous sphere
$$I = \frac{2}{5} m r^2$$
Rolling without slipping implies
$$\omega = \frac{v}{r}$$
Solving for the speed as a function of θ gives
$$v^2(\theta) = \frac{10}{7} g (R + r) (1 - \cos \theta)$$
Taking the positive root for speed
$$v(\theta) = \sqrt{\frac{10}{7} g (R + r) (1 - \cos \theta)}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form v(θ) = ..., and your response should be written with g, R, r, θ.

subquestions.subproblem: Calculate the angle at which the small sphere flies off the large one.
subquestions.solution:
At the instant of flying off
$$N = 0$$
Radial force balance gives
$$m g \cos \theta - N = \frac{m v^2}{R + r}$$
Using the rolling speed from part (a), the loss-of-contact angle satisfies
$$\cos \theta_c = \frac{10}{17}$$
Thus
$$\theta_c = \arccos \left( \frac{10}{17} \right)$$
This result holds provided the coefficient of friction is sufficiently large that rolling without slipping persists up to \theta_c
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express θ_c as a numerical value in radians, rounded to 3 significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: If one now allows for sliding with a coefficient of friction μ, at what point will the small sphere start to slide?
subquestions.solution:
While the small sphere still rolls without sliding, the tangential and rotational equations are
$$m g \sin \theta - f = m \frac{dv}{dt}$$
$$f r = \frac{2}{5} m r^2 \frac{d^2 \varphi}{dt^2}$$
The rolling kinematics give
$$v = (R + r) \frac{d\theta}{dt}$$
$$v = r \frac{d\varphi}{dt}$$
Eliminating the accelerations yields
$$f = \frac{2}{7} m g \sin \theta$$
At the onset of sliding, the friction reaches its limiting value
$$f = \mu N$$
so that
$$\frac{2}{7} m g \sin \theta = \mu \left( m g \cos \theta - \frac{m v^2}{R + r} \right)$$
Using the rolling-without-slipping speed from part (a)
$$2 \sin \theta = 17 \mu \cos \theta - 10 \mu$$
Solving for the onset angle
$$\cos \theta_s = \frac{170 \mu^2 \pm \sqrt{756 \mu^2 + 4}}{289 \mu^2 + 4}$$
To ensure that loss of contact occurs after sliding begins, we require
$$\cos \theta_s > \cos \theta_c$$
When this can be satisfied by the value of \mu, we generally select the upper sign, giving
$$\theta_s = \arccos \left( \frac{170 \mu^2 + \sqrt{756 \mu^2 + 4}}{289 \mu^2 + 4} \right)$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form θ_s = ..., and your response should be written with μ.

grading_standard.formula: $$\frac{2}{7} m g \sin \theta = \mu \left( m g \cos \theta - \frac{m v^2}{R + r} \right)$$

context: A uniform slender plank (rod) of length 2a and mass m is held so that one end leans against a frictionless vertical wall and the other end rests on a frictionless horizontal floor, making an initial angle \theta_0 with the floor. When the plank is released from rest at \theta = \theta_0, it slides under gravity while remaining in contact with the wall and the floor. Let \theta(t) denote the instantaneous angle of the plank with the floor, and let g denote the acceleration due to gravity. The center of mass is at the midpoint, a from either end. Overdots denote time derivatives with respect to time t. For part (b), let x(t) denote the horizontal coordinate of the center of mass measured from the lower end along the floor, and let N_1 be the normal reaction force exerted by the wall on the upper end.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the expression (as an integral if you like) for the time that it will take for the plank to reach a new angle \theta
subquestions.solution:
Since there is no friction, mechanical energy is conserved. The kinetic energy is the sum of the translational kinetic energy of the center of mass and the rotational kinetic energy about the center of mass, and the potential energy is m g a \sin \theta. Using I_{cm} = \frac{1}{3} m a^2 for a slender rod of length 2a,
$$\frac{1}{2} m a^2 \dot{\theta}^2 + \frac{1}{2} \frac{1}{3} m a^2 \dot{\theta}^2 + m g a \sin \theta = m g a \sin \theta_0$$
Cancelling m and a where appropriate gives
$$\frac{2}{3} a \dot{\theta}^2 = g \big(\sin \theta_0 - \sin \theta\big)$$
Solving for \dot{\theta} and noting the negative sign because \theta decreases as t increases,
$$\dot{\theta} = - \sqrt{\frac{3 g}{2 a} \big(\sin \theta_0 - \sin \theta\big)}$$
Integrating to obtain the elapsed time t to reach angle \theta from \theta_0,
$$t = \int_0^t dt$$
$$t = - \int_{\theta_0}^{\theta} \frac{d\theta}{\sqrt{\frac{3 g}{2 a} \big(\sin \theta_0 - \sin \theta\big)}}$$
Note that the factor \frac{1}{3} m a^2 is the moment of inertia of the plank about a horizontal axis through its center of mass.
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of t = ... as an explicit expression (you may use an integral with respect to \theta) for the elapsed time to reach angle \theta from \theta_0, and your response should be written with \theta, \theta_0, a, g only.

subquestions.subproblem: At what value of \theta will the upper end of the plank leave the wall?
subquestions.solution:
With the lower end taken as origin on the floor and the positive x axis along the floor toward the wall, the horizontal coordinate of the center of mass is
$$x = a \cos \theta$$
Differentiating twice with respect to time gives
$$\ddot{x} = - a \big(\dot{\theta}^2 \cos \theta + \ddot{\theta} \sin \theta\big)$$
The horizontal force on the plank is the wall's normal reaction N_1, so
$$N_1 = m \ddot{x}$$
At the instant the plank leaves the wall,
$$N_1 = 0$$
Hence the kinematic condition at separation is
$$\dot{\theta}^2 \cos \theta = - \ddot{\theta} \sin \theta$$
Differentiate the energy result \frac{2}{3} a \dot{\theta}^2 = g \big(\sin \theta_0 - \sin \theta\big) with respect to time to obtain
$$\ddot{\theta} = - \frac{3 g}{4 a} \cos \theta$$
Substituting this and the energy relation into the separation condition yields
$$\sin \theta = 2 \big(\sin \theta_0 - \sin \theta\big)$$
Solving for \sin \theta gives
$$\sin \theta = \frac{2}{3} \sin \theta_0$$
Therefore the angle at which the upper end leaves the wall is
$$\theta = \arcsin\Big(\frac{2}{3} \sin \theta_0\Big)$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \theta = ... , and your response should be written with \theta_0 only.

context: A thin uniform stick of length L and mass m has its lower end in contact with a perfectly smooth horizontal table. It is released from rest at an angle θ_0 to the vertical at time t=0. Let N denote the vertical normal reaction force exerted by the table on the stick at the contact point, g the acceleration due to gravity, θ(t) the angle the stick makes with the vertical, and y(t) the vertical coordinate of the center of mass measured upward from the table. The stick’s moment of inertia about a horizontal axis through its center of mass is I_cm = (1/12) m L^2. Find N at an infinitesimally small time after release (t=0^+).
solution:
With no friction, the only forces on the stick are the table’s normal force N (upward) and gravity m g (downward). The vertical translation of the center of mass at t=0^+ obeys

$$
N - m g = m 
\frac{d^2 y}{d t^2}
$$

Taking torques about the center of mass at t=0^+ gives

$$
\frac{1}{2} N L \sin \theta_0 = \frac{1}{12} m L^2 \frac{d^2 \theta}{d t^2}
$$

where \(\frac{1}{12} m L^2\) is the moment of inertia about a horizontal axis through the center of mass of the stick. The center-of-mass height is

$$
y = \frac{1}{2} L \cos \theta
$$

Differentiating twice with respect to time yields

$$
\frac{d^2 y}{d t^2} = - \frac{1}{2} L \left( \left(\frac{d \theta}{d t}\right)^2 \cos \theta + \frac{d^2 \theta}{d t^2} \sin \theta \right)
$$

At release,

$$
\frac{d \theta}{d t}(0) = 0
$$

$$
\theta(0) = \theta_0
$$

so initially

$$
\frac{d^2 y}{d t^2} = - \frac{1}{2} L \frac{d^2 \theta}{d t^2} \sin \theta_0
$$

From the vertical force balance,

$$
N = m g + m \frac{d^2 y}{d t^2}
$$

Substituting the kinematic relation gives

$$
N = m g - \frac{1}{2} m L \frac{d^2 \theta}{d t^2} \sin \theta_0
$$

From the torque equation,

$$
\frac{d^2 \theta}{d t^2} = \frac{6 N \sin \theta_0}{m L}
$$

Hence,

$$
N = m g - 3 N \sin^2 \theta_0
$$

Solving for N yields

$$
N = \frac{m g}{1 + 3 \sin^2 \theta_0}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of N = ..., and your response should be written with m, g, θ_0.

\frac{d^2 y}{d t^2}
$$

$$
N = m g - \frac{1}{2} m L \frac{d^2 \theta}{d t^2} \sin \theta_0
$$

context: Two long uniform rods A and B each of length L=1\unit{m} lie parallel to each other on a frictionless horizontal plane with axes (x,y). Rod B is initially at rest along y=0 from x=0 to x=1\unit{m}. Rod A, of mass m_A=1\unit{kg}, moves in the positive y direction with speed 10\unit{m/s} and initially extends from x=-1+\epsilon to x=\epsilon\unit{m}, where 0<\epsilon\ll 1\unit{m}. At time t=0 the right end of A reaches y=0 and A collides elastically with the left end of B. Rod B has mass m_B=2\unit{kg}. Ignore any subsequent collisions after the first contact. Define the following unknowns for the motion immediately after the collision: v_A and v_B are the y-components of the center-of-mass velocities of rods A and B, respectively, and \omega_A and \omega_B are their angular velocities about their centers of mass. Let I denote the scalar impulse delivered by A to B during the collision, directed along +y. Use the standard moment of inertia of a uniform rod of length L about its center of mass, I_{cm}=(1/12)mL^2. Define the initial total kinetic energy as E_i and the final total kinetic energy as E_f. Find v_A, \omega_A, v_B, and \omega_B after the collision, and verify energy conservation by checking E_f=E_i.
solution:
Let I be the impulse exerted by rod A on rod B during the collision, directed along +y. Let v_A, \omega_A, v_B, \omega_B denote, respectively, the center-of-mass y-velocities and angular velocities about the center of the mass of rods A and B immediately after the collision. Let m_A and m_B be the masses of A and B, respectively, and L=1\unit{m} their common length. The rod moment of inertia about its center is I_{cm}=(1/12)mL^2.

From linear impulse-momentum for rod A along y we have
$$
-I=m_A\bigl(v_A-10\unit{m/s}\bigr)
$$

From angular impulse-momentum about the center of mass of rod A, using the lever arm L/2 for the end contact and I_{cm,A}=(1/12)m_A L^2 with L=1\unit{m}, we have
$$
\frac{1}{2}I=\frac{1}{12}m_A\omega_A
$$

From linear impulse-momentum for rod B along y we have
$$
I=m_B v_B
$$

From angular impulse-momentum about the center of mass of rod B, using I_{cm,B}=(1/12)m_B L^2 with L=1\unit{m}, we have
$$
\frac{1}{2}I=\frac{1}{12}m_B\omega_B
$$

For a perfectly elastic collision, the relative y-velocity of the contact points reverses in direction while keeping its magnitude. With the contact points at the right end of A and the left end of B, this gives
$$
\bigl(v_B+\tfrac{1}{2}\omega_B\bigr)-\bigl(v_A-\tfrac{1}{2}\omega_A\bigr)=10\unit{m/s}
$$

Solving the above equations yields
$$
I=\frac{5 m_A m_B}{m_A+m_B}
$$

Substituting m_A=1\unit{kg} and m_B=2\unit{kg} gives
$$
I=\frac{10}{3}\unit{N s}
$$

The post-collision center-of-mass velocities are
$$
v_A=10\unit{m/s}-\frac{I}{m_A}
$$

$$
v_A=\frac{20}{3}\unit{m/s}
$$

$$
v_B=\frac{I}{m_B}
$$

$$
v_B=\frac{5}{3}\unit{m/s}
$$

The post-collision angular velocities are
$$
\omega_A=\frac{6I}{m_A}
$$

$$
\omega_A=20\unit{rad/s}
$$

$$
\omega_B=\frac{6I}{m_B}
$$

$$
\omega_B=10\unit{rad/s}
$$

The initial total kinetic energy is
$$
E_i=\frac{1}{2}m_A\bigl(10\unit{m/s}\bigr)^2
$$

$$
E_i=50\unit{J}
$$

The final total kinetic energy is
$$
E_f=\frac{1}{2}m_A v_A^2+\frac{1}{2}m_B v_B^2+\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{12}m_A\omega_A^2+\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{12}m_B\omega_B^2
$$

$$
E_f=50\unit{J}
$$

$$
E_f=E_i
$$

Thus energy is conserved and the subsequent motion is given by v_A=20/3\unit{m/s}, \omega_A=20\unit{rad/s}, v_B=5/3\unit{m/s}, and \omega_B=10\unit{rad/s}.
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express v_A (m/s), ω_A (rad/s), v_B (m/s), ω_B (rad/s), E_i (J), and E_f (J) as numerical values in SI units. Round each reported value to 3 significant figures.

context: A solid billiard ball of radius R and mass M is initially at rest on a horizontal table. It is struck by a horizontal cue stick at a height h above the table surface, as shown in Fig. 1.171. The moment of inertia of the ball about its center is I = 2/5 M R^2. Find the value of h such that immediately after the impulsive hit the ball will roll without slipping. Definitions for the analysis: f is the magnitude of the impact force exerted by the cue, Δt is the contact duration, Δv is the change in the center-of-mass speed, Δω is the change in the angular speed about the center, v is the center-of-mass speed immediately after impact, and ω is the angular speed immediately after impact. The rolling-without-slipping condition is v = R ω, and the torque lever arm about the center during impact is h − R.
solution:
During the short impact, the linear impulse and angular impulse about the center are
$$
M \Delta v = f \Delta t
$$
$$
I \Delta \omega = f ( h - R ) \Delta t
$$
with
$$
I = \frac{2}{5} M R^2
$$
Eliminating f \Delta t gives
$$
\Delta v = \frac{2 R^2 \Delta \omega}{5 ( h - R )}
$$
Since the ball starts from rest, the post-impact speeds satisfy
$$
v = \frac{2 R^2 \omega}{5 ( h - R )}
$$
The rolling-without-slipping condition is
$$
v = R \omega
$$
Solving for h yields
$$
5 ( h - R ) = 2 R
$$
$$
h = \frac{7}{5} R
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of h = ..., and your response should be written with R only.

context: A uniform solid ball of mass m and radius a rolls without slipping on a level surface with initial center-of-mass speed v and angular speed ω, so v = a ω. It collides inelastically with a vertical step of height h satisfying 0 < h < a at the impact point A, as shown in Fig. 1.172. During the impulsive contact, there is no slipping at A and the center of mass is momentarily at rest immediately after the impact, so the ball instantaneously rotates about A with angular speed ω'. Let J and J' denote the angular momentum about A just before and just after the collision, respectively. Let I_cm = (\frac{2}{5}) m a^2 be the moment of inertia of the solid sphere about its center, and let I' = I_cm + m a^2 be the moment of inertia about a horizontal axis through A. Let g denote the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration. Find, in terms of a, h, and g, the minimum initial speed v_min for which the ball will trip up over the step.
solution:
Define J and J' as the angular momentum about A immediately before and after the collision, respectively. The angular momentum about A just before impact is
$$
J = m v (a - h) + \frac{2}{5} m a^2 \omega
$$
Using rolling without slipping before impact,
$$
v = a \omega
$$
Substituting gives
$$
J = \frac{7}{5} m v a - m v h
$$
Immediately after impact, the ball rotates about A with angular speed \omega', so
$$
J' = \frac{7}{5} m a^2 \omega'
$$
Conservation of angular momentum about A during the impulsive contact gives
$$
\frac{7}{5} m a^2 \omega' = \frac{7}{5} m v a - m v h
$$
Solving for \omega' yields
$$
\omega' = \left(1 - \frac{5 h}{7 a}\right) \frac{v}{a}
$$
The moment of inertia about A is
$$
I' = \frac{2}{5} m a^2 + m a^2
$$
Hence
$$
I' = \frac{7}{5} m a^2
$$
For just tripping up, the post-collision rotational kinetic energy equals the gain in gravitational potential energy
$$
\frac{1}{2} I' \omega'^2 = m g h
$$
Substituting I' and \omega' gives
$$
\frac{7}{10} m a^2 \left(1 - \frac{5 h}{7 a}\right)^2 \left(\frac{v}{a}\right)^2 = m g h
$$
Solving for the minimum initial speed v_min gives
$$
v_{min} = \frac{a \sqrt{70 g h}}{7 a - 5 h}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of v_min = ..., and your response should be written with a, h, g.

grading_standard.formula: $$J = \frac{7}{5} m v a - m v h$$
$$\frac{7}{5} m a^2 \omega' = \frac{7}{5} m v a - m v h$$
$$\frac{7}{10} m a^2 \left(1 - \frac{5 h}{7 a}\right)^2 \left(\frac{v}{a}\right)^2 = m g h$$

context: A stepladder consists of two identical uniform legs, each modeled as a slender rod of length l and mass m, held together by a hinge at the top at point A and a horizontal rope near the bottom. The legs rest on a horizontal, frictionless surface at 60^\circ as shown in Fig. 1.175. At the instant the rope is suddenly cut, find the acceleration of the hinge A. Use an inertial coordinate system with x horizontal and y vertically downward. For one leg, let B be the contact point with the floor at the bottom, and C its center of mass. Let \theta(t) be the angle of the leg with the horizontal, with \theta=60^\circ at that instant. Let I be the mass moment of inertia of one leg about C. Let N be the vertical normal reaction of the floor on the leg at B, and F the horizontal interaction force exerted by the other leg on this leg at the hinge A. Let a_A denote the magnitude of the vertical acceleration of point A, and let a_{Cx}, a_{Cy} be the components of the acceleration of C. Take g as the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration with units \unit{m/s^2}.
solution:
By symmetry, the forces that the two legs exert on each other at the hinge A are horizontal, so the acceleration of A is purely vertical and directed downward.

For one leg, the translational equations for the center of mass C are
$$
m g - N = m a_{Cy}
$$
$$
F = m a_{Cx}
$$
The rotational equation about C is
$$
\frac{1}{2} N l \cos 60^\circ - \frac{1}{2} F l \sin 60^\circ = I \ddot{\theta}
$$
with
$$
I = \frac{1}{12} m l^2
$$
which gives
$$
N - \sqrt{3} F = \frac{1}{3} m l \ddot{\theta}
$$
Kinematics of A in terms of C give the velocity relations
$$
\dot{x}_A = \dot{x}_C - \frac{1}{2} l \dot{\theta} \sin 60^\circ
$$
$$
\dot{y}_A = \dot{y}_C + \frac{1}{2} l \dot{\theta} \cos 60^\circ
$$
and the acceleration relations
$$
 a_{Ax} = a_{Cx} - \frac{1}{2} l \ddot{\theta} \sin 60^\circ
$$
$$
 a_{Ay} = a_{Cy} + \frac{1}{2} l \ddot{\theta} \cos 60^\circ
$$
Since the acceleration of A is vertical, we have
$$
 a_{Ax} = 0
$$
Let a_A denote the vertical acceleration of A, so
$$
 a_A = a_{Cy} + \frac{1}{2} l \ddot{\theta} \cos 60^\circ
$$
For point B, the vertical acceleration is
$$
 a_{By} = a_{Cy} - \frac{1}{2} l \ddot{\theta} \cos 60^\circ
$$
At the instant the rope is cut, B has no vertical acceleration, hence
$$
 a_{By} = 0
$$
Using \sin 60^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} and \cos 60^\circ = \frac{1}{2}, we obtain
$$
 0 = a_{Cx} - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} l \ddot{\theta}
$$
$$
 a_A = a_{Cy} + \frac{1}{4} l \ddot{\theta}
$$
$$
 a_{Cy} = \frac{1}{4} l \ddot{\theta}
$$
$$
 a_{Cx} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} l \ddot{\theta}
$$
Substituting these into the equations of motion yields
$$
 \ddot{\theta} = \frac{3 g}{4 l}
$$
Therefore
$$
 a_A = \frac{1}{2} l \ddot{\theta}
$$
which gives
$$
 a_A = \frac{3}{8} g
$$
directed vertically downward
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form a_A = [expression in terms of g], and you must also state the direction explicitly as either 'upward' or 'downward'. Use only the variable g in your expression.

context: A particle of mass m and speed v collides elastically with the end of a uniform thin rod of mass M and length l, as shown in Fig. 1.177. The rod is initially at rest. After the collision, the particle of mass m is stationary. Calculate M. Variables used in the solution: v_c is the velocity of the center of mass of the rod after the collision, ω is the angular velocity of the rod about its center of mass after the collision, and I is the moment of inertia of the rod about its center of mass.
solution:
Let v_c be the velocity of the center of mass of the rod and ω the angular velocity of the rod about the center of mass. Conservation of linear momentum and mechanical energy for this elastic collision give

$$
m v = M v_c
$$

$$
\frac{1}{2} m v^2 = \frac{1}{2} M v_c^2 + \frac{1}{2} I \omega^2
$$

For a uniform thin rod about its center of mass,

$$
I = \frac{1}{12} M l^2
$$

Conservation of angular momentum about the center of the rod during the collision gives

$$
\frac{1}{2} l m v = I \omega
$$

Solving the above equations yields

$$
M = 4 m
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of M = ... , and your response should be written using only m and numerical constants.

context: A uniform thin cylindrical rigid rod of length L and mass m is supported at its ends by two massless vertical springs with spring constants k_1 and k_2. In equilibrium the rod is horizontal, as shown in Fig. 1.178. Consider small-amplitude motion about equilibrium under circumstances where the springs and the rod can move only vertically. Use y_1 and y_2 for the vertical displacements of the left and right ends of the rod, measured upward from the equilibrium configuration. Seek normal-mode solutions of the form y_1 = A_1 e^{i \omega t} and y_2 = A_2 e^{i \omega t}, where A_1 and A_2 are complex amplitudes, t is time, i is the imaginary unit, and \omega is the angular eigenfrequency. For a uniform rod

Define y_1 and y_2 as the vertical displacements of the left and right ends of the rod, measured upward from equilibrium, and take normal-mode solutions y_1 = A_1 e^{i \omega t}, y_2 = A_2 e^{i \omega t}. Here A_1 and A_2 are complex amplitudes, t is time in \unit{s}, i is the imaginary unit with i^2 = -1, and \omega is the angular eigenfrequency in \unit{rad/s}. Let I be the moment of inertia of the uniform rod about its center for rotation about an axis perpendicular to the rod, with I = \frac{1}{12} m L^2, where L is in \unit{m}, m is in \unit{kg}, and k_1, k_2 are in \unit{N/m}.

$$y_1 = A_1 e^{i \omega t}$$
$$y_2 = A_2 e^{i \omega t}$$
$$i^2 = -1$$
$$I = \frac{1}{12} m L^2$$
$$(k_1 - \frac{1}{2} m \omega^2) A_1 + (k_2 - \frac{1}{2} m \omega^2) A_2 = 0$$
$$\left( \frac{I \omega^2}{L} - \frac{1}{2} L k_1 \right) A_1 + \left( \frac{1}{2} L k_2 - \frac{I \omega^2}{L} \right) A_2 = 0$$
$$\frac{I m \omega^4}{L} - \left( \frac{I}{L} + \frac{1}{4} m L \right) (k_1 + k_2) \omega^2 + L k_1 k_2 = 0$$

$$\omega^2 = \frac{2}{m} \left[ (k_1 + k_2) \pm \sqrt{k_1^2 - k_1 k_2 + k_2^2} \right]$$
$$\omega = \sqrt{ \frac{2}{m} \left[ (k_1 + k_2) \pm \sqrt{k_1^2 - k_1 k_2 + k_2^2} \right] }$$
When k_1 = k_2 = k, denote the two eigenfrequencies by \omega_1 and \omega_2, given by
$$\omega_1 = \sqrt{\frac{2 k}{m}}$$
$$\omega_2 = \sqrt{\frac{6 k}{m}}$$
