context: A rigid conical trash-can lid is supported by a pivot at the center O. Let C be the center of mass, and let r denote the vector from O to C, with magnitude r_0=|r|. The lid is tipped and spun rapidly with angular velocity ω about its symmetry axis. Let m be the mass of the lid, g the gravitational acceleration vector of magnitude g pointing vertically downward, L the angular momentum of the lid about O (in an inertial frame), M the torque of gravity about O, and ω_p the precession angular velocity vector about the vertical (parallel to g). For a rapidly spinning symmetric cone, L is directed along the symmetry axis. Define the sense variables s_ω and s_p as follows: when viewed from above along the vertical axis, s_ω=+1 for counterclockwise spin and s_ω=-1 for clockwise spin; s_p is defined analogously for the precession about the vertical. Determine whether the lid precesses in the same or opposite sense to the spin by giving the relation between s_p and s_ω. Document your answer with the governing equations and refer to the vector diagram in Fig. 1.182.
solution:
The gravitational torque about O is
$$
M = r \times m g
$$
In an inertial frame the rate of change of angular momentum equals the torque
$$
\frac{dL}{dt} = M
$$
Define the precession angular velocity by
$$
\frac{dL}{dt} = \omega_p \times L
$$
For a rapidly spinning symmetric cone, L is parallel to r, so
$$
r = \frac{r_0}{L} L
$$
Substituting into the torque gives
$$
M = \frac{r_0 m}{L} L \times g
$$
Reordering the cross product yields
$$
M = - \frac{r_0 m}{L} g \times L
$$
Equating with the definition of precession gives
$$
\omega_p \times L = - \frac{r_0 m}{L} g \times L
$$
Hence the precession angular velocity vector is
$$
\omega_p = - \frac{r_0 m}{L} g
$$
Its magnitude is
$$
|\omega_p| = \frac{r_0 m g}{L}
$$
With the viewing convention defined in the problem statement, the precession sense relative to the spin sense is
$$
s_p = - s_\omega
$$
Thus the axis of symmetry of the lid precesses about the vertical in the sense opposite to the spin, as shown in Fig. 1.182.
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of s_p = ..., and your response should be written with s_p and s_ω only.

context: A rigid, horizontal, massless square frame carries four identical disks rotating as shown in Fig. 1.183. Each disk has mass m, moment of inertia I_0 about its own spin axis, and spin angular speed \omega_0. The frame pivots freely about a support at one corner O. Let c be the center of mass of the four-disk system (located at the square's center), and let D=|OC| be the distance from O to c. The spin directions are as in Fig. 1.184 so that the resultant spin angular momentum of the system is directed along OC and is horizontal. Let g denote the gravitational acceleration vector (of magnitude g, directed downward). Let L denote the total angular momentum of the system about O, M the torque about O due to gravity, \Omega the vector precessional angular velocity, and \Omega_p its magnitude (the precession rate). Find \Omega_p and the sense of precession as seen from above.
solution:
The angular momentum of each disk about its spin axis has magnitude I_0 \omega_0, with directions as indicated in Fig. 1.184. The total angular momentum of the system about O has magnitude
$$
L = 2 \sqrt{2} I_0 \omega_0
$$
and it is directed along OC, hence horizontal. The torque due to gravity about O is
$$
M = OC \times 4 m g
$$
For steady precession we have
$$
\frac{dL}{dt} = M
$$
and
$$
M = \Omega \times L
$$
From these relations, the precessional angular velocity is
$$
\Omega = - \frac{2 \sqrt{2} D m g}{2 \sqrt{2} I_0 \omega_0}
$$
which simplifies to
$$
\Omega = - \frac{D m g}{I_0 \omega_0}
$$
Therefore, the precession rate (the magnitude of \Omega) is
$$
\Omega_p = \frac{D m g}{I_0 \omega_0}
$$
and the sense of precession is anticlockwise when viewed from above.
final_answer_instructions: Provide two parts: (1) an algebraic expression in the form \Omega_p = ... , using only the variables D, m, g, I_0, and \omega_0; and (2) a one-sentence statement of the sense of precession in exactly one of the following forms: 'The precession is clockwise as seen from above.' or 'The precession is anticlockwise as seen from above.'

context: We consider an ideal free symmetric gyro, i.e., a rotationally symmetric rigid body with principal moments of inertia I_1 = I_2 < I_3, suspended so it can rotate freely about its center of mass with no external torque. Let ω(t) denote the instantaneous angular velocity vector, L(t) denote the instantaneous angular momentum vector, and u(t) denote the unit vector along the body symmetry axis associated with I_3. Work in an inertial fixed frame Oxyz with unit vectors i, j, k, and in a rotating body frame Ox^{\prime}y^{\prime}z^{\prime} with unit vectors i^{\prime}, j^{\prime}, k^{\prime}, where k^{\prime} is aligned with the symmetry axis. The orientation is described by the Euler angles θ, \varphi, ψ as in Fig. 1.185. Choose the fixed frame at t = 0 with the z-axis along L(0) and the y-axis perpendicular to ω_0 = ω(0). Choose the body frame at t = 0 with k^{\prime} along the symmetry axis u_0 = u(0) and i^{\prime} in the plane spanned by k^{\prime} and k, so that initially y^{\prime} aligns with y and \varphi(0) = 0, ψ(0) = 0. Define θ_0 = θ(0). Define u_0 = u(0) with components u_{0x}, u_{0y}, u_{0z} in the fixed frame. Define ω_0 = ω(0) with components ω_{0x}, ω_{0y}, ω_{0z} in the fixed frame and ω_{0 x^{\prime}}, ω_{0 y^{\prime}}, ω_{0 z^{\prime}} in the body frame. Let L_m = |L(t)| and ω_m = |ω(t)| denote magnitudes. Let α be the angle between ω(t) and the fixed z-axis, and β the angle between ω(t) and the body z^{\prime}-axis. Derive explicit expressions for L(t), ω(t), and u(t) in terms of the initial values u_0 and ω_0
solution:
At t = 0 let L(0), ω(0), and the symmetry axis u(0) be coplanar. Use the fixed frame Oxyz with z along L(0) and y perpendicular to ω(0), and the rotating body frame Ox^{\prime}y^{\prime}z^{\prime} with z^{\prime} along the symmetry axis and x^{\prime} in the plane of z^{\prime} and z at t = 0. The Euler angles are θ, \varphi, ψ with \varphi(0) = 0 and ψ(0) = 0.

In the rotating frame, the angular velocity components in terms of θ, \varphi, ψ are
$$
ω_{x^{\prime}} = \frac{d\theta}{dt} \sin \psi - \frac{d\varphi}{dt} \sin \theta \cos \psi
$$
$$
ω_{y^{\prime}} = \frac{d\theta}{dt} \cos \psi + \frac{d\varphi}{dt} \sin \theta \sin \psi
$$
$$
ω_{z^{\prime}} = \frac{d\varphi}{dt} \cos \theta + \frac{d\psi}{dt}
$$
Since x^{\prime}, y^{\prime}, z^{\prime} are principal axes and I_1 = I_2, the angular momentum in the body frame is
$$
L(t) = I_1 ω_{x^{\prime}} i^{\prime} + I_1 ω_{y^{\prime}} j^{\prime} + I_3 ω_{z^{\prime}} k^{\prime}
$$
With no external torque, L(t) is constant in the fixed frame and remains along k. The Euler equation for the z^{\prime} component is
$$
I_3 \frac{d ω_{z^{\prime}}}{dt} - ( I_1 - I_2 ) ω_{x^{\prime}} ω_{y^{\prime}} = 0
$$
For I_1 = I_2 we obtain
$$
\frac{d ω_{z^{\prime}}}{dt} = 0
$$
Hence
$$
ω_{z^{\prime}} = ω_{0 z^{\prime}}
$$
The magnitude L_m satisfies
$$
L_m^2 = I_1^2 ( ω_{x^{\prime}}^2 + ω_{y^{\prime}}^2 ) + I_3^2 ω_{0 z^{\prime}}^2
$$
Thus
$$
ω_{x^{\prime}}^2 + ω_{y^{\prime}}^2 = ω_{0 x^{\prime}}^2 + ω_{0 y^{\prime}}^2
$$
Because initially y^{\prime} coincides with y and ω_{0y} = 0, we have
$$
ω_{0 y^{\prime}} = 0
$$
Therefore
$$
ω_{x^{\prime}}^2 + ω_{y^{\prime}}^2 = ω_{0 x^{\prime}}^2
$$
In the fixed frame the constant vector is
$$
L(t) = L_m k
$$
with
$$
L_m = \sqrt{ I_1^2 ω_{0 x^{\prime}}^2 + I_3^2 ω_{0 z^{\prime}}^2 }
$$
In the rotating frame we also have
$$
L(t) = - L_m \sin \theta \cos \psi i^{\prime} + L_m \sin \theta \sin \psi j^{\prime} + L_m \cos \theta k^{\prime}
$$
Comparing the k^{\prime} component gives
$$
L_m \cos \theta = I_3 ω_{0 z^{\prime}}
$$
Therefore
$$
\theta = \theta_0
$$
and
$$
\frac{d\theta}{dt} = 0
$$
From the i^{\prime} component we have
$$
- L_m \sin \theta \cos \psi = I_1 ω_{x^{\prime}}
$$
Using
$$
ω_{x^{\prime}} = - \frac{d\varphi}{dt} \sin \theta \cos \psi
$$
we obtain
$$
\frac{d\varphi}{dt} = \frac{ L_m }{ I_1 }
$$
From the k^{\prime} component we have
$$
I_3 \left( \frac{d\varphi}{dt} \cos \theta + \frac{d\psi}{dt} \right) = L_m \cos \theta
$$
Hence
$$
\frac{d\psi}{dt} = \frac{ L_m \cos \theta }{ I_3 } - \frac{ L_m \cos \theta }{ I_1 }
$$
Using
$$
L_m \cos \theta = I_3 ω_{0 z^{\prime}}
$$
we get
$$
\frac{d\psi}{dt} = \left( 1 - \frac{ I_3 }{ I_1 } \right) ω_{0 z^{\prime}}
$$
With \varphi(0) = 0 and ψ(0) = 0 we have
$$
\varphi(t) = \frac{d\varphi}{dt} t
$$
$$
\psi(t) = \frac{d\psi}{dt} t
$$
For the symmetry-axis unit vector in the fixed frame we have
$$
\nu(t) = \sin \theta \cos \varphi i + \sin \theta \sin \varphi j + \cos \theta k
$$
At t = 0 with \theta = \theta_0 and \varphi(0) = 0,
$$\nu(0) = \sin \theta_0 i + \cos \theta_0 k
$$
Defining u_{0x} = \sin \theta_0 and u_{0z} = \cos \theta_0 and using \varphi(t) = \frac{d\varphi}{dt} t, we obtain
$$\nu(t) = u_{0x} \cos \left( \frac{d\varphi}{dt} t \right) i + u_{0x} \sin \left( \frac{d\varphi}{dt} t \right) j + u_{0z} k
$$
In the rotating frame, using \theta = \theta_0 and \frac{d\theta}{dt} = 0,
$$
ω(t) = - \frac{d\varphi}{dt} \sin \theta_0 \cos \psi i^{\prime} + \frac{d\varphi}{dt} \sin \theta_0 \sin \psi j^{\prime} + \left( \frac{d\varphi}{dt} \cos \theta_0 + \frac{d\psi}{dt} \right) k^{\prime}
$$
At t = 0 with \varphi(0) = 0 and ψ(0) = 0,
$$
ω_0 = - \frac{d\varphi}{dt} \sin \theta_0 i^{\prime} + \left( \frac{d\varphi}{dt} \cos \theta_0 + \frac{d\psi}{dt} \right) k^{\prime}
$$
Therefore
$$
ω(t) = ω_{0 x^{\prime}} \cos \psi i^{\prime} - ω_{0 x^{\prime}} \sin \psi j^{\prime} + ω_{0 z^{\prime}} k^{\prime}
$$
The magnitude satisfies
$$
ω_m = \sqrt{ ω_{0 x^{\prime}}^2 + ω_{0 z^{\prime}}^2 }
$$
Also
$$
ω_m = |ω_0|
$$
The angle with the fixed z-axis satisfies
$$
\cos \alpha = \frac{ ω_z }{ ω_m }
$$
with
$$
ω_z = \frac{d\varphi}{dt} + \frac{d\psi}{dt} \cos \theta_0
$$
Thus
$$
\cos \alpha = \frac{ \frac{d\varphi}{dt} + \frac{d\psi}{dt} \cos \theta_0 }{ ω_m }
$$
The angle with the body z^{\prime}-axis satisfies
$$
\cos \beta = \frac{ ω_{z^{\prime}} }{ ω_m }
$$
with
$$
ω_{z^{\prime}} = \frac{d\varphi}{dt} \cos \theta_0 + \frac{d\psi}{dt}
$$
Thus
$$
\cos \beta = \frac{ \frac{d\varphi}{dt} \cos \theta_0 + \frac{d\psi}{dt} }{ ω_m }
$$
In the fixed frame, using \theta = \theta_0,
$$
ω(t) = \frac{d\psi}{dt} \sin \theta_0 \cos \varphi i + \frac{d\psi}{dt} \sin \theta_0 \sin \varphi j + \left( \frac{d\psi}{dt} \cos \theta_0 + \frac{d\varphi}{dt} \right) k
$$
At t = 0 we have
$$
ω_0 = \frac{d\psi}{dt} \sin \theta_0 i + \left( \frac{d\psi}{dt} \cos \theta_0 + \frac{d\varphi}{dt} \right) k
$$
Thus
$$
ω(t) = ω_{0x} \cos \left( \frac{d\varphi}{dt} t \right) i + ω_{0x} \sin \left( \frac{d\varphi}{dt} t \right) j + ω_{0z} k
$$
Finally, the explicit results in terms of initial values are
$$
L(t) = L_m k
$$
$$
L_m = \sqrt{ I_1^2 ω_{0 x^{\prime}}^2 + I_3^2 ω_{0 z^{\prime}}^2 }
$$
$$
\frac{d\varphi}{dt} = \frac{ L_m }{ I_1 }
$$
$$
\frac{d\psi}{dt} = \left( 1 - \frac{ I_3 }{ I_1 } \right) ω_{0 z^{\prime}}
$$
$$
\nu(t) = u_{0x} \cos \left( \frac{d\varphi}{dt} t \right) i + u_{0x} \sin \left( \frac{d\varphi}{dt} t \right) j + u_{0z} k
$$
$$
ω(t) = ω_{0x} \cos \left( \frac{d\varphi}{dt} t \right) i + ω_{0x} \sin \left( \frac{d\varphi}{dt} t \right) j + ω_{0z} k
$$
The vectors u(t) and ω(t) both precess about L(t) with angular speed \frac{d\varphi}{dt}, while the body spins about its symmetry axis with angular speed \frac{d\psi}{dt}

context: A thin disk of mass M and radius A is connected by two identical springs of spring constant k to two fixed points on a frictionless tabletop. Each spring has unstretched length l_0, and in the symmetric equilibrium configuration each is stretched to length l > l_0. Consider small oscillations confined to the plane of the table. Let x denote the small displacement of the disk’s center of mass along the common line of the springs from its equilibrium position, and let θ denote the small angular displacement of the disk about its center. Let F_1 and F_2 denote the tensions in the left and right springs, respectively. Let I be the moment of inertia of the disk about its center, and let φ be the small geometric angle defined in the figure between a spring and the radius from the disk’s center to the point of spring attachment. Let ω_1 and ω_2 be the angular frequencies of the two normal modes, and let f_1 and f_2 be the corresponding frequencies in hertz defined by f = ω/(2π). Find ω_1 and ω_2 for small oscillations, and describe the motion in each normal mode.
solution:
The motion is confined to the plane of the table. Define the small translational displacement x of the center of mass and the small rotation θ about the center. To first order in θ, the spring forces are
$$
F_1 = k (l + x - l_0)
$$
$$
F_2 = k (l - x - l_0)
$$
The translational equation of motion is
$$
M \ddot{x} = F_2 - F_1
$$
Using the linearized forces gives
$$
F_2 - F_1 = -2 k x
$$
Hence
$$
\ddot{x} + \frac{2 k}{M} x = 0
$$
For rotation about the center, the torque equation is
$$
I \ddot{\theta} = (F_2 + F_1) A \sin \varphi
$$
For a thin disk
$$
I = \frac{1}{2} M A^2
$$
The geometry gives the relation
$$
\frac{\sin(\pi - \varphi)}{l + A + x} = \frac{\sin \theta}{l + x}
$$
For small angles and small x, this implies
$$
\sin \varphi \approx \frac{l + A}{l} \sin \theta
$$
and therefore
$$
\sin \varphi \approx \frac{l + A}{l} \theta
$$
Since
$$
F_1 + F_2 = 2 k (l - l_0)
$$
we obtain
$$
\ddot{\theta} + \frac{4 k (l - l_0) (l + A)}{M l A} \theta = 0
$$
Therefore, the angular frequencies of the normal modes are
$$
\omega_1 = \sqrt{\frac{2 k}{M}}
$$
$$
\omega_2 = \sqrt{\frac{4 k (l - l_0) (l + A)}{M l A}}
$$
The corresponding frequencies in hertz are
$$
f_1 = \frac{\omega_1}{2 \pi}
$$
$$
f_2 = \frac{\omega_2}{2 \pi}
$$
Mode descriptions: In the first normal mode, the disk undergoes pure translation with x oscillating and \theta = 0. In the second normal mode, the disk undergoes pure rotation with \theta oscillating and x = 0.
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should include two parts: (1) Algebraic expressions for the two angular frequencies in the explicit forms 'ω1 = ...' and 'ω2 = ...'. Write ω1 using only the variables M and k, and write ω2 using only the variables M, k, l, l_0, and A. (2) A concise text description of the motion in each normal mode, given exactly as two sentences: 'Mode 1: ...' and 'Mode 2: ...'. In each sentence, explicitly state which of x and θ oscillates and which is zero.

context: A heavy symmetric top with one point fixed is precessing at a steady angular velocity Ω about the vertical axis z. The symmetry axis of the top is z′, which is inclined at an angle θ with respect to the z-axis. The spin about the symmetry axis z′ is denoted by ω′. The top has mass m, its center of gravity is at a distance h from the fixed point, and the acceleration due to gravity is g. Use the coordinate systems indicated in Fig. 1.193, with the axes z, z′, x, and x′ in the same plane at the time under consideration. Assume the principal moments of inertia satisfy I1 = I2 and let I3 be the moment of inertia about the symmetry axis z′. Let the Euler angles be φ (precession about z), θ (inclination between z and z′), and ψ (spin about z′). Time derivatives are denoted by d/dt. In steady precession, θ is constant, the precession rate about z is Ω, and the spin rate about z′ is ω′. Let ω′min denote the minimum spin about z′ required for steady precession. Determine ω′min in terms of m, g, h, I1, I3, and θ.
solution:
In the rotating body frame O x′ y′ z′ attached to the top, the torque due to gravity is perpendicular to the xz-plane and has components

$$
\tau_{x'} = m g h \sin \theta \sin \psi
$$

$$
\tau_{y'} = m g h \sin \theta \cos \psi
$$

$$
\tau_{z'} = 0
$$

Euler's equations in the body frame for a symmetric top with I1 = I2 are

$$
I_1 \frac{d\omega_{x'}}{dt} - (I_1 - I_3) \omega_{y'} \omega_{z'} = m g h \sin \theta \sin \psi
$$

$$
I_1 \frac{d\omega_{y'}}{dt} - (I_3 - I_1) \omega_{x'} \omega_{z'} = m g h \sin \theta \cos \psi
$$

$$
I_3 \frac{d\omega_{z'}}{dt} = 0
$$

The angular velocity components in the body frame, with constant inclination, satisfy

$$
\frac{d\theta}{dt} = 0
$$

$$
\omega_{x'} = - \frac{d\varphi}{dt} \sin \theta \cos \psi
$$

$$
\omega_{y'} = \frac{d\varphi}{dt} \sin \theta \sin \psi
$$

$$
\omega_{z'} = \frac{d\varphi}{dt} \cos \theta + \frac{d\psi}{dt}
$$

For steady precession the precession rate is constant and satisfies

$$
\frac{d\varphi}{dt} = \Omega
$$

$$
\frac{d^2 \varphi}{dt^2} = 0
$$

Substituting into the first Euler equation gives

$$
\Omega^2 (I_1 - I_3) \cos \theta - \Omega I_3 \frac{d\psi}{dt} + m g h = 0
$$

Defining the spin about z′ by

$$
\omega' = \frac{d\psi}{dt}
$$

yields

$$
\omega' = \frac{m g h + (I_1 - I_3) \Omega^2 \cos \theta}{I_3 \Omega}
$$

For Ω to be real, the discriminant condition implies

$$
I_3^2 \omega'^2 - 4 (I_1 - I_3) m g h \cos \theta \geq 0
$$

Therefore the minimum spin required for steady precession is

$$
\omega'_{\min} = \frac{1}{I_3} \sqrt{4 (I_1 - I_3) m g h \cos \theta}
$$

and hence

$$
\omega' \geq \omega'_{\min}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of ω'_min = ..., expressed solely in terms of m, g, h, I1, I3, and θ. Do not include any other variables or numerical evaluations.

context: The game of Jacks is played with metal pieces that can be approximated by six equal point masses m located at distances l from the center along the positive and negative directions of three orthogonal body-fixed principal axes x', y', z', as shown in Fig. 1.194. The total mass is M=6m. Gravity acts downward with magnitude g and units \unit{m/s^2}. The length parameter l has units \unit{m}. The orientation of the jack is described by Euler angles (varphi, theta, psi): varphi is the precession angle about the vertical, theta is the angle between the vertical and the body z' axis, and psi is the spin angle about the body z' axis. Define the spin angular velocity s=dot psi and the precession rate Omega=dot varphi. The body angular velocity vector omega has components (omega_{x'}, omega_{y'}, omega_{z'}) in the body frame. The gravitational torque vector tau has components (tau_{x'}, tau_{y'}, tau_{z'}) in the body frame. In steady precession about the vertical (Fig. 1.195), the analysis below relates s, Omega, and theta. For convenience when indicating constancy, we will also use the statement omega_{z'} is constant during steady precession.

subquestions.subproblem: If you spin the jack around one of its principal axes so that there is a steady precession around the vertical (Fig. 1.195), what is the relation between the spin velocity s, the precession rate Omega, and the angle theta between the vertical and the rotation axis of the jack?
subquestions.solution:
In the rotating body frame, the gravitational torque components are
$$
\tau_{x'}=6 m g l \sin \theta \sin \psi
$$
$$
\tau_{y'}=6 m g l \sin \theta \cos \psi
$$
$$
\tau_{z'}=0
$$
The angular velocity components are
$$
\omega_{x'}=\dot \theta \sin \psi-\dot \varphi \sin \theta \cos \psi
$$
$$
\omega_{y'}=\dot \theta \cos \psi+\dot \varphi \sin \theta \sin \psi
$$
$$
\omega_{z'}=\dot \psi+\dot \varphi \cos \theta
$$
Euler's equations then give
$$
5 \dot \omega_{x'}-3 \omega_{y'} \omega_{z'}=\frac{3 g}{l} \sin \theta \sin \psi
$$
$$
5 \dot \omega_{y'}+3 \omega_{z'} \omega_{x'}=\frac{3 g}{l} \sin \theta \cos \psi
$$
$$
4 \dot \omega_{z'}=0
$$
The last equation implies
$$
\dot \omega_{z'}=0
$$
Using the kinematic relation for \omega_{z'} we have
$$
\omega_{z'}=\dot \psi+\dot \varphi \cos \theta
$$
Defining the spin velocity and precession rate gives
$$
 s=\dot \psi
$$
$$
 \Omega=\dot \varphi
$$
Hence the desired relation is
$$
\omega_{z'}=s+\Omega \cos \theta
$$
and \omega_{z'} is constant during steady precession
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given as a single equation in the form ω_{z'} = ..., and your response should be written with the variables s, Ω, θ only.

subquestions.subproblem: What must the spin velocity s be for the jack to spin stably around a vertical axis, i.e., theta=0? (Princeton)
subquestions.solution:
For a nearly vertical spin axis, use the small-angle approximations
$$
\sin \theta \approx \theta
$$
$$
\cos \theta \approx 1
$$
Combining the first two Euler equations appropriately yields the linearized equation of motion
$$
5 \ddot \theta+\left(2 \Omega s-3 \Omega^{2}-\frac{3 g}{l}\right) \theta=0
$$
with
$$
\Omega=\dot \varphi
$$
$$
 s=\dot \psi
$$
For stable spin at \theta=0, the coefficient of \theta must be positive
$$
2 \Omega s-3 \Omega^{2}-\frac{3 g}{l}>0
$$
which gives the required condition on the spin velocity
$$
 s>\frac{3 \Omega}{2}+\frac{3 g}{2 l \Omega}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be an inequality in the form s > ..., and your response should be written with the variables Ω, g, l only.

context: A propeller-driven airplane flies in a horizontal circle, counterclockwise when viewed from above, with a constant angular velocity χ with respect to an inertial frame. Its propeller turns at a constant angular velocity dψ/dt clockwise as seen by the pilot. Use an inertial frame Oxyz with the z-axis vertical up, and a rotating frame o x'y'z' fixed to the propeller with the x'-axis along the propeller spin axis and the z'-axis along a propeller blade. At the instant under consideration, take the x-axis to coincide with the x'-axis. The principal moments of inertia about x', y', z' are I1, I2, I3, respectively; for a flat, four-bladed propeller by symmetry I2 = I3, and define I = I2 = I3. Let ω denote the angular velocity of the propeller expressed in the rotating frame with components ω_{x'}, ω_{y'}, ω_{z'}. Let M denote the torque exerted on the propeller shaft with components M_{x'}, M_{y'}, M_{z'}. The propeller spin angle is ψ with ψ̇ = dψ/dt and ψ = ψ̇ t, and the airplane’s turn rate is χ.

subquestions.subproblem: For a flat,four-bladed propeller,what relations exist among the momentsof inertia?
subquestions.solution:
Choose the frames as stated in the context. By symmetry, these axes are principal axes and satisfy
$$I_2 = I$$
$$I_3 = I$$
$$I_1 = 2 I$$
The angular velocity components in the rotating frame are
$$\omega_{x'} = \dot{\psi}$$
$$\omega_{y'} = \chi \sin \psi$$
$$\omega_{z'} = \chi \cos \psi$$
with
$$\psi = \dot{\psi} t$$
Euler's equations about x', y', z' give
$$I_1 \frac{d\omega_{x'}}{dt} - (I_2 - I_3)\omega_{y'} \omega_{z'} = M_{x'}$$
$$I_2 \frac{d\omega_{y'}}{dt} - (I_3 - I_1)\omega_{z'} \omega_{x'} = M_{y'}$$
$$I_3 \frac{d\omega_{z'}}{dt} - (I_1 - I_2)\omega_{x'} \omega_{y'} = M_{z'}$$
With I_2 = I_3 and constant \chi and \(\dot{\psi}\), these yield
$$M_{x'} = 0$$
$$M_{y'} = 2 I \dot{\psi} \chi \cos (\dot{\psi} t)$$
$$M_{z'} = - 2 I \dot{\psi} \chi \sin (\dot{\psi} t)$$
The torque magnitude is
$$M = 2 I \dot{\psi} \chi$$
Equivalently,
$$M_{y'} = M \cos \psi$$
$$M_{z'} = - M \sin \psi$$
Thus M lies in the plane of the propeller and is directed along the y-axis of the fixed frame
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should provide the relations among the principal moments in the form I1 = ..., I2 = ..., I3 = ..., and your response should only use the symbols I1, I2, I3, I.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the magnitude and direction of the torque that must be applied to the propeller shaft by the bearings to maintain level flight in a circle.
subquestions.solution:
Let M_req denote the required torque magnitude. From part (a), the necessary torque is
$$M_{req} = 2 I \dot{\psi} \chi$$
Its components in the rotating frame are
$$M_{x'} = 0$$
$$M_{y'} = M_{req} \cos \psi$$
$$M_{z'} = - M_{req} \sin \psi$$
This torque lies in the plane of the propeller and is directed along the y-axis of the fixed frame
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should include both: (i) the torque magnitude in the form M_req = ..., and (ii) the torque components in the rotating frame in the form M_{x'} = ..., M_{y'} = ..., M_{z'} = .... The right-hand sides of your expressions should use only the symbols I, ψ̇, χ, ψ; do not use M_req on the right-hand side.

context: A perfectly uniform rigid ball of diameter 20 \unit{cm} and density 5 \unit{g/cm^3} rotates freely in space at 1 \unit{rev/s}. An intelligent flea of mass 10^{-3} \unit{g} lives in a small massless house fixed to the ball's surface at a rotational pole, as shown in Fig. 1.197. The flea quickly walks to latitude 45^{\circ} and waits there. Neglect the small precession during the flea's motion. How long should it wait so that the ball's equator passes through the house? Use the following definitions: R is the ball's radius, M is the ball's mass, m is the flea's mass, \rho is the ball's density, \omega is the angular speed magnitude before the flea moves, t is time, t_{wait} is the required waiting time, I_1=I_2 and I_3 are the principal moments of inertia about body axes Ox'y'z' with z' through the flea's new position, \omega_{x'}, \omega_{y'}, \omega_{z'} are the components of the angular velocity in the body frame, and \Omega is the body's torque-free precession rate about z'. Take an inertial frame Oxyz with z along the original \omega and a body-fixed frame Ox'y'z' attached to the ball with x and x' in the plane of z and z' at t=0, as in Fig. 1.198. The center of mass is at the ball's center O since m \ll M, and \omega at t=0 equals its value just before the flea moved.
solution:
With Ox'y'z' the new principal axes, Euler's equations for torque-free rotation are
$$
I_1 \frac{d\omega_{x'}}{dt} - \left(I_1 - I_3\right) \omega_{y'} \omega_{z'} = 0
$$
$$
I_1 \frac{d\omega_{y'}}{dt} - \left(I_3 - I_1\right) \omega_{z'} \omega_{x'} = 0
$$
$$
I_3 \frac{d\omega_{z'}}{dt} = 0
$$
From the last equation, \omega_{z'} is constant in time
$$
\omega_{z'} = \omega_{0 z'}
$$
Eliminating \omega_{y'} gives a simple harmonic equation for \omega_{x'}
$$
\frac{d^2 \omega_{x'}}{dt^2} + \Omega^2 \omega_{x'} = 0
$$
The precession rate is
$$
\Omega = \left|\frac{I_3 - I_1}{I_1}\right| \omega_{0 z'}
$$
A general solution for the transverse components is
$$
\omega_{x'} = A \cos\left(\Omega t + \phi\right)
$$
$$
\omega_{y'} = A \sin\left(\Omega t + \phi\right)
$$
where A and \phi are constants determined by the initial conditions. Because the flea sits at latitude 45^{\circ}, the axes z and z' are separated by 45^{\circ}, so at t=0 the components of \omega in the body frame are
$$
\omega_{0 x'} = - \frac{\omega}{\sqrt{2}}
$$
$$
\omega_{0 y'} = 0
$$
$$
\omega_{0 z'} = \frac{\omega}{\sqrt{2}}
$$
These initial conditions give
$$
A = \frac{\omega}{\sqrt{2}}
$$
$$
\phi = \pi
$$
Hence, for all t,
$$
\omega_{x'} = \frac{\omega}{\sqrt{2}} \cos\left(\Omega t + \pi\right)
$$
$$
\omega_{y'} = \frac{\omega}{\sqrt{2}} \sin\left(\Omega t + \pi\right)
$$
$$
\omega_{z'} = \frac{\omega}{\sqrt{2}}
$$
Thus \omega precesses about the z' axis with constant magnitude and constant \omega_{z'}. The precession rate can be written as
$$
\Omega = \left|\frac{I_3 - I_1}{I_1}\right| \frac{\omega}{\sqrt{2}}
$$
The equator passes through the flea's house when \omega is midway between the x' and z' axes, which requires
$$
\omega_{x'} = \frac{\omega}{\sqrt{2}}
$$
$$
\omega_{y'} = 0
$$
$$
\omega_{z'} = \frac{\omega}{\sqrt{2}}
$$
This occurs when
$$
\Omega t = \pi
$$
Therefore the required waiting time is
$$
 t_{wait} = \frac{\pi}{\Omega}
$$
Using the principal moments for a uniform sphere with a small point mass fixed on its surface, we have
$$
I_1 \approx \frac{2}{5} M R^2
$$
$$
I_3 - I_1 \approx - m R^2
$$
Hence
$$
\left|\frac{I_1}{I_3 - I_1}\right| \approx \frac{2 M R^2}{5 m R^2}
$$
$$
\frac{2 M R^2}{5 m R^2} = \frac{2 M}{5 m}
$$
Substituting into t_{wait} gives
$$
 t_{wait} = \frac{\sqrt{2} \pi}{\omega} \left|\frac{I_1}{I_3 - I_1}\right|
$$
$$
 t_{wait} \approx \frac{2 \sqrt{2} \pi}{5 \omega m} M
$$
With
$$
M = \frac{4}{3} \pi R^3 \rho
$$
and the data
$$
R = 10 \unit{cm}
$$
$$
\rho = 5 \unit{g/cm^3}
$$
$$
\omega = 2 \pi \unit{s^{-1}}
$$
$$
 m = 10^{-3} \unit{g}
$$
we obtain the numerical estimate
$$
 t_{wait} \approx 6 \times 10^6 \unit{s}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express t_wait as a numerical value in seconds. If an approximation is used, round your result to 1 significant figure.

context: A horizontal uniform bar of mass m and length 2a hangs by two parallel, inextensible strings of length 2a attached to its two ends. The strings are fixed at support points located at (a, 0, 2a) and (-a, 0, 2a) in a right-handed Cartesian frame (x, y, z). At t = 0 the bar lies along the x-axis in the plane z = 0 and is suddenly given an angular velocity ω about the vertical z-axis through its center. Let g be the acceleration due to gravity. Let h denote the maximum vertical rise of the bar's center of mass relative to its initial level. Let T(t) denote the tension in each string and let ΔT denote the initial increase in T over its static value mg/2. Let I be the moment of inertia of the bar about the vertical axis through its center. Let E denote the total mechanical energy. Let θ(t) be the angle the bar makes with the x-axis in the xy-plane, and z(t) be the height of the bar's center of mass. Define the end of the bar at x > 0 as point A and its corresponding support as A′, with coordinates A = (a cos θ, a sin θ, z) and A′ = (a, 0, 2a). Derivatives with respect to time t are written using d/dt. Calculate

subquestions.subproblem: the distance h to which the bar rises,
subquestions.solution:
Take the xy-plane as the reference level for potential energy. The total mechanical energy of the bar at t = 0, when it is given angular velocity ω, is
$$E = \frac{1}{2} I \omega^2$$
For a uniform bar of length 2a about a vertical axis through its center,
$$I = \frac{1}{3} m a^2$$
Thus
$$E = \frac{m a^2 \omega^2}{6}$$
At the highest position h the energy is purely gravitational potential energy, so
$$m g h = \frac{m a^2 \omega^2}{6}$$
Hence
$$h = \frac{a^2 \omega^2}{6 g}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form h = ... , and your response should only involve the variables a, ω, g.

subquestions.subproblem: the initial increase in tension in each string.
subquestions.solution:
Due to symmetry, the bar remains horizontal during the motion while it rotates about the z-axis. For one end A of the bar and its support A′, their coordinates are A = (a cos θ, a sin θ, z) and A′ = (a, 0, 2a). The string is inextensible, so the distance A A′ stays equal to 2a, giving
$$a^2 (1 - \cos \theta)^2 + a^2 \sin^2 \theta + (2 a - z)^2 = 4 a^2$$
This simplifies to
$$z^2 - 4 a z + 2 a^2 (1 - \cos \theta) = 0$$
Differentiating once with respect to time t gives
$$2 z \frac{dz}{dt} - 4 a \frac{dz}{dt} + 2 a^2 \sin \theta \frac{d\theta}{dt} = 0$$
Differentiating again with respect to time t gives
$$2 \left( \frac{dz}{dt} \right)^2 + 2 z \frac{d^2 z}{dt^2} - 4 a \frac{d^2 z}{dt^2} + 2 a^2 \left( \sin \theta \frac{d^2 \theta}{dt^2} + \cos \theta \left( \frac{d\theta}{dt} \right)^2 \right) = 0$$
Hence
$$\frac{d^2 z}{dt^2} = \frac{\left( \frac{dz}{dt} \right)^2 + a^2 \left( \sin \theta \frac{d^2 \theta}{dt^2} + \cos \theta \left( \frac{d\theta}{dt} \right)^2 \right)}{2 a - z}$$
At the initial instant
$$t = 0$$
$$\theta = 0$$
$$z = 0$$
$$\frac{dz}{dt} = 0$$
$$\frac{d\theta}{dt} = \omega$$
so
$$\frac{d^2 z}{dt^2} = \frac{1}{2} a \omega^2$$
The total vertical force on the bar is therefore increased by
$$m \frac{d^2 z}{dt^2}$$
Since the two strings share this equally, the initial increase in the tension of each string is
$$\Delta T = \frac{1}{2} m \frac{d^2 z}{dt^2}$$
Thus
$$\Delta T = \frac{1}{4} m a \omega^2$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form ΔT = ... , and your response should only involve the variables m, a, ω.

context: A string is stretched between two rigid supports that are 100 cm apart. Let the string length be L and the wavelengths corresponding to the only excitable frequencies in the 100 Hz to 350 Hz range, namely 160 Hz, 240 Hz, and 320 Hz, be λ_0, λ_1, and λ_2, respectively. The string has fixed ends, so it supports standing waves with mode index n, a positive integer. Determine λ_0, λ_1, and λ_2.
solution:
For a string with fixed ends, the allowed wavelengths satisfy n λ = 2L, where n is a positive integer and L is the string length

$$
L = 100 \unit{cm}
$$

Let the wavelengths corresponding to 160 \unit{Hz}, 240 \unit{Hz}, and 320 \unit{Hz} be λ_0, λ_1, and λ_2, respectively. Then

$$
n \lambda_0 = 2L
$$

$$
(n+1) \lambda_1 = 2L
$$

$$
(n+2) \lambda_2 = 2L
$$

Since the wave speed is the same for all modes, f λ is constant for these three modes, so

$$
160 \unit{Hz} \lambda_0 = 240 \unit{Hz} \lambda_1
$$

$$
240 \unit{Hz} \lambda_1 = 320 \unit{Hz} \lambda_2
$$

Hence

$$
n = 2
$$

Therefore

$$
\lambda_0 = 100 \unit{cm}
$$

$$
\lambda_1 = 67 \unit{cm}
$$

$$
\lambda_2 = 50 \unit{cm}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express λ_0, λ_1, and λ_2 as numerical values with units of cm, written in the form λ_0 = ..., λ_1 = ..., λ_2 = ....

context: A taut string of length l, linear mass density rho (mass per unit length), and uniform tension F is considered. Let y(x,t) denote the transverse displacement of the string, and let theta(x,t) be the small angle the string makes with the x-axis. Let v be the wave speed along the string, lambda the wavelength of a standing wave, and omega the angular frequency of a vibrational mode. Consider a short segment of horizontal length Delta x and arc length Delta l; the tensions at its two ends have magnitudes F_1 and F_2, directed tangentially to the string and making angles theta and theta+Delta theta with the x-axis, respectively. Let f_x and f_y denote the x- and y-components of the net force on this short segment. In the small-oscillation limit, |theta| is small and Delta l approximates Delta x. For standing-wave modes with fixed ends, the boundaries are at x=0 and x=l.

subquestions.subproblem: Give the equation which relates the fundamental frequency of a string to the physical and geometrical properties of the string. Use omega for the fundamental angular frequency, l for the string length, F for the tension, and rho for the linear mass density.
subquestions.solution: $$\omega=\frac{\pi}{l}\sqrt{\frac{F}{\rho}}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form omega = ..., and your response should use only the variables l, F, and rho.

subquestions.subproblem: Derive your result from Newton's equations by analyzing a small section of the string undergoing small transverse oscillations.
subquestions.solution:
Consider a small segment of the string of horizontal length Delta x and arc length Delta l. Let the tensions at its two ends have magnitudes F_1 and F_2 and make angles theta and theta+Delta theta with the x-axis, respectively. The x-component of the net force on the segment is zero for small oscillations
$$f_x=F_2\cos(\theta+\Delta\theta)-F_1\cos\theta$$
Using a first-order expansion for small angles
$$f_x\approx (F_2-F_1)\cos\theta - F_2\Delta\theta\sin\theta$$
To first order in small quantities
$$f_x\approx F_2-F_1$$
Hence
$$F_2\approx F_1$$
Denote this common magnitude by F to first order. The y-component of the net force on the segment is
$$f_y=F\sin(\theta+\Delta\theta)-F\sin\theta$$
Using a first-order expansion
$$f_y\approx F\frac{d\sin\theta}{d\theta}\Delta\theta$$
Therefore
$$f_y=F\cos\theta\frac{d\theta}{dx}\Delta x$$
For small angles
$$f_y\approx F\frac{d\theta}{dx}\Delta x$$
The small-slope relations are
$$\theta\approx\frac{dy}{dx}$$
$$\frac{d\theta}{dx}=\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$$
Newton's second law for the segment gives
$$\rho\Delta l\frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial t^2}=f_y$$
Substituting the expression for f_y and using Delta l\approx Delta x yields
$$\rho\Delta l\frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial t^2}=F\frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial x^2}\Delta x$$
Canceling the common factor and using Delta l\approx Delta x leads to the wave equation
$$\frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial x^2}-\frac{\rho}{F}\frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial t^2}=0$$
The wave speed is
$$v=\sqrt{\frac{F}{\rho}}$$
For the fundamental mode with fixed ends, the wavelength is
$$\lambda=2l$$
The angular frequency of the fundamental mode is
$$\omega=\frac{\2\pi v}{\lambda}$$
Using lambda=2l gives
$$\omega=\frac{\pi v}{l}$$
Substituting v=\sqrt{F/\rho} gives
$$\omega=\frac{\pi}{l}\sqrt{\frac{F}{\rho}}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form omega = ..., and your response should use only the variables l, F, and rho.

grading_standard.formula: $$\rho\Delta l\frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial t^2}=F\frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial x^2}\Delta x$$

context: A violin string of length L is fastened at both ends. The fundamental (open string) frequency is f_0. The violinist bows the string at a distance L/4 from one end and touches the string lightly at the midpoint L/2. Let lambda_0 denote the wavelength corresponding to f_0 for the open string. Under the imposed bowing and touching conditions, let lambda denote the allowed wavelength of an excited mode. Let f_min denote the lowest frequency that can be excited under these conditions, and let f_1 denote the frequency of the first overtone under these conditions. All answers should be expressed in terms of f_0.

subquestions.subproblem: Under these conditions,what is the lowest frequency he can excite? Sketch the shape of the string.
subquestions.solution: For the open string, the wavelength corresponding to f_0 satisfies $$\lambda_0/2=L$$ When the violinist bows at L/4 from one end and touches the string at L/2, the former point is a node and the latter point an antinode, so the allowed wavelength is $$\lambda=L$$ Using the inverse proportionality of frequency and wavelength for standing waves, $$\frac{f_{\min}}{f_0}=\frac{\lambda_0}{\lambda}$$ Hence the lowest frequency is $$f_{\min}=2 f_0$$ The string shape is as shown in Fig. 1.204 under these constraints
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of f_min = ..., and your response should be written with f_min and f_0 only.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the frequency of the first overtone under these conditions? (Wisconsin)
subquestions.solution: The frequency of the first overtone is $$f_1=4 f_0$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of f_1 = ..., and your response should be written with f_1 and f_0 only.

context: A guitar string is fixed at both ends and vibrates in its fundamental mode. The string length is l = 80 cm, the fundamental frequency is f = 400 Hz, the maximum transverse displacement at the middle is y0 = 2 cm, and the tension is T = 10^6 dyne. Use Cartesian coordinates with the x-axis along the equilibrium position of the string and the origin at the left support x = 0. Let y(x,t) be the transverse displacement at position x and time t. Let θ(x,t) be the small angle that the string makes with the x-axis; at the support we write θ(t) = θ(0,t). The component of the force on the left support that is perpendicular to the equilibrium position is denoted F_y(t). Assume small slopes so that sin θ ≈ θ ≈ ∂y/∂x. Let v be the wave speed, λ the wavelength, and ω the angular frequency, with λ = 2l in the fundamental mode. Find the maximum value F_{y,max} of F_y(t).
solution:
For small slopes at the support, the perpendicular force satisfies

$$
F_y(t) = T \sin \theta(t)
$$

With the small-angle approximation,

$$
\theta(t) \approx \frac{\partial y}{\partial x}(0,t)
$$

Therefore,

$$
F_y(t) \approx T \frac{\partial y}{\partial x}(0,t)
$$

In the fundamental mode,

$$
\lambda = 2 l
$$

The angular frequency is

$$
\omega = \frac{2 \pi v}{\lambda}
$$

A suitable sinusoidal form consistent with \lambda = 2l is

$$
y(x,t) = y_0 \sin\Big( \omega t - \frac{\pi x}{l} \Big)
$$

The spatial derivative is

$$
\frac{\partial y}{\partial x} = - y_0 \frac{\pi}{l} \cos\Big( \omega t - \frac{\pi x}{l} \Big)
$$

Evaluated at the support x = 0,

$$
\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}(0,t) = - y_0 \frac{\pi}{l} \cos(\omega t)
$$

Hence,

$$
F_y(t) = T \frac{\partial y}{\partial x}(0,t)
$$

$$
F_y(t) = - \frac{\pi T y_0}{l} \cos(\omega t)
$$

With the given data,

$$
y_0 = 2 \unit{cm}
$$

$$
l = 80 \unit{cm}
$$

Thus,

$$
F_y(t) = - \frac{2 \pi T}{80} \cos(\omega t)
$$

The maximum magnitude is

$$
F_{y,\max} = \frac{\pi T}{40}
$$

With the given tension,

$$
T = 10^6 \unit{dyne}
$$

Therefore,

$$
F_{y,\max} = \frac{\pi}{40} \times 10^6 \unit{dyne}
$$

$$
F_{y,\max} \approx 7.85 \times 10^4 \unit{dyne}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express F_{y,max} as a numerical value with units of dyne, written in the form 'F_{y,max} = [value] dyne', rounded to 3 significant figures.

context: A transverse traveling sinusoidal wave on a long stretched wire with mass per unit length \(\rho\) (SI units \unit{kg/m}) has angular frequency \(\omega\) (SI units \unit{rad/s}) and wave speed \(c\) (SI units \unit{m/s}). The maximum transverse displacement amplitude is \(y_0\) with \(y_0 \ll \lambda\), where \(\lambda\) is the wavelength, and the wave propagates in the +\(x\) direction. Let \(y(x,t)\) denote the transverse displacement at position \(x\) (SI units \unit{m}) and time \(t\) (SI units \unit{s}). Let \(E\) denote the energy per unit length (energy density) along the wire, \(P\) the power transmitted along the wire, and \(F_y(t)\) the transverse force applied at \(x=0\) by the generator. Let \(\Delta_t\) denote a time interval.

subquestions.subproblem: Write an expression for the displacement y as a function of t and x, where x is distance measured along the wire.
subquestions.solution: $$y(x,t)=y_0 \sin[\omega(t-x/c)]$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form y(x,t) = [expression], and your response should be written only with the variables y_0, \omega, x, t, c.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the energy density (energy/unit length)?
subquestions.solution: Every point the wave travels through undergoes simple harmonic motion. For the displacement in part (a), the time derivative is $$\frac{\partial y}{\partial t}=\omega y_0 \cos[\omega(t-x/c)]$$ The maximum vibrational speed is \(\omega y_0\). For an element of the wire from \(x\) to \(x+\Delta x\), its mass is $$\Delta m=\rho \Delta x$$ The total mechanical energy of that element equals the maximum kinetic energy $$\Delta E=\frac{1}{2}\Delta m \, \omega^{2} y_0^{2}$$ Hence the energy per unit length is $$E=\frac{1}{2}\rho \omega^{2} y_0^{2}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form E = [expression], and your response should be written only with the variables \rho, \omega, y_0.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the power transmitted along the wire?
subquestions.solution: As the wave travels at speed \(c\), the energy crossing a point in time \(\Delta_t\) is \(E c \Delta_t\). Hence the power is $$P=E c$$ Using the result from part (b) gives $$P=\frac{1}{2}\rho c \omega^{2} y_0^{2}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form P = [expression], and your response should be written only with the variables \rho, c, \omega, y_0.

subquestions.subproblem: If the wave is generated by a mechanical device at x = 0 find the transverse force F_y(t) that it exerts on the wire.
subquestions.solution: The tension \(T\) in the string satisfies $$c=\sqrt{\frac{T}{\rho}}$$ The transverse force applied at \(x=0\) is $$F_y(t)=-T \left(\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}\right)_{x=0}$$ From part (a), the spatial derivative is $$\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}=-\frac{\omega}{c} y_0 \cos[\omega(t-x/c)]$$ Therefore $$F_y(t)=\rho c \omega y_0 \cos(\omega t)$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form F_y(t) = [expression], and your response should be written only with the variables \rho, c, \omega, y_0, t.

context: A piano string of length l is fixed at both ends. The string has linear mass density sigma and is under tension T. Let y(x,t) denote the transverse displacement of a point located at position x along the string at time t, where 0 \leq x \leq l. The wave speed is v = \sqrt{T/\sigma}. In the separation-of-variables method we write y(x,t) = X(x) A(t) with separation constant k. Mode indices n and m denote positive integers. The nth-mode period, frequency, and wavelength are denoted by T_n, \nu_n, and \lambda_n, respectively. In part (b) the string is initially displaced by a small distance s at x = l/2 so that s \ll l, forming an isosceles triangle, and then released from rest. The coefficients A_n and B_n are Fourier sine series coefficients for the normal modes.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the allowed solutions for the vibrations of the string. What are the allowed frequencies and wavelengths?
subquestions.solution:
The vibration of the string is governed by the wave equation
$$
\frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial x^2} - \frac{\sigma}{T} \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial t^2} = 0
$$
subject to the boundary conditions
$$
y(0,t) = 0
$$
$$
y(l,t) = 0
$$
Assume a separable solution
$$
y(x,t) = X(x) A(t)
$$
Substitution gives
$$
\frac{1}{X} \frac{d^2 X}{dx^2} = \frac{\sigma}{T A} \frac{d^2 A}{dt^2}
$$
Each side must equal a constant, chosen as
$$
-k^2
$$
The resulting ordinary differential equations are
$$
\frac{d^2 X}{dx^2} + k^2 X = 0
$$
$$
\frac{d^2 A}{dt^2} + v^2 k^2 A = 0
$$
with
$$
v = \sqrt{\frac{T}{\sigma}}
$$
The general solutions are
$$
X(x) = c_1 \cos(kx) + c_2 \sin(kx)
$$
$$
A(t) = b_1 \cos(v k t) + b_2 \sin(v k t)
$$
Applying the boundary conditions X(0) = 0 and X(l) = 0 gives
$$
c_1 = 0
$$
$$
\sin(k l) = 0
$$
Hence
$$
k l = n \pi
$$
for
$$
n = 1,2,3,\ldots
$$
Thus the allowed general solution is
$$
y(x,t) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left[ A_n \cos\left( \frac{n \pi v t}{l} \right) + B_n \sin\left( \frac{n \pi v t}{l} \right) \right] \sin\left( \frac{n \pi x}{l} \right)
$$
The period of the nth mode is
$$
T_n = \frac{2 l}{n v}
$$
The frequency of the nth mode is
$$
\nu_n = \frac{1}{T_n}
$$
$$
\nu_n = \frac{n v}{2 l}
$$
$$
\nu_n = \frac{n}{2 l} \sqrt{\frac{T}{\sigma}}
$$
The wavelength of the nth mode is
$$
\lambda_n = \frac{v}{\nu_n}
$$
$$
\lambda_n = \frac{2 l}{n}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should include: (i) the normal-mode expansion written in the form y(x,t) = sum_{n=1}^infty [A_n cos(...) + B_n sin(...)] sin(...); write it only with the symbols A_n, B_n, n, π, v, l, x, t. (ii) the nth allowed frequency in the form ν_n = ..., written only with n, v, l. (iii) the nth allowed wavelength in the form λ_n = ..., written only with n, l. Do not introduce any additional symbols.

subquestions.subproblem: At time t = 0 the string is pulled a distance s from equilibrium at its midpoint so that it forms an isosceles triangle and is then released (s \ll l; see Fig. 1.208). Find the ensuing motion of the string using the Fourier analysis method.
subquestions.solution:
The initial displacement is
$$
s \ll l
$$
On 0 \leq x \leq \frac{l}{2} we have
$$
y(x,0) = \frac{2 s x}{l}
$$
On \frac{l}{2} \leq x \leq l we have
$$
y(x,0) = \frac{2 s (l - x)}{l}
$$
The initial velocity is
$$
\left. \frac{\partial y}{\partial t} \right|_{t=0} = 0
$$
Hence
$$
B_n = 0
$$
Expand the initial shape in the sine series
$$
y(x,0) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} A_n \sin\left( \frac{n \pi x}{l} \right)
$$
Multiply by \sin(m \pi x / l) and integrate over 0 \leq x \leq l to get
$$
A_m = \frac{2}{l} \int_0^l y(x,0) \sin\left( \frac{m \pi x}{l} \right) dx
$$
Split the integral at x = l/2
$$
A_m = \frac{2}{l} \left[ \int_0^{l/2} \frac{2 s x}{l} \sin\left( \frac{m \pi x}{l} \right) dx + \int_{l/2}^{l} \frac{2 s (l - x)}{l} \sin\left( \frac{m \pi x}{l} \right) dx \right]
$$
Use the identities
$$
\int x \sin(a x) dx = \frac{\sin(a x)}{a^2} - \frac{x \cos(a x)}{a}
$$
$$
\int_0^l \sin\left( \frac{n \pi x}{l} \right) \sin\left( \frac{m \pi x}{l} \right) dx = 0 \quad \text{for} \quad n \neq m
$$
$$
\int_0^l \sin^2\left( \frac{m \pi x}{l} \right) dx = \frac{l}{2}
$$
Carrying out the calculation yields
$$
A_m = \frac{8 s}{(m \pi)^2} \sin\left( \frac{m \pi}{2} \right)
$$
Therefore, the motion of the string is
$$
y(x,t) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{8 s}{(n \pi)^2} \sin\left( \frac{n \pi}{2} \right) \cos\left( \frac{n \pi v t}{l} \right) \sin\left( \frac{n \pi x}{l} \right)
$$
with
$$
v = \sqrt{\frac{T}{\sigma}}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be a single Fourier-sine series for the motion in the form y(x,t) = sum_{n=1}^infty C_n cos(...) sin(...), where the coefficient C_n = ... is written only in terms of s, n, and π. Your response should use only the symbols s, n, π, v, l, x, t (and numerical constants as needed). Do not introduce any additional symbols.

grading_standard.formula: $$A(t) = b_1 \cos(v k t) + b_2 \sin(v k t)$$
$$y(x,t) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left[ A_n \cos\left( \frac{n \pi v t}{l} \right) + B_n \sin\left( \frac{n \pi v t}{l} \right) \right] \sin\left( \frac{n \pi x}{l} \right)$$
$$A_m = \frac{2}{l} \left[ \int_0^{l/2} \frac{2 s x}{l} \sin\left( \frac{m \pi x}{l} \right) dx + \int_{l/2}^{l} \frac{2 s (l - x)}{l} \sin\left( \frac{m \pi x}{l} \right) dx \right]$$

context: A spring of rest length X and force constant k has total mass m. One end is fixed at x=0 and the other end at x=X is attached to a point mass M. The spring lies horizontally, and M moves on a frictionless surface. Let x denote the coordinate along the spring from the fixed end. Let \xi(x,t) be the longitudinal displacement field of the spring measured from equilibrium. Let a be the cross-sectional area of the spring and \sigma its Young's modulus. Define K_0 = a \sigma and the mass density per unit length \rho = m/X. The fixed-end boundary condition is \xi(0,t) = 0. The end x = X is attached to M, so the boundary condition there follows from Newton's second law for M. The wave speed along the spring is denoted by v, the angular frequency by \omega, the phase by \varphi, and the wavenumber by K. When solving the spatial equation, A and B denote constants of integration.

subquestions.subproblem: Derive a wave equation for longitudinal oscillation of this system.
subquestions.solution:
Consider a small section of the spring of length \Delta x extending from x to x + \Delta x. The tensile force in the spring at position x is
$$
F(x,t) = K_0 \frac{\partial \xi}{\partial x}(x,t)
$$
The net force on the section [x, x + \Delta x] is
$$
F(x+\Delta x,t) - F(x,t)
$$
By Newton's second law, this equals
$$
\rho \Delta x \frac{\partial^2 \xi}{\partial t^2}(x,t)
$$
Dividing by \Delta x and taking the limit \Delta x \to 0 gives
$$
\frac{\partial^2 \xi}{\partial t^2} = \frac{K_0}{\rho} \frac{\partial^2 \xi}{\partial x^2}
$$
Using \rho = m/X, this can be written as
$$
\frac{\partial^2 \xi}{\partial x^2} - \frac{m}{K_0 X} \frac{\partial^2 \xi}{\partial t^2} = 0
$$
The wave speed is
$$
v = \sqrt{\frac{K_0}{\rho}}
$$
Using \rho = m/X, this becomes
$$
v = \sqrt{\frac{K_0 X}{m}}
$$
With k = K_0/X, we also have
$$
k = \frac{K_0}{X}
$$
Hence
$$
v = X \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \(\frac{\partial^2 \xi}{\partial t^2} = \;\cdots\; \frac{\partial^2 \xi}{\partial x^2}\), and your response should be written with \(\xi, x, t, K_0, \rho\).

subquestions.subproblem: Find the frequency of the lowest mode as a function of mass for the case where M and k are finite and m \ll M (Princeton).
subquestions.solution:
Try a separable solution of the form
$$
\xi(x,t) = \xi_0(x) \cos(\omega t + \varphi)
$$
Substitution into the wave equation yields
$$
\frac{d^2 \xi_0}{dx^2} + K^2 \xi_0 = 0
$$
with
$$
K^2 = \frac{m \omega^2}{K_0 X}
$$
and
$$
K^2 = \frac{\omega^2}{v^2}
$$
The general solution is
$$
\xi_0(x) = A \sin(Kx) + B \cos(Kx)
$$
The fixed-end boundary condition is
$$
\xi(0,t) = 0
$$
which implies
$$
\xi_0(0) = 0
$$
so
$$
B = 0
$$
At x = X, Newton's second law for the attached mass M gives
$$
M \frac{\partial^2 \xi}{\partial t^2}(X,t) = - K_0 \frac{\partial \xi}{\partial x}(X,t)
$$
Using the assumed time dependence, the frequency condition becomes
$$
K X \tan(K X) = \frac{m}{M}
$$
For m \ll M and the lowest mode, use the approximation
$$
\tan(K X) = K X
$$
which gives
$$
\frac{\omega^2 m}{k} = \frac{m}{M}
$$
Hence the lowest angular frequency is
$$
\omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{M}}
$$
For a more accurate approximation, use
$$
\tan(K X) = K X + \frac{1}{3} (K X)^3
$$
Retaining these terms gives
$$
(K X)^2 = \frac{m}{M} \left[ 1 + \frac{1}{3} (K X)^2 \right]^{-1}
$$
Approximating the inverse to first order yields
$$
(K X)^2 = \frac{m}{M} \left[ 1 - \frac{1}{3} (K X)^2 \right]
$$
Solving for K^2 gives
$$
K^2 = \frac{3 m}{(3 M + m) X^2}
$$
Therefore
$$
\omega = \sqrt{\frac{3 k}{3 M + m}}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \(\omega = \;\cdots\), and your response should be written with \(k, M, m\).

context: Consider small transverse oscillations y(x,t) of a light, flexible string of length l and uniform mass per unit length ρ. Let x measure distance along the string from the end attached to a vertical pole at x=0 to the other end at x=l. Let T(x) denote the static tension distribution along the string. Let τ denote a constant end tension when the string is held at both ends under uniform tension. Let F_y(x) denote the internal transverse force in the string at position x. Let Δx denote a small element of string length used for force balance. In the rotating case, let ω be the angular frequency of steady rotation about the pole, and let Ω be the angular eigenfrequency of a small transverse oscillation about the steady configuration. Define the dimensionless coordinate ξ = x/l. Let P_n(ξ) denote the Legendre polynomial of integer degree n. Unless otherwise stated, gravity is neglected, oscillations are small, and y is measured perpendicular to the x-axis.

subquestions.subproblem: Suppose you have a string of uniform mass per unit length ρ and length l held at both ends under tension τ. Set up the equation for small transverse oscillations of the string and then find the eigenfrequencies.
subquestions.solution:
We have
$$F_y(x+\Delta x) - F_y(x) = \bigl(T \frac{\partial y}{\partial x}\bigr)_{x+\Delta x} - \bigl(T \frac{\partial y}{\partial x}\bigr)_x$$
$$F_y(x+\Delta x) - F_y(x) \approx \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\bigl[\frac{1}{2} \rho \omega^2 (l^2 - x^2) \frac{\partial y}{\partial x}\bigr] \Delta x$$
Newton's second law gives
$$\rho \Delta x \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial t^2} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\bigl[\frac{1}{2} \rho \omega^2 (l^2 - x^2) \frac{\partial y}{\partial x}\bigr] \Delta x$$
or
$$\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\bigl[(l^2 - x^2) \frac{\partial y}{\partial x}\bigr] = \frac{2}{\omega^2} \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial t^2}$$
for small transverse oscillations
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Provide two parts: (i) the governing PDE for the small transverse oscillations as a single equation relating y(x,t), its derivatives with respect to x and t, and the parameters τ and ρ only. Use only the symbols x, t, y, τ, and ρ. (ii) the eigenfrequencies as a single explicit formula in the form Ω_n = ..., written using only τ, ρ, l, and n.

subquestions.subproblem: Now consider the case where the string is free at one end and attached to a vertical pole at the other end, and is rotating about the pole at an angular frequency ω (neglect gravity) as shown in Fig. 1.211. Set up the equation for small transverse oscillations for this case.
subquestions.solution:
Take a rotating frame Oxyz attached to the string with the y-axis along the axis of rotation and the x-axis along the string. There is a fictitious centrifugal force acting on the string which is balanced by the tension. Consider a section Δx of the string. The difference of tension across its ends is
$$-\Delta T = \rho \Delta x \, x \omega^2$$
whence
$$\frac{dT}{dx} = - \rho \omega^2 x$$
Integrating and applying the boundary condition at the free end, we have
$$T(x=l) = 0$$
which gives
$$T(x) = \frac{1}{2} \rho \omega^2 (l^2 - x^2)$$
Following the procedure of part (a), the small transverse oscillations obey
$$\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\bigl[(l^2 - x^2) \frac{\partial y}{\partial x}\bigr] = \frac{2}{\omega^2} \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial t^2}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be the governing partial differential equation for y(x,t) in the rotating, free-end case, written as a single equation involving only the symbols x, t, y, l, and ω.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the eigenfrequencies. (Hint: the equation you get should look familiar in terms of the Legendre polynomials.) (CUSPEA)
subquestions.solution:
Try a solution of the type
$$y(x,t) = y(x) e^{-i \Omega t}$$
Let
$$\xi = \frac{x}{l}$$
The above equation then becomes
$$(1 - \xi^2) \frac{d^2 y}{d \xi^2} - 2 \xi \frac{d y}{d \xi} + \frac{2 \Omega^2}{\omega^2} y = 0$$
This differential equation has finite solutions if
$$\frac{2 \Omega^2}{\omega^2} = n(n+1)$$
The equation is Legendre's differential equation and the solutions are Legendre polynomials P_n(ξ). Thus the eigenfrequencies are
$$\frac{\Omega}{2 \pi} = \frac{\omega}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\frac{1}{2} n(n+1)}$$
We must also satisfy the boundary condition at the pole
$$y(0,t) = 0$$
This limits the allowable n to odd integers because
$$P_n(0) = 0$$
only for odd n, hence
$$n = 1, 3, 5, \dots$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should consist of two algebraic statements: (i) an explicit formula in the form Ω = ..., using only ω and n; and (ii) the allowed values of n specified using set notation in the form n ∈ {1, 3, 5, …}.

grading_standard.formula: $$F_y(x+\Delta x) - F_y(x) = \bigl(T \frac{\partial y}{\partial x}\bigr)_{x+\Delta x} - \bigl(T \frac{\partial y}{\partial x}\bigr)_x$$
$$F_y(x+\Delta x) - F_y(x) \approx \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\bigl[\frac{1}{2} \rho \omega^2 (l^2 - x^2) \frac{\partial y}{\partial x}\bigr] \Delta x$$
$$\rho \Delta x \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial t^2} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\bigl[\frac{1}{2} \rho \omega^2 (l^2 - x^2) \frac{\partial y}{\partial x}\bigr] \Delta x$$
$$\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\bigl[(l^2 - x^2) \frac{\partial y}{\partial x}\bigr] = \frac{2}{\omega^2} \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial t^2}$$
$$\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\bigl[(l^2 - x^2) \frac{\partial y}{\partial x}\bigr] = \frac{2}{\omega^2} \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial t^2}$$

context: A long, uniform string of linear mass density μ is held under constant tension T. Small-amplitude transverse waves of angular frequency ω propagate along the string from left to right. At x=0, a point mass m is attached to the string. Let R denote the fraction of the incident energy flux that is reflected by the inhomogeneity. In part (b), the point mass m is replaced by a short string segment of length l and linear mass density μ_m with μ_m >> μ; its mass equals m, so an equivalent length λ is defined by λ = m / μ_m. The wave speed on the uniform string is v = sqrt(T/μ).

subquestions.subproblem: Calculate the fraction R of the incident energy that is reflected by the point mass m.
subquestions.solution: $$R=\frac{m^2 \omega^2}{4 T \mu + m^2 \omega^2}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of R = ..., and your response should be written with T, μ, m, ω.

subquestions.subproblem: Suppose that the point mass m is replaced by a short string segment of linear density μ_m >> μ and length l such that λ = m / μ_m. For what range of l values (for fixed m) does the answer for part (a) remain approximately correct?
subquestions.solution: $$l \ll \frac{2 \pi}{\omega} \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given as an inequality for l in the form l << ..., and your response should be written with T, μ, ω.

context: A perfectly flexible string with uniform linear mass density ρ and length L hangs from a fixed support at x=0 with its bottom end free at x=L, as in Fig. 1.214. Use a right-handed coordinate system Oxyz with the x-axis directed downward along the string. Let y(x,t) denote the small transverse displacement of the string in one plane, t is time, T(x) is the tension in the string at position x, and g is the gravitational acceleration. For separation of variables, write y(x,t)=ξ(x)τ(t), where ξ(x) is the spatial mode shape and τ(t) is the time-dependent amplitude. Let λ>0 be the separation constant determined by the boundary conditions. The boundary conditions for the transverse motion are y(0,t)=0 (top fixed) and y(L,t) is finite (bottom end free). In part (b), a power-series solution ξ(x)=∑ a_n (x−L)^n about x=L is used, with coefficients a_n determined by a recurrence. Define f(z)=∑_{n=0}^{∞} (-1)^n z^n/(n!)^2, and use Newton's method α_{k+1}=α_k−f(α_k)/f'(α_k) to approximate the smallest positive root of f(λL)=0, where α_k denotes successive approximations to λL. Let ν be the oscillation frequency in hertz, and ν_min the frequency of the lowest normal mode. Constants A and B denote arbitrary constants determined by initial conditions. Let Δx denote a small element length of the string used in the derivation.

subquestions.subproblem: Derive the partial differential equation describing small transverse (in one plane) oscillations of the string, and from it, the differential equation for the form of the normal modes.
subquestions.solution:
For a small element of length Δx, Newton's second law gives
$$
ρ Δx \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial t^2} = \bigl[T \frac{\partial y}{\partial x}\bigr]_{x+Δx} - \bigl[T \frac{\partial y}{\partial x}\bigr]_x
$$
Dividing by Δx and taking the limit Δx→0 yields
$$
ρ \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial t^2} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x} \left( T \frac{\partial y}{\partial x} \right)
$$
The tension at position x equals the weight of the portion below x
$$
T(x) = \int_x^L ρ g dx
$$
$$
T(x) = ρ g (L - x)
$$
Substituting T(x) into the equation of motion gives the PDE for small transverse oscillations
$$
\frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial t^2} = g \frac{\partial}{\partial x} \left[ (L - x) \frac{\partial y}{\partial x} \right]
$$
Use separation of variables y(x,t)=ξ(x)τ(t)
$$
\frac{1}{g τ} \frac{d^2 τ}{d t^2} = \frac{1}{ξ} \frac{d}{d x} \left[ (L - x) \frac{d ξ}{d x} \right]
$$
Each side depends on a different variable, so set both equal to a constant −λ with λ>0
$$
\frac{d}{d x} \left[ (L - x) \frac{d ξ}{d x} \right] + λ ξ = 0
$$
$$
\frac{d^2 τ}{d t^2} + λ g τ = 0
$$
The boundary conditions are
$$
y(0,t) = 0
$$
with y(L,t) finite, which imply
$$
ξ(0) = 0
$$
with ξ(L) finite
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should include: (i) the governing PDE written explicitly as an equality between derivatives of y using only the symbols y, x, t, g, and L; (ii) the separated spatial ODE written using only ξ, x, L, and λ; (iii) the separated temporal ODE written using only τ, t, g, and λ; and (iv) the boundary conditions stated in the form ξ(0) = 0 with ξ(L) finite.

subquestions.subproblem: Solve this differential equation using standard power-series methods (do not transform it into Bessel's equation), and, using approximate numerical methods, solve for the frequency of the lowest normal mode. (Princeton)
subquestions.solution:
The ξ-equation can be written as
$$
(x - L) \frac{d^2 ξ}{d x^2} + \frac{d ξ}{d x} - λ ξ = 0
$$
Seek a power series about x=L
$$
ξ(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n (x - L)^n
$$
Differentiate termwise
$$
\frac{d ξ}{d x} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} (n+1) a_{n+1} (x - L)^n
$$
$$
\frac{d^2 ξ}{d x^2} = \sum_{n=2}^{\infty} n (n-1) a_n (x - L)^{n-2}
$$
Multiply by (x−L)
$$
(x - L) \frac{d^2 ξ}{d x^2} = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n (n+1) a_{n+1} (x - L)^n
$$
Substitute into the ODE and equate coefficients
$$
(a_1 - λ a_0) + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \bigl[(n+1)^2 a_{n+1} - λ a_n\bigr] (x - L)^n = 0
$$
Thus the recurrence relations are
$$
a_1 = λ a_0
$$
$$
a_{n+1} = \frac{λ}{(n+1)^2} a_n
$$
The first few coefficients are
$$
a_2 = \frac{λ}{2^2} a_1
$$
$$
a_1 = λ a_0
$$
$$
a_2 = \frac{λ^2}{2^2} a_0
$$
$$
a_3 = \frac{λ}{3^2} a_2
$$
$$
a_2 = \frac{λ}{2^2} a_1
$$
$$
a_1 = λ a_0
$$
$$
a_3 = \frac{λ^3}{(3 \cdot 2)^2} a_0
$$
In general
$$
a_n = \frac{λ^n}{(n!)^2} a_0
$$
Hence
$$
ξ(x) = a_0 \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{λ^n}{(n!)^2} (x - L)^n
$$
The boundary condition ξ(0)=0 gives
$$
f(λ L) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^n (λ L)^n}{(n!)^2}
$$
$$
f(λ L) = 0
$$
An explicit expansion begins as
$$
f(λ L) = 1 - λ L + \frac{1}{4} λ^2 L^2 - \cdots
$$
For an approximate solution, truncate at n=2
$$
f(λ L) \approx 1 - λ L + \frac{1}{4} (λ L)^2
$$
Use Newton's method
$$
α_{k+1} = α_k - \frac{f(α_k)}{f'(α_k)}
$$
For the truncated polynomial
$$
f'(λ L) \approx -1 + \frac{1}{2} λ L
$$
Starting with
$$
α_1 = 0
$$
we obtain
$$
α_2 = 1
$$
$$
f(α_2) \approx \frac{1}{4}
$$
$$
α_3 = 1 - \frac{\frac{1}{4}}{-\frac{1}{2}}
$$
$$
α_3 = \frac{3}{2}
$$
$$
f(α_3) \approx \frac{1}{16}
$$
Therefore the smallest positive root is approximated by
$$
λ_{\min} = \frac{3}{2 L}
$$
For this mode the time dependence is
$$
τ(t) = A \cos(\sqrt{λ g} t) + B \sin(\sqrt{λ g} t)
$$
The corresponding frequency of the lowest normal mode is
$$
ν_{\min} \approx \frac{1}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\frac{3 g}{2 L}}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should include: (i) the spatial mode shape as a power series about x = L in the form ξ(x) = a_0 · [series in (x−L)] with coefficients written using only a_0, λ, x, and L; and (ii) the lowest-mode frequency stated explicitly as ν_min = [expression] using only g, L, and numerical constants.

grading_standard.formula:
$$
ρ Δx \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial t^2} = \bigl[T \frac{\partial y}{\partial x}\bigr]_{x+Δx} - \bigl[T \frac{\partial y}{\partial x}\bigr]_x
$$

$$
ρ \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial t^2} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x} \left( T \frac{\partial y}{\partial x} \right)
$$

$$
\frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial t^2} = g \frac{\partial}{\partial x} \left[ (L - x) \frac{\partial y}{\partial x} \right]
$$

$$
\frac{1}{g τ} \frac{d^2 τ}{d t^2} = \frac{1}{ξ} \frac{d}{d x} \left[ (L - x) \frac{d ξ}{d x} \right]
$$

$$
\frac{d}{d x} \left[ (L - x) \frac{d ξ}{d x} \right] + λ ξ = 0
$$

$$
(x - L) \frac{d^2 ξ}{d x^2} + \frac{d ξ}{d x} - λ ξ = 0
$$

$$
f(λ L) = 1 - λ L + \frac{1}{4} λ^2 L^2 - \cdots
$$

$$
τ(t) = A \cos(\sqrt{λ g} t) + B \sin(\sqrt{λ g} t)
$$

context: An infinite string with constant tension T and linear mass density \sigma undergoes small transverse displacements y(x,t). Define the wave speed by v=\sqrt{T/\sigma}. The initial displacement and velocity are given by y(x,0)=f(x) and \frac{\partial y}{\partial t}(x,0)=g(x), respectively. Find the motion y(x,t) for all t>0. In the solution below, f_1 and f_2 are auxiliary functions, C is an integration constant, and f_1'(x)=\frac{d f_1}{dx}(x), f_2'(x)=\frac{d f_2}{dx}(x).
solution:
The displacement satisfies the one-dimensional wave equation
$$
\frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial x^2} - \frac{1}{v^2} \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial t^2} = 0
$$
with wave speed
$$
v = \sqrt{\frac{T}{\sigma}}
$$
A general solution is the sum of right- and left-traveling waves
$$
y(x,t) = f_1(x+vt) + f_2(x-vt)
$$
The initial conditions are
$$
y(x,0) = f(x)
$$
$$
\frac{\partial y}{\partial t}(x,0) = g(x)
$$
From these, we obtain
$$
f_1(x) + f_2(x) = f(x)
$$
$$
f_1'(x) - f_2'(x) = \frac{g(x)}{v}
$$
Integrating the second relation gives
$$
f_1(x) - f_2(x) = \frac{1}{v} \int^x g(x') dx' + C
$$
Solving for f_1 and f_2 yields
$$
f_1(x) = \frac{1}{2} \left[ f(x) + \frac{1}{v} \int^x g(x') dx' + C \right]
$$
$$
f_2(x) = \frac{1}{2} \left[ f(x) - \frac{1}{v} \int^x g(x') dx' - C \right]
$$
Substituting into the general solution gives
$$
y(x,t) = f_1(x+vt) + f_2(x-vt)
$$
which simplifies to the d'Alembert formula
$$
y(x,t) = \frac{1}{2} \left[ f(x+vt) + f(x-vt) + \frac{1}{v} \int_{x-vt}^{x+vt} g(x') dx' \right]
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of y(x,t) = ... , and your response should be written using only the symbols x, t, v, f(·), and g(·). Do not introduce any auxiliary functions (such as f1, f2) or arbitrary constants.

context: A long wave packet with amplitude A, composed predominantly of angular frequencies very near the central value ω_0, propagates on an infinitely long string of linear mass density μ and tension T, as shown in Fig. 1.218. A bead of mass m is attached to the string at x = 0, as shown in Fig. 1.219. Let y(x,t) denote the small transverse displacement of the string. The wave speed is denoted by v, and for a monochromatic component of angular frequency ω, the wavenumber is k = ω/v. For waves near ω_0 we write, for x < 0, y_1(x,t) as a superposition of an incident wave of amplitude A and a reflected wave of amplitude B; for x > 0, y_2(x,t) is a transmitted wave of amplitude C. The angles that the string makes with the x-axis immediately to the left and right of the bead are θ_1 and θ_2, respectively. The imaginary unit is i with i^2 = -1, and C^* denotes the complex conjugate of C. The magnitude of the complex transmitted amplitude is |C|, defined by |C| = sqrt(C^* C). The task is to find the transmitted amplitude |C| and, in the limit of large m and large ω_0, determine how |C| scales with ω_0.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the amplitude of the transmitted wave packet?
subquestions.solution:
The equation of motion for small transverse oscillations on the string is the wave equation
$$
\frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial x^2} - \frac{\mu}{T} \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial t^2} = 0
$$
The wave speed is
$$
v = \pm \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}
$$
For a monochromatic component of angular frequency \omega, the wavenumber is
$$
k = \frac{\omega}{v}
$$
Equivalently
$$
k = \omega \sqrt{\frac{\mu}{T}}
$$
For waves with angular frequencies very nearly \omega_0, the fields can be written as
$$
y_1 = A e^{i(k x - \omega_0 t)} + B e^{-i(k x - \omega_0 t)}
$$
$$
y_2 = C e^{i(k x - \omega_0 t)}
$$
Continuity of displacement at the bead gives, at x = 0,
$$
A + B = C
$$
The equation of motion of the bead at x = 0 is
$$
m \left(\frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial t^2}\right)_{x=0} = - T \sin \theta_1 + T \sin \theta_2
$$
For small angles, \sin \theta \approx \theta, so
$$
m \left(\frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial t^2}\right)_{x=0} \approx - T \theta_1 + T \theta_2
$$
With small-slope approximations,
$$
\theta_1 \approx \left(\frac{\partial y_1}{\partial x}\right)_{x=0}
$$
$$
\theta_2 \approx \left(\frac{\partial y_2}{\partial x}\right)_{x=0}
$$
Thus
$$
m \left(\frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial t^2}\right)_{x=0} \approx - T \left(\frac{\partial y_1}{\partial x}\right)_{x=0} + T \left(\frac{\partial y_2}{\partial x}\right)_{x=0}
$$
Substituting the harmonic forms and canceling the common time factor yields
$$
- m \omega_0^2 C = - i k T (A - B) + i k T C
$$
Hence
$$
A - B = \left(1 + \frac{m \omega_0^2}{i k T}\right) C
$$
Together with A + B = C, we obtain
$$
C = \frac{2 A}{2 + \frac{m \omega_0^2}{i k T}}
$$
The magnitude of the transmitted amplitude is
$$
|C| = \sqrt{C^* C}
$$
Thus
$$
|C| = \frac{2 A}{\sqrt{4 + \frac{m^2 \omega_0^4}{k^2 T^2}}}
$$
Using k = \omega_0 \sqrt{\frac{\mu}{T}}, this becomes
$$
|C| = \frac{2 A}{\sqrt{4 + \frac{m^2 \omega_0^4}{\mu T}}}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form |C| = ..., and your response should use only the variables A, m, ω_0, μ, and T.

subquestions.subproblem: In the limit of large m and high frequency (large ω_0), how does the amplitude of the transmitted wave depend on ω_0?
subquestions.solution:
In the limit of large m and large \omega_0 we have
$$
|C| \approx \frac{2 A}{m \omega_0} \sqrt{\mu T}
$$
Therefore
$$
|C| \propto \frac{1}{\omega_0}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given as a proportionality of the form |C| ∝ ..., and your response should involve only the variable ω_0.

grading_standard.formula: $$y_1 = A e^{i(k x - \omega_0 t)} + B e^{-i(k x - \omega_0 t)}$$
$$m \left(\frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial t^2}\right)_{x=0} \approx - T \left(\frac{\partial y_1}{\partial x}\right)_{x=0} + T \left(\frac{\partial y_2}{\partial x}\right)_{x=0}$$
$$- m \omega_0^2 C = - i k T (A - B) + i k T C$$

context: An organ pipe of length l, open at both ends and aligned with the airflow, is used in a subsonic wind tunnel to measure the Mach number M of air in the tunnel, where M=v/c and v is the uniform airflow speed while c is the speed of sound in still air. When the pipe is fixed in the tunnel, it resonates with a fundamental period t (the same quantity denoted by δt in the original statement). Let t0 be the fundamental period of the pipe in still air. Assume the fundamental mode of an open-open pipe has wavelength λ=2l and that the effective wave speed relative to the pipe is the speed of sound in still air adjusted by the pipe’s motion relative to the medium. Given v/c=1/2, calculate the ratio of periods t/t0.
solution:
For an open-open organ pipe, the fundamental wavelength satisfies
$$
\frac{\lambda}{2}=l
$$
The fundamental period equals wavelength divided by the effective wave speed relative to the pipe c_{eff}:
$$
 t=\frac{\lambda}{c_{eff}}
$$
Using the fundamental wavelength, we have
$$
 t=\frac{2l}{c_{eff}}
$$
In still air, c_{eff}=c, so the fundamental period is
$$
 t_0=\frac{2l}{c}
$$
With airflow speed v in the tunnel, we may model the situation as the pipe moving at velocity −v through still air, giving
$$
 c_{eff}=c-(-v)
$$
For v/c=1/2, the effective wave speed is
$$
 c_{eff}=\frac{3c}{2}
$$
Hence the period in the tunnel is
$$
 t=\frac{2l}{\frac{3c}{2}}
$$
Which gives
$$
 t=\frac{4l}{3c}
$$
Therefore the desired ratio is
$$
 \frac{t}{t_0}=\frac{\frac{4l}{3c}}{\frac{2l}{c}}
$$
And finally
$$
 \frac{t}{t_0}=\frac{2}{3}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the ratio t/t0 as a numerical value.

context: Two media have a planar, perfectly impermeable interface at z=0 as shown in Fig. 1.223. Plane acoustic waves of pressure amplitude A and frequency f are generated in medium (1), propagating normally toward medium (2). Medium (1) has density \(\rho_1\) and sound speed \(c_1\), while medium (2) has density \(\rho_2\) and sound speed \(c_2\). Let the z-axis be perpendicular to the interface with the origin at the interface. Let p(z,t) denote the acoustic pressure and v(z,t) the particle velocity along z. Define the acoustic impedance in medium j as \(Z_j=\rho_j c_j\). The incident, reflected, and transmitted pressure amplitudes are A, A_r, and B, respectively. The angular frequency is \(\omega=2\pi f\).

subquestions.subproblem: What are the appropriate boundary conditions at the interface?
subquestions.solution:
The boundary conditions at the interface are the continuity of acoustic pressure and the continuity of the normal component of particle velocity at z=0.
$$p_i(0,t)+p_r(0,t)=p_t(0,t)$$
$$v_i(0,t)+v_r(0,t)=v_t(0,t)$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should consist of two equations expressing continuity of acoustic pressure and continuity of normal particle velocity at z=0, written using the symbols p_i, p_r, p_t, v_i, v_r, v_t (evaluated at z=0).

subquestions.subproblem: Apply these boundary conditions to derive the pressure amplitude A_r of the wave reflected back into medium (1) and the pressure amplitude B of the wave transmitted into medium (2).
subquestions.solution:
Take the z-axis perpendicular to the interface with the origin on the interface. Let the pressure fields be
$$p_i(z,t)=A e^{i(\omega t-k_1 z)}$$
$$p_r(z,t)=A_r e^{i(\omega t+k_1 z)}$$
$$p_t(z,t)=B e^{i(\omega t-k_2 z)}$$
with
$$k_j=\frac{\omega}{c_j}$$
The particle velocities for plane waves are
$$v_i(z,t)=\frac{A}{Z_1} e^{i(\omega t-k_1 z)}$$
$$v_r(z,t)=-\frac{A_r}{Z_1} e^{i(\omega t+k_1 z)}$$
$$v_t(z,t)=\frac{B}{Z_2} e^{i(\omega t-k_2 z)}$$
Applying the boundary conditions at z=0 gives
$$A+A_r=B$$
$$\frac{A}{Z_1}-\frac{A_r}{Z_1}=\frac{B}{Z_2}$$
Solving for the amplitudes yields
$$A_r=A\frac{Z_2-Z_1}{Z_1+Z_2}$$
$$B=A\frac{2 Z_2}{Z_1+Z_2}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of A_r = ... and B = ..., and your response should be written only with the variables A, Z_1, Z_2.

context: Let the speed of sound in air be c. A point source of sound moves at constant speed v along the +x direction through still air. The inertial frame Oxy is fixed to the air with origin O at x = 0, y = 0. Time is t. At time t the source is at the point S on the +x axis. Define a source-fixed frame Sx'y' with origin at S and axes parallel to x and y. The angle phi parameterizes points on circles centered at O by x = r cos phi and y = r sin phi. The semi-vertex angle of the cone in part (b) is denoted by theta.

subquestions.subproblem: For v < c: A pulse of sound is emitted at the origin O at time t = 0. At time t, sketch the wavefront and the simultaneous position S of the source at x = v t. Label O, S, and the axes. Write equations for the position of the wavefront as seen from the source at time t in the source-fixed coordinates x', y'.
subquestions.solution: Let S be the position of the source at time t at x = v t, y = 0. Define the frames Oxy and Sx'y' with parallel axes and origins at O and S, respectively. The coordinate transformation is $$x' = x - v t$$ $$y' = y$$ In the O-frame, the wavefront at time t is the circle of radius c t parameterized by $$x = c t \cos \varphi$$ $$y = c t \sin \varphi$$ with parameter range $$0 \leq \varphi$$ $$\varphi \leq 2\pi$$ Expressed in the S-frame, the wavefront is $$x' = c t \cos \varphi - v t$$ $$y' = c t \sin \varphi$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be the parametric equations of the wavefront in the source-fixed coordinates (x', y') at time t, given in the form x' = ... and y' = ..., and your response should use only the variables c, v, t, and φ (with x' and y' on the left-hand sides).

subquestions.subproblem: For v > c: A source emits a continuous signal while moving. Sketch the wavefront set up by the moving source and indicate the geometric construction that yields your result. Write an equation relating the shape of the wavefront to the known quantities in the problem. (Wisconsin)
subquestions.solution: Let the source move from O to S during the interval from t = 0 to the observation time t. Consider emissions at times t_1, t_2, ... when the source was at points S_1, S_2, ... along its path, with distances from O given by $$OS_1 = v t_1$$ $$OS_2 = v t_2$$ At the observation time t, the radii of the circular wavefronts from these emissions are $$r_0 = c t$$ $$r_i = c (t - t_i)$$ For each emission time t_i, the ratio of radius to source displacement equals $$\frac{c t}{v t} = \frac{c}{v}$$ and also $$\frac{c (t - t_i)}{v (t - t_i)} = \frac{c}{v}$$ Hence the envelope of these circles is a right circular cone with vertex at S and semi-vertex angle theta satisfying $$\sin \theta = \frac{c}{v}$$ Equivalently, the semi-vertex angle is $$\theta = \arcsin \frac{c}{v}$$ Thus the resultant wavefront of the continuous signal is this cone with vertex at the moving source
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be a single equation relating the semi-vertex angle θ of the cone to the speeds, given in the form sin θ = ..., and your response should use only the variables θ, c, and v.

context: An airplane flies horizontally at constant speed v = 600 \unit{m/s} at a constant altitude h = 8000 \unit{m}. The speed of sound in air is c = 300 \unit{m/s}. An observer stands at point A on the ground. Let A' be the point on the airplane's straight-line path directly above A, so AA' = h.
