context: Three point-like masses move without friction inside a fixed circular tube of radius R in a uniform gravitational field of magnitude g directed downward, as shown in Fig. 2.65. Two outer masses are equal to m and the central mass is M. The masses are connected in a line by two massless springs of constant κ, with zero natural length; the masses may pass through one another. Let K=κ. Find, using Lagrange's method, the normal modes of small vibrations about the position of equilibrium and describe each mode. Use the following definitions and conventions: - R has units \unit{m}. - g has units \unit{m/s^2}. - K has units \unit{N/m}. - m and M have units \unit{kg}. - Label the masses along the tube as i=1,2,3 from one outer mass to the other outer mass, with the central mass i=2. - Let the tube be centered so that the lowest point corresponds to angular coordinate θ=0, and define small angular deviations θ_i of each mass. - Introduce the small horizontal coordinates x_i=R θ_i for i=1,2,3. Retain terms up to second order in x_i and \dot{x}_i.
solution:
Choose Cartesian coordinates (ξ, η) as in Fig. 2.66, with the i-th mass at angle θ_i located at (R sin θ_i, R(1−cos θ_i)). For small oscillations define the generalized coordinates x_i=R θ_i and expand to second order.

$$
x_i=R \theta_i
$$

$$
y_i=\frac{1}{2} R \theta_i^2
$$

Keeping terms up to second order in x_i and \dot{x}_i, the kinetic energy is

$$
T=\frac{1}{2} m \dot{x}_1^2+\frac{1}{2} M \dot{x}_2^2+\frac{1}{2} m \dot{x}_3^2
$$

The potential energy consists of the two springs and gravity

$$
V=\frac{1}{2} K (x_1-x_2)^2+\frac{1}{2} K (x_2-x_3)^2+\frac{1}{2} \frac{m g}{R} x_1^2+\frac{1}{2} \frac{M g}{R} x_2^2+\frac{1}{2} \frac{m g}{R} x_3^2
$$

The Lagrangian is

$$
L=T-V
$$

Lagrange's equations yield

$$
m \ddot{x}_1+\left(K+\frac{m g}{R}\right) x_1-K x_2=0
$$

$$
M \ddot{x}_2+\left(2K+\frac{M g}{R}\right) x_2-K(x_1+x_3)=0
$$

$$
m \ddot{x}_3+\left(K+\frac{m g}{R}\right) x_3-K x_2=0
$$

Seek normal modes of the form

$$
x_j=A_j e^{i \omega t}
$$

This gives the homogeneous linear system

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
K+\frac{m g}{R}-m \omega^2 & -K & 0 \\
-K & 2K+\frac{M g}{R}-M \omega^2 & -K \\
0 & -K & K+\frac{m g}{R}-m \omega^2
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
A_1 \\
A_2 \\
A_3
\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}
0 \\
0 \\
0
\end{pmatrix}
$$

Nontrivial solutions require

$$
\det\begin{pmatrix}
K+\frac{m g}{R}-m \omega^2 & -K & 0 \\
-K & 2K+\frac{M g}{R}-M \omega^2 & -K \\
0 & -K & K+\frac{m g}{R}-m \omega^2
\end{pmatrix}=0
$$

The three nonnegative roots are the normal-mode angular frequencies

$$
\omega_1=\sqrt{\frac{g}{R}+\frac{K}{m}}
$$

$$
\omega_2=\sqrt{\frac{g}{R}+\frac{K}{2 m}+\frac{K}{M}-K \sqrt{\frac{1}{4 m^2}+\frac{1}{m M}+\frac{1}{M^2}}}
$$

$$
\omega_3=\sqrt{\frac{g}{R}+\frac{K}{2 m}+\frac{K}{M}+K \sqrt{\frac{1}{4 m^2}+\frac{1}{m M}+\frac{1}{M^2}}}
$$

From the first and third equations one obtains the amplitude relations

$$
\frac{A_2}{A_1}=1+\frac{m g}{R K}-\frac{m \omega^2}{K}
$$

$$
\frac{A_2}{A_3}=1+\frac{m g}{R K}-\frac{m \omega^2}{K}
$$

From the middle equation

$$
K A_1-\left(2K+\frac{M g}{R}-M \omega^2\right) A_2+K A_3=0
$$

For the mode at \omega_1 the amplitudes are antisymmetric in the outer masses with a stationary center

$$
A_3=-A_1
$$

$$
A_2=0
$$

For the symmetric modes at \omega_2 and \omega_3 the outer amplitudes are equal in sign, and the center moves with opposite or same phase, respectively

$$
B_3=B_1
$$

$$
\frac{B_2}{B_1}<0
$$

$$
C_3=C_1
$$

$$
\frac{C_2}{C_1}>0
$$

Equivalently, the three mode shapes can be written as column vectors of outer and center amplitudes

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
A_1 \\
0 \\
- A_1
\end{pmatrix}
$$

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
B_1 \\
B_2 \\
B_1
\end{pmatrix}
$$

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
C_1 \\
C_2 \\
C_1
\end{pmatrix}
$$

The ratios for the symmetric modes are

$$
B_2=\left[\frac{1}{2}-\frac{m}{M}-m \sqrt{\frac{1}{4 m^2}+\frac{1}{m M}+\frac{1}{M^2}}\right] B_1
$$

$$
C_2=\left[\frac{1}{2}-\frac{m}{M}+m \sqrt{\frac{1}{4 m^2}+\frac{1}{m M}+\frac{1}{M^2}}\right] C_1
$$

These three normal modes are depicted qualitatively in Fig. 2.67.

context: A flyball governor consists of two identical balls of mass m attached by massless arms of length l to a sliding sleeve of mass M on a vertical shaft, as shown in Fig. 2.68. The arms make an angle θ with the vertical shaft axis (the z-axis). The sleeve of mass M can slide without friction along the shaft. Air resistance and the masses of the arms are neglected, and the diameter of the mass M is assumed small. The gravitational acceleration is g. In parts (a) and (b), the shaft is constrained to rotate with constant angular velocity ω_0 about the z-axis. In part (c), the shaft is allowed to rotate freely, and its rotation angle about the shaft is denoted by φ with angular velocity ω=˙φ. The equilibrium angle is denoted by θ_0, and the small-oscillation frequency is denoted by f. The top of the shaft is taken as the reference for the vertical distance of the sleeve; the sleeve’s vertical position is z_M = -2 l cos θ, so its distance below the top is 2 l cos θ.

subquestions.subproblem: Calculate the equilibrium height of the mass M when the shaft rotates at angular velocity ω_0.
subquestions.solution:
Use a rotating coordinate frame with the x-axis in the plane of the governor arms, and the z-axis along the shaft. In this frame the position vectors of the two balls of mass m and the sleeve of mass M are
$$r_{m,1}=(-l \sin \theta,0,-l \cos \theta)$$
$$r_{m,2}=(l \sin \theta,0,-l \cos \theta)$$
$$r_M=(0,0,-2 l \cos \theta)$$
In an inertial frame with the same origin and z-axis, the velocities satisfy
$$\dot r' = \dot r + \omega_0 \times r$$
with angular velocity vector
$$\omega_0=(0,0,\omega_0)$$
Hence the velocities are
$$\dot r_{m,1}'=(-l \dot \theta \cos \theta, l \omega_0 \sin \theta, l \dot \theta \sin \theta)$$
$$\dot r_{m,2}'=(l \dot \theta \cos \theta, -l \omega_0 \sin \theta, l \dot \theta \sin \theta)$$
$$\dot r_M'=(0,0,-2 l \dot \theta \sin \theta)$$
The kinetic energy is
$$T = m l^2 \omega_0^2 \sin^2 \theta + m l^2 \dot \theta^2 + 2 M l^2 \dot \theta^2 \sin^2 \theta$$
The potential energy is
$$V = -2 m g l \cos \theta - 2 M g l \cos \theta$$
The Lagrangian is
$$L = T - V = m l^2 \omega_0^2 \sin^2 \theta + m l^2 \dot \theta^2 + 2 M l^2 \dot \theta^2 \sin^2 \theta + 2 (M + m) g l \cos \theta$$
Lagrange's equation gives
$$\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot \theta}\right) - \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta} = 0$$
which yields
$$2 (m + 2 M \sin^2 \theta) l \ddot \theta + 2 M l \dot \theta^2 \sin 2 \theta - m l \omega_0^2 \sin 2 \theta + 2 (m + M) g \sin \theta = 0$$
At equilibrium,
$$\ddot \theta = 0$$
$$\dot \theta = 0$$
$$\theta = \theta_0$$
and the equation of motion reduces to
$$m l \omega_0^2 \sin 2 \theta_0 = 2 (m + M) g \sin \theta_0$$
The equilibrium solutions are
$$\theta_0 = 0$$
$$\cos \theta_0 = \frac{(m + M) g}{m l \omega_0^2}$$
The distances of the sleeve mass M below the top of the shaft at these equilibria are
$$2 l \cos \theta_0 = 2 l$$
$$2 l \cos \theta_0 = \frac{2 (m + M) g}{m \omega_0^2}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should give the sleeve’s equilibrium distance(s) below the top of the shaft in the form d_eq = ..., written using only l, m, M, g, and ω_0 (and numerical constants if needed).

subquestions.subproblem: Calculate the frequency f of small oscillations around the nontrivial equilibrium in part (a) while the shaft is constrained to rotate at angular velocity ω_0.
subquestions.solution:
When \(\theta_0=0\), the governor collapses and there is no oscillation. Consider the nontrivial equilibrium satisfying \(\cos \theta_0 = \frac{(m + M) g}{m l \omega_0^2}\). Let
$$\theta' = \theta - \theta_0$$
so that
$$\dot \theta = \dot \theta'$$
For small oscillations with \(\theta' \ll 1\), expand
$$\sin \theta \approx \sin \theta_0 + \theta' \cos \theta_0$$
$$\sin 2 \theta \approx \sin 2 \theta_0 + 2 \theta' \cos 2 \theta_0$$
Linearizing the equation of motion about \(\theta_0\) and using the equilibrium condition yields
$$(m + 2 M \sin^2 \theta_0) l \ddot \theta' + \big[(m + M) g \cos \theta_0 - m l \omega_0^2 \cos 2 \theta_0\big] \theta' = 0$$
Therefore, the small-oscillation frequency is
$$f = \frac{1}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\frac{(m + M) g \cos \theta_0 - m l \omega_0^2 \cos 2 \theta_0}{(m + 2 M \sin^2 \theta_0) l}}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form f = ..., written using only m, M, g, l, ω_0, θ_0, and mathematical constants such as π. Here θ_0 denotes the nontrivial equilibrium angle defined in part (a).

subquestions.subproblem: Suppose the shaft is now allowed to rotate freely. Does the frequency of small oscillations change? If so, calculate the new value.
subquestions.solution:
Let φ be the rotation angle about the shaft, with angular velocity \(\omega = \dot \varphi\). The Lagrangian becomes
$$L = m l^2 \dot \varphi^2 \sin^2 \theta + m l^2 \dot \theta^2 + 2 M l^2 \dot \theta^2 \sin^2 \theta + 2 (m + M) g l \cos \theta$$
Lagrange's equations yield the first integral
$$\dot \varphi \sin^2 \theta = c$$
where c is a constant of motion, and the θ-equation
$$2 (m + 2 M \sin^2 \theta) l \ddot \theta + 2 M l \dot \theta^2 \sin 2 \theta - m l \dot \varphi^2 \sin 2 \theta + 2 (m + M) g \sin \theta = 0$$
Eliminating \(\dot \varphi\) using \(\dot \varphi = c \sin^{-2} \theta\) gives
$$(m + 2 M \sin^2 \theta) l \ddot \theta + M l \dot \theta^2 \sin 2 \theta - m l c^2 \frac{\cos \theta}{\sin^3 \theta} + (m + M) g \sin \theta = 0$$
At equilibrium,
$$\ddot \theta = 0$$
$$\dot \theta = 0$$
$$\theta = \theta_0$$
which implies
$$m l c^2 \frac{\cos \theta_0}{\sin^3 \theta_0} = (m + M) g \sin \theta_0$$
For small oscillations about \(\theta_0\), let \(\theta = \theta_0 + \theta'\) with \(\theta' \ll 1\). Then
$$m l c^2 \frac{\cos \theta}{\sin^3 \theta} \approx m l c^2 \frac{\cos \theta_0 - \theta' \sin \theta_0}{(\sin \theta_0 + \theta' \cos \theta_0)^3}$$
$$m l c^2 \frac{\cos \theta}{\sin^3 \theta} \approx m l c^2 \frac{\cos \theta_0}{\sin^3 \theta_0} \big(1 - \theta' \tan \theta_0 - 3 \theta' \cot \theta_0\big)$$
Using the equilibrium relation to replace \(m l c^2 \frac{\cos \theta_0}{\sin^3 \theta_0}\), this becomes
$$m l c^2 \frac{\cos \theta}{\sin^3 \theta} \approx (m + M) g \sin \theta_0 \left[1 - \left(\frac{1 + 2 \cos^2 \theta_0}{\sin \theta_0 \cos \theta_0}\right) \theta'\right]$$
Substituting into the linearized equation of motion yields
$$(m + 2 M \sin^2 \theta_0) l \ddot \theta' + (m + M) g \frac{1 + 3 \cos^2 \theta_0}{\cos \theta_0} \theta' = 0$$
Hence, the frequency of small oscillations is
$$f = \frac{1}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\frac{(m + M) g (1 + 3 \cos^2 \theta_0)}{(m + 2 M \sin^2 \theta_0) l \cos \theta_0}}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form f = ..., written using only m, M, g, l, θ_0, and mathematical constants such as π. Here θ_0 denotes the equilibrium angle for the freely rotating case.

$$2 (m + 2 M \sin^2 \theta) l \ddot \theta + 2 M l \dot \theta^2 \sin 2 \theta - m l \omega_0^2 \sin 2 \theta + 2 (m + M) g \sin \theta = 0$$
$$(m + 2 M \sin^2 \theta_0) l \ddot \theta' + \big[(m + M) g \cos \theta_0 - m l \omega_0^2 \cos 2 \theta_0\big] \theta' = 0$$

context: A particle of mass m moves under uniform gravity on a smooth surface given by z = x^2 + y^2 - x y, where x, y, z are Cartesian coordinates and the z-axis is vertical, pointing upwards. The gravitational acceleration has magnitude g with SI units \unit{m/s^2}, and the gravitational potential energy is V = m g z. Time is denoted by t. In parts (b) and (c), small oscillations about the stable equilibrium are considered; the angular frequency is denoted by \omega, and the complex amplitudes in the trial solutions are x_0 and y_0. The normal-mode angular frequencies are denoted by \omega_1 and \omega_2.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the equations of motion of the particle.
subquestions.solution:
The surface constraint is given by
$$z = x^2 + y^2 - x y$$
Differentiating with respect to time gives
$$\dot z = 2 x \dot x + 2 y \dot y - y \dot x - x \dot y$$
This can be written as
$$\dot z = \dot x (2 x - y) + \dot y (2 y - x)$$
The kinetic energy is
$$T = \frac{1}{2} m (\dot x^2 + \dot y^2 + \dot z^2)$$
Using the constraint, we have
$$\dot z^2 = \dot x^2 (2 x - y)^2 + \dot y^2 (2 y - x)^2 + 2 \dot x \dot y (2 x - y)(2 y - x)$$
Thus
$$T = \frac{1}{2} m [ \dot x^2 + \dot y^2 + \dot x^2 (2 x - y)^2 + \dot y^2 (2 y - x)^2 + 2 \dot x \dot y (2 x - y)(2 y - x) ]$$
The potential energy is
$$V = m g (x^2 + y^2 - x y)$$
The Lagrangian is
$$L = T - V$$
Lagrange's equations are
$$\frac{d}{dt} \bigg( \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot q_i} \bigg) - \frac{\partial L}{\partial q_i} = 0$$
Using q_1 = x and q_2 = y, the equations of motion are
$$\frac{d}{dt} [ \dot x + \dot x (2 x - y)^2 + \dot y (2 x - y)(2 y - x) ] = 2 \dot x^2 (2 x - y) - \dot y^2 (2 y - x) + 2 \dot x \dot y (2 y - x) - \dot x \dot y (2 x - y) - 2 g x + g y$$
$$\frac{d}{dt} [ \dot y + \dot y (2 y - x)^2 + \dot x (2 x - y)(2 y - x) ] = 2 \dot y^2 (2 y - x) - \dot x^2 (2 x - y) + 2 \dot x \dot y (2 x - y) - \dot x \dot y (2 y - x) - 2 g y + g x$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given as two Euler–Lagrange equations in the expanded form d/dt[...]=..., not explicitly solved for accelerations: d/dt[A_x(x, y, \dot{x}, \dot{y})] = B_x(x, y, \dot{x}, \dot{y}, g) and d/dt[A_y(x, y, \dot{x}, \dot{y})] = B_y(x, y, \dot{x}, \dot{y}, g). Use only x, y, \dot{x}, \dot{y}, and g.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the frequencies of the normal-modes for small oscillations about the position of stable equilibrium.
subquestions.solution:
From the potential energy we have
$$\frac{\partial V}{\partial x} = m g (2 x - y)$$
$$\frac{\partial V}{\partial y} = m g (2 y - x)$$
Equilibrium occurs at the origin x = 0, y = 0. For small oscillations about the origin, the linearized equations of motion are
$$\ddot x + 2 g x - g y = 0$$
$$\ddot y + 2 g y - g x = 0$$
Consider solutions of the form
$$x = x_0 e^{i \omega t}$$
$$y = y_0 e^{i \omega t}$$
The secular equation is
$$( g - \omega^2 )( 3 g - \omega^2 ) = 0$$
The normal-mode angular frequencies are
$$\omega_1 = \sqrt{g}$$
$$\omega_2 = \sqrt{3 g}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given as two equations: \omega_1 = ... and \omega_2 = ..., where each right-hand side is written only in terms of g.

subquestions.subproblem: If the particle is displaced from equilibrium slightly and then released,what must be the ratio of the x and y displacements to guarantee that only the higher frequency normal-mode is excited?
subquestions.solution:
From the eigenvector condition we have
$$\frac{y_0}{x_0} = \frac{2 g - \omega^2}{g}$$
For the higher frequency mode with \omega^2 = 3 g, the ratio is
$$\frac{y_0}{x_0} = -1$$
Therefore, the initial displacements of x and y must be equal in magnitude and opposite in sign so that only the higher frequency normal-mode is excited.
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the ratio y_0/x_0 as a numerical value.

$$\frac{d}{dt} [ \dot x + \dot x (2 x - y)^2 + \dot y (2 x - y)(2 y - x) ] = 2 \dot x^2 (2 x - y) - \dot y^2 (2 y - x) + 2 \dot x \dot y (2 y - x) - \dot x \dot y (2 x - y) - 2 g x + g y$$

context: A rigid structure consists of three massless rods joined at point B. Points A and C are at the free ends of rods AB and BC, with AB=BC=L. The third rod BD has length l and makes equal angles ABD=DBC=θ with the other two rods. Two identical point masses, each of mass m, are attached at A and C. The structure is supported at point D and oscillates in a vertical plane with small amplitude about D under uniform gravitational acceleration g with units \unit{m/s^2}. Choose the motion to lie in the xy-plane with origin at D and the y-axis vertically upward. Let b=AD=CD be the fixed distance from D to each mass. Let α and φ be angles measured from the vertical such that the angle between AD and the vertical is α+φ and the angle between CD and the vertical is α−φ. Define α=θ+ψ, where ψ is determined by the geometry via the sine law b/sin θ=l/sin ψ. The generalized coordinate is φ, assumed small for the small-oscillation analysis. Denote the coordinates of the mass at A by (x_A,y_A) and at C by (x_C,y_C). Dots denote time derivatives. Let T be the total kinetic energy, V the potential energy, and Λ the Lagrangian defined by Λ=T−V. Let ω be the small-oscillation angular frequency. Determine ω and the stability condition on l under which small oscillations about equilibrium are stable. In the final answers, write the angular frequency as ω and the stability condition as an inequality for l.
solution:
By the law of cosines for triangle ABD (and CBD), the fixed distance b is
$$
b=\sqrt{L^2+l^2-2Ll\cos\theta}
$$
By definition of the angles,
$$
\alpha=\theta+\psi
$$
The geometry fixes ψ by the sine law
$$
\frac{b}{\sin\theta}=\frac{l}{\sin\psi}
$$
Choose coordinates with origin at D and y-axis upward. The coordinates of the mass at A are
$$
x_A=-b\sin(\alpha+\varphi)
$$
$$
y_A=-b\cos(\alpha+\varphi)
$$
The coordinates of the mass at C are
$$
x_C=b\sin(\alpha-\varphi)
$$
$$
y_C=-b\cos(\alpha-\varphi)
$$
Differentiating, the velocities of the mass at A are
$$
\dot x_A=-b\dot\varphi\cos(\alpha+\varphi)
$$
$$
\dot y_A=b\dot\varphi\sin(\alpha+\varphi)
$$
The velocities of the mass at C are
$$
\dot x_C=-b\dot\varphi\cos(\alpha-\varphi)
$$
$$
\dot y_C=-b\dot\varphi\sin(\alpha-\varphi)
$$
The kinetic energy is
$$
T=\frac{1}{2}m(\dot x_A^2+\dot y_A^2)+\frac{1}{2}m(\dot x_C^2+\dot y_C^2)
$$
After simplification, the kinetic energy becomes
$$
T=mb^2\dot\varphi^2
$$
The potential energy is
$$
V=-mgb[\cos(\alpha+\varphi)+\cos(\alpha-\varphi)]
$$
The Lagrangian is
$$
\Lambda=T-V
$$
Substituting T and V gives
$$
\Lambda=mb^2\dot\varphi^2+mgb[\cos(\alpha+\varphi)+\cos(\alpha-\varphi)]
$$
Lagrange's equation is
$$
\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{\partial \Lambda}{\partial \dot\varphi})-\frac{\partial \Lambda}{\partial \varphi}=0
$$
The equation of motion becomes
$$
2mb^2\ddot\varphi+mgb[\sin(\alpha+\varphi)-\sin(\alpha-\varphi)]=0
$$
For small oscillations, use the approximation
$$
\sin(\alpha\pm\varphi)\approx\sin\alpha\pm\varphi\cos\alpha
$$
The linearized equation of motion is
$$
b\ddot\varphi+g\cos\alpha\varphi=0
$$
The angular frequency satisfies
$$
\omega^2=\frac{g\cos\alpha}{b}
$$
Hence the angular frequency is
$$
\omega=\sqrt{\frac{g\cos\alpha}{b}}
$$
To express cos α in terms of L, l, and θ, use
$$
\cos\alpha=\cos\theta\cos\psi-\sin\theta\sin\psi
$$
From the sine law,
$$
\sin\psi=\frac{l\sin\theta}{b}
$$
Using the identity for cos ψ,
$$
\cos\psi=\frac{\sqrt{b^2-l^2\sin^2\theta}}{b}
$$
Therefore,
$$
\cos\alpha=\frac{\sqrt{b^2-l^2\sin^2\theta}\cos\theta-l\sin^2\theta}{b}
$$
With
$$
b^2=L^2+l^2-2Ll\cos\theta
$$
this simplifies to
$$
\cos\alpha=\frac{L\cos\theta-l}{b}
$$
Therefore the angular frequency is
$$
\omega=\sqrt{\frac{g(L\cos\theta-l)}{L^2+l^2-2Ll\cos\theta}}
$$
For stability, evaluate the curvature of the potential at equilibrium φ=0
$$
\frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial\varphi^2}=mgb[\cos(\alpha+\varphi)+\cos(\alpha-\varphi)]
$$
At equilibrium, this gives
$$
\frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial\varphi^2}=2mgb\cos\alpha
$$
Stability requires
$$
\cos\alpha>0
$$
Using the expression for cos α, the stability condition is
$$
L\cos\theta-l>0
$$
Equivalently,
$$
l<L\cos\theta
$$
final_answer_instructions: Provide two final expressions: (1) The small-oscillation angular frequency in the form 'ω = ...', expressed only in terms of g, L, l, and θ; (2) The stability condition as a single inequality solving for l on one side, expressed only in terms of L and θ. Do not use any auxiliary variables such as b, α, ψ, or φ in your final expressions.

context: A flyball governor for a steam engine consists of two balls, each of mass m, attached by means of four hinged arms, each of length l, to sleeves located on a vertical rod. The lower sleeve has mass M and negligible moment of inertia, and is free to slide up and down the rod without friction. The upper sleeve is fastened to the rod. The system is constrained to rotate with constant angular velocity \omega about the vertical rod in a uniform gravitational field of acceleration g. Use the generalized coordinate \theta, defined as the angle that each arm makes with the vertical. Let z denote the height of the lower sleeve above its lowest position. Let L denote the Lagrangian, H the Hamiltonian, T the kinetic energy, and V the potential energy. Let p_{\theta} denote the momentum conjugate to \theta and \Omega the small-oscillation angular frequency about steady motion.

subquestions.subproblem: Choose suitable coordinates and write the Lagrangian and Hamiltonian functions for the system. Neglect weights of arms and rod, and neglect friction.
subquestions.solution:
Choose \theta as the generalized coordinate, the angle between each arm and the vertical.
$$L=T-V$$
$$L=m l^2 \omega^2 \sin^2 \theta + m l^2 \dot{\theta}^2 + 2 M l^2 \dot{\theta}^2 \sin^2 \theta + 2 (m+M) g l \cos \theta$$
$$H=\dot{\theta} p_{\theta} - L$$
$$p_{\theta}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{\theta}}$$
$$p_{\theta}=2 (m + 2 M \sin^2 \theta) l^2 \dot{\theta}$$
$$H=\dot{\theta} p_{\theta} - m l^2 \omega^2 \sin^2 \theta - (m + 2 M \sin^2 \theta) l^2 \dot{\theta}^2 - 2 (m+M) g l \cos \theta$$
$$H=\frac{p_{\theta}^2}{4 (m + 2 M \sin^2 \theta) l^2} - m l^2 \omega^2 \sin^2 \theta - 2 (m+M) g l \cos \theta$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should present: (i) L(\theta,\dot{\theta}) = ... ; (ii) p_{\theta}(\theta,\dot{\theta}) = ... ; and (iii) H(\theta,p_{\theta}) = ... . Use only the symbols m, M, l, \omega, g, \theta, \dot{\theta}, and p_{\theta} as appropriate (L and p_{\theta} in terms of m, M, l, \omega, g, \theta, \dot{\theta}; H in terms of m, M, l, \omega, g, \theta, p_{\theta}).

subquestions.subproblem: Discuss the motion.
subquestions.solution:
Lagrange's equation
$$\frac{d}{dt} \left( \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{\theta}} \right) - \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta} = 0$$
leads to
$$(m + 2 M \sin^2 \theta) l \ddot{\theta} + 2 M l \dot{\theta}^2 \sin 2\theta - m l \omega^2 \sin 2\theta + 2 (m+M) g \sin \theta = 0$$
The lower sleeve of mass M oscillates up and down the vertical rod about an equilibrium position \theta_0 determined by
$$\cos \theta_0 = \frac{(m+M) g}{m l \omega^2}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should include two items: (i) the equation of motion written explicitly as F(\theta,\dot{\theta},\ddot{\theta}; m, M, l, \omega, g) = 0; and (ii) the steady-angle condition written explicitly in the form "\cos \theta_0 = ...". Use only the symbols m, M, l, \omega, g, \theta, \dot{\theta}, \ddot{\theta}, and \theta_0, where \theta_0 denotes the steady angle.

subquestions.subproblem: Determine the height z of the lower sleeve above its lowest position, as a function of \omega, for steady motion. Find the frequency of small oscillations about this steady motion.
subquestions.solution:
At steady rotation with equilibrium angle \theta_0, the z coordinate of the lower sleeve relative to its lowest position is
$$z = 2 l - 2 l \cos \theta_0$$
Using the equilibrium condition, this becomes
$$z = 2 l \left(1 - \frac{(m+M) g}{m l \omega^2}\right)$$
The angular frequency of small oscillations about the equilibrium position is
$$\Omega = \sqrt{ \frac{ (m+M) g \cos \theta_0 - m l \omega^2 \cos 2\theta_0 }{ (m + 2 M \sin^2 \theta_0) l } }$$
$$\Omega = \omega \sqrt{ \frac{ m \sin^2 \theta_0 }{ m + 2 M \sin^2 \theta_0 } }$$
with
$$\sin^2 \theta_0 = 1 - \left( \frac{ (m+M) g }{ m l \omega^2 } \right)^2$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should present: (i) the steady-motion height as z = ... expressed as a function of \omega; and (ii) the small-oscillation angular frequency as \Omega = ... . Express z using only m, M, l, \omega, g; and express \Omega using only m, M, l, \omega, g, and \theta_0, where \theta_0 denotes the steady angle defined in part (b).

grading_standard.formula: $$L=m l^2 \omega^2 \sin^2 \theta + m l^2 \dot{\theta}^2 + 2 M l^2 \dot{\theta}^2 \sin^2 \theta + 2 (m+M) g l \cos \theta$$
$$H=\dot{\theta} p_{\theta} - m l^2 \omega^2 \sin^2 \theta - (m + 2 M \sin^2 \theta) l^2 \dot{\theta}^2 - 2 (m+M) g l \cos \theta$$
$$H=\frac{p_{\theta}^2}{4 (m + 2 M \sin^2 \theta) l^2} - m l^2 \omega^2 \sin^2 \theta - 2 (m+M) g l \cos \theta$$
$$(m + 2 M \sin^2 \theta) l \ddot{\theta} + 2 M l \dot{\theta}^2 \sin 2\theta - m l \omega^2 \sin 2\theta + 2 (m+M) g \sin \theta = 0$$

context: A light, uniform U-shaped tube has two vertical legs of length h joined by a horizontal segment of length l. It is partially filled with mercury of total mass M and linear mass density ρ (mass per unit length along the tube). The total length of the mercury column is s = l + 2 h. The tube is mounted so that it can rotate about the axis of one of the vertical legs. Neglect friction, the mass and moment of inertia of the glass tube, and the moment of inertia of the mercury on the rotation axis. Let g be the acceleration due to gravity. Let z be the displacement of the top of the mercury column from its symmetric equilibrium position, defined so that when one top descends by z the other rises by z. Let θ be the rotation angle of the tube about the vertical rotation axis. Let x denote the coordinate along the horizontal segment measured from the rotation axis toward the opposite vertical leg, with 0 ≤ x ≤ l. Let T be the kinetic energy, V the gravitational potential energy, and L = T − V the Lagrangian. Let p_z and p_θ be the canonical momenta conjugate to z and θ, respectively. Let H be the Hamiltonian. Overdots denote derivatives with respect to time t. In part (a), ω denotes the small-oscillation angular frequency when the tube is not spinning. In part (b), ω_0 and z_0 are the initial angular velocity and initial displacement at t = 0, respectively. The constant A and the small-oscillation frequency Ω about an equilibrium in the spinning case are defined in the solution below

subquestions.subproblem: Calculate the potential energy of the mercury column and describe its possible motion when the tube is not spinning.
subquestions.solution:
Let an external force F act quasistatically on the descending top to move it by dz
$$F = 2 ρ g z$$
The differential work done is
$$dW = F dz$$
The change in potential energy satisfies
$$dV = dW$$
Integrating from 0 to z gives
$$V = ρ g z^2$$
The Lagrangian when the tube is not spinning is
$$L = \frac{1}{2} ρ s \dot z^2 - ρ g z^2$$
The total column length is
$$s = l + 2 h$$
Lagrange's equation yields
$$\ddot z + \frac{2 g}{s} z = 0$$
Thus the mercury column oscillates about equilibrium with angular frequency
$$\omega = \sqrt{\frac{2 g}{s}}$$
In terms of l and h this is
$$\omega = \sqrt{\frac{2 g}{l + 2 h}}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Provide two algebraic expressions as your final answer: 1) V(z) = ... using only the symbols ρ, g, z; 2) ω = ... using only the symbols g, l, h. Do not introduce any additional symbols.

subquestions.subproblem: The tube is set in rotation with an initial angular velocity ω_0 with the mercury column at rest vertically with a displacement z_0 from equilibrium. 1) Give the Lagrangian for the system. 2)Give the equation of motion. 3) What quantities are conserved in the motion? Give expressions for these quantities. 4) Describe the motion qualitatively as completely as you can.
subquestions.solution:
When the tube is spinning, the system has two generalized coordinates z and θ.
1) The kinetic energy is
$$T = \frac{1}{2} ρ (h - z) \dot z^2 + \frac{1}{2} ρ \int_0^l (\dot z^2 + x^2 \dot θ^2) dx + \frac{1}{2} ρ (h + z) (\dot z^2 + l^2 \dot θ^2)$$
The potential energy is
$$V = ρ g z^2$$
The Lagrangian is
$$L = T - V$$
After evaluating the integral and collecting terms, the Lagrangian becomes
$$L = \frac{1}{2} ρ s \dot z^2 + \frac{1}{2} ρ \left( \frac{l}{3} + h + z \right) l^2 \dot θ^2 - ρ g z^2$$
2) The Lagrange equations are
$$\frac{d}{dt} \left( \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot q_i} \right) - \frac{\partial L}{\partial q_i} = 0$$
The equation of motion for z is
$$s \ddot z + 2 g z - \frac{1}{2} l^2 \dot θ^2 = 0$$
The conjugate momentum to θ is
$$p_θ = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot θ}$$
Its explicit form is
$$p_θ = ρ \left( \frac{l}{3} + h + z \right) l^2 \dot θ$$
Since θ is cyclic, we have
$$p_θ = \text{constant}$$
The initial conditions at t = 0 are
$$\dot θ(0) = \omega_0$$
$$\dot z(0) = 0$$
$$z(0) = z_0$$
Therefore
$$p_θ = ρ \left( \frac{l}{3} + h + z_0 \right) l^2 \omega_0$$
3) The Hamiltonian is
$$H = p_z \dot z + p_θ \dot θ - L$$
Evaluating gives
$$H = \frac{1}{2} ρ s \dot z^2 + \frac{1}{2} ρ \left( \frac{l}{3} + h + z \right) l^2 \dot θ^2 + ρ g z^2$$
The momentum conjugate to z is
$$p_z = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot z}$$
Its explicit form is
$$p_z = ρ s \dot z$$
In canonical variables the Hamiltonian is
$$H = \frac{p_z^2}{2 ρ s} + \frac{p_θ^2}{2 \left( \frac{l}{3} + h + z \right) ρ l^2} + ρ g z^2$$
Since H has no explicit time dependence, we have
$$H = \text{constant}$$
In addition, we have
$$p_θ = \text{constant}$$
Using the initial conditions gives
$$H = \frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{l}{3} + h + z_0 \right) ρ l^2 \omega_0^2 + ρ g z_0^2$$
4) The motion consists of two coupled parts: rotation with the tube and axial motion of the mercury column. The angular velocity \dot θ decreases when z increases and increases when z decreases so that p_θ remains constant. Eliminating \dot θ using p_θ, the equation of motion for z becomes
$$s \ddot z + 2 g z = \frac{A}{\left( \frac{l}{3} + h + z \right)^2}$$
The constant A is
$$A = \frac{p_θ^2}{2 ρ^2 l^2}$$
Generally speaking, there are three equilibrium positions corresponding to the three roots of
$$2 g z = \frac{A}{\left( \frac{l}{3} + h + z \right)^2}$$
Let z_1 be any equilibrium such that
$$2 g z_1 = \frac{A}{\left( \frac{l}{3} + h + z_1 \right)^2}$$
For small oscillations write z = z_1 + z' with |z'| small, giving the linearized equation
$$s \ddot z' + 2 g z' = - \frac{2 A z'}{\left( \frac{l}{3} + h + z_1 \right)^3}$$
The small-oscillation angular frequency about z_1 is
$$\Omega = \sqrt{\frac{2 g}{s} + \frac{2 A}{s \left( \frac{l}{3} + h + z_1 \right)^3}}$$
Since Ω is real, these equilibrium positions are stable
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Provide algebraic expressions only (overdots denote time derivatives): 1) Lagrangian: Give a single expression in the form L = ... using only the symbols ρ, s, l, h, z, ż, θ̇, g. 2) Equation of motion for z: Give one scalar equation in the form ... = 0 using only the symbols s, g, z, z̈, l, θ̇. 3) Conserved quantities: Provide p_θ = ... using only ρ, l, h, z, θ̇; and H = ... using only ρ, s, l, h, z, ż, θ̇, g. Also provide their constant values at t = 0 as p_θ = ... using only ρ, l, h, z_0, ω_0 and H = ... using only ρ, l, h, z_0, ω_0, g. No text-based description is required in your final answer.

$$T = \frac{1}{2} ρ (h - z) \dot z^2 + \frac{1}{2} ρ \int_0^l (\dot z^2 + x^2 \dot θ^2) dx + \frac{1}{2} ρ (h + z) (\dot z^2 + l^2 \dot θ^2)$$

context: A point particle of mass m slides without friction on the inside of a smooth paraboloid of revolution whose axis is vertical. The surface is given by z = A r^2, where r is the distance from the axis and z is measured vertically upward, with A > 0 a constant. Use cylindrical coordinates (r, \varphi, z) and take r and \varphi as generalized coordinates, with the holonomic constraint z = A r^2. Let g be the constant gravitational acceleration directed downward. Use T for kinetic energy, V for potential energy, L for the Lagrangian, p_r and p_\varphi for the momenta conjugate to r and \varphi, H for the Hamiltonian, and \omega for the angular frequency of small oscillations about the lowest point r = 0. Find:

subquestions.subproblem: The Lagrangian of the system.
subquestions.solution:
The Lagrangian is
$$L = T - V$$
The kinetic energy is
$$T = \frac{1}{2} m \dot{r}^2 + \frac{1}{2} m r^2 \dot{\varphi}^2 + \frac{1}{2} m \dot{z}^2$$
The potential energy is
$$V = m g z$$
The holonomic constraint is
$$z = A r^2$$
Differentiating the constraint gives
$$\dot{z} = 2 A r \dot{r}$$
Substituting into L yields
$$L = \frac{1}{2} m (1 + 4 A^2 r^2) \dot{r}^2 + \frac{1}{2} m r^2 \dot{\varphi}^2 - A m g r^2$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of L = ..., and your response should be written using only the symbols m, A, g, r, \dot{r}, \dot{\varphi}.

subquestions.subproblem: The generalized momenta and the corresponding Hamiltonian.
subquestions.solution:
The generalized momentum conjugate to r is
$$p_r = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{r}}$$
Explicitly
$$p_r = m (1 + 4 A^2 r^2) \dot{r}$$
The generalized momentum conjugate to \varphi is
$$p_{\varphi} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{\varphi}}$$
Explicitly
$$p_{\varphi} = m r^2 \dot{\varphi}$$
The Hamiltonian is
$$H = p_r \dot{r} + p_{\varphi} \dot{\varphi} - L$$
In terms of velocities
$$H = \frac{1}{2} m (1 + 4 A^2 r^2) \dot{r}^2 + \frac{1}{2} m r^2 \dot{\varphi}^2 + A m g r^2$$
In terms of the momenta
$$H = \frac{p_r^2}{2 m (1 + 4 A^2 r^2)} + \frac{p_{\varphi}^2}{2 m r^2} + A m g r^2$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should present three expressions: (i) p_r = ... written only with m, A, r, \dot{r}; (ii) p_{\varphi} = ... written only with m, r, \dot{\varphi}; and (iii) H = ... written only with r, p_r, p_{\varphi}, m, A, g.

subquestions.subproblem: The equation of motion for the coordinate r as a function of time.
subquestions.solution:
The Euler–Lagrange equation for r gives
$$(1 + 4 A^2 r^2) \ddot{r} + 4 A^2 r \dot{r}^2 + 2 A g r = 0$$
The lowest point of the paraboloid is at
$$r = 0$$
For small oscillations near r = 0, the linearized equation is
$$\ddot{r} + 2 A g r = 0$$
The angular frequency of these small oscillations is
$$\omega = \sqrt{2 A g}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be a single explicit differential equation for r(t), set equal to zero, written only with r, \dot{r}, \ddot{r}, A, g.

subquestions.subproblem: If \frac{d \varphi}{d t} = 0, show that the particle can execute small oscilations about the lowest point of the paraboloid,and find the frequency of these oscillations.
subquestions.solution:
Imposing the condition
$$\dot{\varphi} = 0$$
reduces the motion to the radial equation found above near r = 0,
$$\ddot{r} + 2 A g r = 0$$
Thus the particle executes small oscillations about r = 0 with angular frequency
$$\omega = \sqrt{2 A g}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \omega = ..., and your response should be written using only A and g.

grading_standard.formula: $$L = \frac{1}{2} m (1 + 4 A^2 r^2) \dot{r}^2 + \frac{1}{2} m r^2 \dot{\varphi}^2 - A m g r^2$$
$$H = \frac{1}{2} m (1 + 4 A^2 r^2) \dot{r}^2 + \frac{1}{2} m r^2 \dot{\varphi}^2 + A m g r^2$$

context: A particle of mass m is confined to one-dimensional motion along the x-axis between two perfectly reflecting walls. The walls move symmetrically toward the center at constant speed V, with V much smaller than the particle's speed. The particle's speed is always much less than the speed of light. Let x(t) denote the instantaneous separation between the walls and let x0 = x(0). Let p denote the magnitude of the particle's linear momentum and p0 = p(0) when the separation is x0. Collisions with the walls are perfectly elastic.

subquestions.subproblem: If the momentum of the particle is p0 when the walls are a distance x0 apart, find the momentum p(t) of the particle at any later time t. Assume all collisions with the walls are perfectly elastic and that at all times the particle's speed is much less than the speed of light.
subquestions.solution:
Consider a collision of the particle with a wall moving toward the particle with speed V. For an incident speed v and reflected speed v', equality of relative speeds before and after the elastic collision gives
$$v + V = v' - V$$
which implies
$$v' = v + 2 V$$
After each collision, the magnitude of the particle's momentum increases by
$$\Delta p = 2 m V$$
When the walls are a distance x apart, the interval between two consecutive collisions is
$$T = \frac{x m}{p}$$
Hence the momentum change in a time dt is
$$dp = \frac{2 m V dt}{T}$$
which gives
$$dp = \frac{2 V p dt}{x}$$
As the walls move toward each other with speed V, with t measured from the instant x = x0, the separation is
$$x = x0 - 2 V t$$
Therefore
$$dp = - \frac{p dx}{x}$$
Integrating from the initial state (p0,x0) to (p,x) gives
$$\int_{p0}^{p} \frac{dp'}{p'} = - \int_{x0}^{x} \frac{dx'}{x'}$$
which yields
$$\ln \frac{p}{p0} = - \ln \frac{x}{x0}$$
so that
$$p x = p0 x0$$
and hence
$$p = \frac{p0 x0}{x}$$
Using x = x0 - 2 V t, the momentum as a function of time is
$$p(t) = \frac{p0 x0}{x0 - 2 V t}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form p(t) = ..., and your response should be written with p0, x0, V, t.

subquestions.subproblem: When the walls are a distance x apart, what average external force F_ext(x) must be applied to each wall in order to move it at constant speed V?
subquestions.solution:
Consider collisions with one wall. The particle's momentum changes from −p to p + 2 m V, so the momentum gained by the particle in one collision is
$$\Delta p = 2 p + 2 m V$$
The interval between two consecutive collisions with the same wall is
$$T' = \frac{2 x m}{p}$$
Thus the rate of change of the particle's momentum due to collisions with that wall is
$$\frac{dp}{dt} = \frac{2 (p + m V)}{T'}$$
which gives
$$\frac{dp}{dt} = \frac{(p + m V) p}{x m}$$
Since p/m \gg V, we have the approximation
$$\frac{dp}{dt} \approx \frac{p^{2}}{x m}$$
Using p = p0 x0 / x, this becomes
$$\frac{dp}{dt} = \frac{p0^{2} x0^{2}}{m x^{3}}$$
This is the average force exerted by the wall on the particle. By Newton's third law, to keep the wall moving at constant speed V, an average external force of the same magnitude must be applied to the wall, so
$$F_{\mathrm{ext}}(x) = \frac{p0^{2} x0^{2}}{m x^{3}}$$
An equivalent derivation uses the Hamiltonian in a frame attached to one wall. In that frame the particle velocity is
$$v_{\mathrm{rel}} = - \frac{p}{m} - V$$
The Hamiltonian is
$$H = \frac{1}{2} m \left( \frac{p}{m} + V \right)^{2}$$
which can be written as
$$H = \frac{1}{2 m} (p + m V)^{2}$$
Under p/m \gg V this reduces to
$$H \approx \frac{p^{2}}{2 m}$$
and using p = p0 x0 / x gives
$$H = \frac{p0^{2} x0^{2}}{2 m x^{2}}$$
Hamilton's equation yields the force on the particle
$$\dot{p} = - \frac{\partial H}{\partial x}$$
so that
$$\dot{p} = \frac{p0^{2} x0^{2}}{m x^{3}}$$
which agrees with the result above
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form F_ext(x) = ..., and your response should be written with p0, x0, m, x.

context: The Poisson bracket for functions a and b of canonical variables q_k and p_k is defined by $$[a,b]=\sum_k\frac{\partial a}{\partial q_k}\frac{\partial b}{\partial p_k}-\sum_k\frac{\partial a}{\partial p_k}\frac{\partial b}{\partial q_k}$$ Consider a two-dimensional oscillator with Cartesian coordinates x and y, mass m, and constants K and C. The kinetic and potential energies are $$T(\dot x,\dot y)=\frac{1}{2}m(\dot x^2+\dot y^2)$$ $$V(x,y)=\frac{1}{2}K(x^2+y^2)+Cxy$$ The Lagrangian is $$L=T-V$$ Let H denote the Hamiltonian constructed from L. An overdot denotes a time derivative. Canonical momenta are conjugate to their corresponding coordinates, for example p_x and p_y are conjugate to x and y, and p_\eta and p_\xi are conjugate to \eta and \xi introduced later. In part (e), indices i and j take values in {1,2}, with x_1=x, x_2=y, p_1=p_x, and p_2=p_y.

subquestions.subproblem: Show that for a dynamical quantity a(q,p,t) the following relation holds $$\frac{da}{dt}=[a,H]+\frac{\partial a}{\partial t}$$ For the two-dimensional oscillator specified in the context, the energies are $$T(\dot x,\dot y)=\frac{1}{2}m(\dot x^2+\dot y^2)$$ $$V(x,y)=\frac{1}{2}K(x^2+y^2)+Cxy$$ where K and C are constants.
subquestions.solution: Using Hamilton's canonical equations $$\dot q_k=\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_k}$$ $$\dot p_k=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial q_k}$$ we find $$\frac{da}{dt}=\sum_k\frac{\partial a}{\partial q_k}\dot q_k+\sum_k\frac{\partial a}{\partial p_k}\dot p_k+\frac{\partial a}{\partial t}$$ $$\frac{da}{dt}=\sum_k\frac{\partial a}{\partial q_k}\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_k}-\sum_k\frac{\partial a}{\partial p_k}\frac{\partial H}{\partial q_k}+\frac{\partial a}{\partial t}$$ $$\frac{da}{dt}=[a,H]+\frac{\partial a}{\partial t}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \(\frac{da}{dt}=\dots\), and your response should be written with only \(a, H, t\).

subquestions.subproblem: Show by a coordinate transformation that this oscillator is equivalent to a nonisotropic harmonic oscillator.
subquestions.solution: Introduce the new variables $$\eta=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(x+y)$$ $$\xi=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(x-y)$$ Then $$x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(\eta+\xi)$$ $$y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(\eta-\xi)$$ For the kinetic energy, $$T=\frac{1}{4}m[(\dot\eta+\dot\xi)^2+(\dot\eta-\dot\xi)^2]$$ $$T=\frac{1}{2}m(\dot\eta^2+\dot\xi^2)$$ For the potential energy, $$V=\frac{1}{4}K[(\eta+\xi)^2+(\eta-\xi)^2]+\frac{1}{2}C(\eta^2-\xi^2)$$ $$V=\frac{1}{2}K(\eta^2+\xi^2)+\frac{1}{2}C(\eta^2-\xi^2)$$ $$V=\frac{1}{2}(K+C)\eta^2+\frac{1}{2}(K-C)\xi^2$$ Therefore, the Lagrangian splits as $$L=L_1+L_2$$ with $$L_1=\frac{1}{2}m\dot\eta^2-\frac{1}{2}(K+C)\eta^2$$ $$L_2=\frac{1}{2}m\dot\xi^2-\frac{1}{2}(K-C)\xi^2$$ Hence \eta and \xi are normal coordinates and the system is equivalent to two harmonic oscillators with angular frequencies $$\omega_1=\sqrt{\frac{K+C}{m}}$$ $$\omega_2=\sqrt{\frac{K-C}{m}}$$ which are generally different, so the oscillator is nonisotropic.
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should provide the coordinate transformation and the two angular frequencies in the form \(\eta=\dots,\ \xi=\dots,\ \omega_1=\dots,\ \omega_2=\dots\), and your response should be written with only \(x, y, \eta, \xi, m, K, C\).

subquestions.subproblem: Find two independent constants of the motion and verify using part (a) that they are constants of motion.
subquestions.solution: The canonical momenta are $$p_\eta=\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot\eta}$$ $$p_\eta=m\dot\eta$$ $$p_\xi=\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot\xi}$$ $$p_\xi=m\dot\xi$$ The Hamiltonian is $$H=p_\eta\dot\eta+p_\xi\dot\xi-L$$ $$H=\frac{1}{2m}p_\eta^2+\frac{1}{2m}p_\xi^2+\frac{1}{2}(K+C)\eta^2+\frac{1}{2}(K-C)\xi^2$$ This can be written as $$H=H_1+H_2$$ with $$H_1=\frac{p_\eta^2}{2m}+\frac{1}{2}(K+C)\eta^2$$ $$H_2=\frac{p_\xi^2}{2m}+\frac{1}{2}(K-C)\xi^2$$ As H_1 and H_2 do not contain t explicitly, $$\frac{dH_1}{dt}=[H_1,H]$$ $$[H_1,H]=[H_1,H_1+H_2]$$ $$[H_1,H]=[H_1,H_1]+[H_1,H_2]$$ $$[H_1,H_2]=\frac{\partial H_1}{\partial \eta}\frac{\partial H_2}{\partial p_\eta}+\frac{\partial H_1}{\partial \xi}\frac{\partial H_2}{\partial p_\xi}-\frac{\partial H_1}{\partial p_\eta}\frac{\partial H_2}{\partial \eta}-\frac{\partial H_1}{\partial p_\xi}\frac{\partial H_2}{\partial \xi}$$ $$[H_1,H_2]=0$$ Hence $$\frac{dH_1}{dt}=0$$ and similarly $$\frac{dH_2}{dt}=0$$ Therefore H_1 and H_2 are two independent constants of the motion.
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should give two independent constants of motion in the form \(H_1=\dots\) and \(H_2=\dots\), and your response should be written with only \(\eta, \xi, p_\eta, p_\xi, m, K, C\).

subquestions.subproblem: Repeat of part (a): Show that for a(q,p,t) the relation holds $$\frac{da}{dt}=[a,H]+\frac{\partial a}{\partial t}$$
subquestions.solution: Using Hamilton's canonical equations $$\dot q_k=\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_k}$$ $$\dot p_k=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial q_k}$$ we find $$\frac{da}{dt}=\sum_k\frac{\partial a}{\partial q_k}\dot q_k+\sum_k\frac{\partial a}{\partial p_k}\dot p_k+\frac{\partial a}{\partial t}$$ $$\frac{da}{dt}=\sum_k\frac{\partial a}{\partial q_k}\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_k}-\sum_k\frac{\partial a}{\partial p_k}\frac{\partial H}{\partial q_k}+\frac{\partial a}{\partial t}$$ $$\frac{da}{dt}=[a,H]+\frac{\partial a}{\partial t}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \(\frac{da}{dt}=\dots\), and your response should be written with only \(a, H, t\).

subquestions.subproblem: If C=0 find a third constant of the motion.
subquestions.solution: If C=0, the oscillator is isotropic and $$\omega_1=\omega_2$$ The Hamiltonian is $$H=\frac{1}{2m}p_\eta^2+\frac{1}{2m}p_\xi^2+\frac{1}{2}K\eta^2+\frac{1}{2}K\xi^2$$ Define $$J=m(\eta p_\xi-\xi p_\eta)$$ Then $$\frac{dJ}{dt}=[J,H]$$ $$[J,H]=\frac{\partial J}{\partial \eta}\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_\eta}-\frac{\partial J}{\partial p_\eta}\frac{\partial H}{\partial \eta}+\frac{\partial J}{\partial \xi}\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_\xi}-\frac{\partial J}{\partial p_\xi}\frac{\partial H}{\partial \xi}$$ $$[J,H]=p_\xi p_\eta+mK\xi\eta-p_\eta p_\xi-mK\eta\xi$$ $$[J,H]=0$$ Hence J is a third constant of the motion.
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form \(J=\dots\) (for the case \(C=0\)), and your response should be written with only \(J, m, \eta, \xi, p_\eta, p_\xi\).

subquestions.subproblem: Show that for the isotropic oscillator the symmetric matrix $$A_{ij}=\frac{p_ip_j}{2m}+\frac{1}{2}Kx_ix_j$$ is a constant of the motion by expressing each element in terms of the known constants of motion. Here i,j∈{1,2} with x_1=x, x_2=y, p_1=p_x, and p_2=p_y.
subquestions.solution: For the isotropic oscillator, C=0 and x and y already are normal coordinates. As shown above, there are three constants of the motion defined by $$E_1=\frac{p_x^2}{2m}+\frac{1}{2}Kx^2$$ $$E_2=\frac{p_y^2}{2m}+\frac{1}{2}Ky^2$$ $$J=m(xp_y-yp_x)$$ The diagonal elements are $$A_{11}=E_1$$ $$A_{22}=E_2$$ For the off-diagonal element, consider $$E_1E_2-\frac{KJ^2}{4m^3}=\left(\frac{p_xp_y}{2m}+\frac{1}{2}Kxy\right)^2$$ Since the left-hand side is constant, $$A_{12}=\frac{p_xp_y}{2m}+\frac{1}{2}Kxy$$ $$A_{21}=\frac{p_xp_y}{2m}+\frac{1}{2}Kxy$$ Hence A_{ij} is a matrix of constant elements.
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should specify the matrix elements in the form \(A_{11}=\dots,\ A_{22}=\dots,\ A_{12}=A_{21}=\dots\) expressed using the known constants of motion, and your response should be written with only \(A_{11}, A_{22}, A_{12}, A_{21}, E_1, E_2, J, m, K\).

grading_standard.formula: $$\frac{da}{dt}=\sum_k\frac{\partial a}{\partial q_k}\dot q_k+\sum_k\frac{\partial a}{\partial p_k}\dot p_k+\frac{\partial a}{\partial t}$$
$$\frac{da}{dt}=\sum_k\frac{\partial a}{\partial q_k}\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_k}-\sum_k\frac{\partial a}{\partial p_k}\frac{\partial H}{\partial q_k}+\frac{\partial a}{\partial t}$$
$$\frac{da}{dt}=\sum_k\frac{\partial a}{\partial q_k}\dot q_k+\sum_k\frac{\partial a}{\partial p_k}\dot p_k+\frac{\partial a}{\partial t}$$
$$\frac{da}{dt}=\sum_k\frac{\partial a}{\partial q_k}\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_k}-\sum_k\frac{\partial a}{\partial p_k}\frac{\partial H}{\partial q_k}+\frac{\partial a}{\partial t}$$

context: A particle of mass m moves in one dimension with coordinate q(t) in a potential energy field V(q) and is retarded by a linear damping force F_d = -2 m gamma dot q proportional to its velocity. Let t denote time and gamma > 0 be the damping coefficient. Use p for the momentum conjugate to q, H for the Hamiltonian, F_2(q,P,t) for a type-2 generating function, and (Q,P) for the transformed canonical variables with transformed Hamiltonian K(Q,P,t). For the harmonic oscillator, use V(q) = (1/2) m omega^2 q^2. In the underdamped case gamma < omega, define omega_1 = sqrt(omega^2 - gamma^2). Let A and varphi denote integration constants determined by initial conditions.

subquestions.subproblem: Show that the equation of motion can be obtained from the Lagrangian $$\mathcal{L} = e^{2 \gamma t} \left[ \frac{1}{2} m \dot{q}^{2} - V(q) \right]$$ and that the Hamiltonian is $$H = \frac{p^{2} e^{-2 \gamma t}}{2 m} + V(q) e^{2 \gamma t}$$ where p is the momentum conjugate to q
subquestions.solution: Lagrange's equation $$\frac{d}{dt} \left( \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot{q}} \right) - \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial q} = 0$$ gives the equation of motion $$m \ddot{q} = - \frac{\partial V}{\partial q} - 2 m \gamma \dot{q}$$ The Hamiltonian is defined by $$H = p \dot{q} - \mathcal{L}$$ with conjugate momentum $$p = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot{q}}$$ For the given Lagrangian this yields $$p = m \dot{q} e^{2 \gamma t}$$ Hence $$H = \left( \frac{1}{2} m \dot{q}^{2} + V(q) \right) e^{2 \gamma t}$$ Eliminating \dot{q} in favor of p gives $$H = \frac{p^{2} e^{-2 \gamma t}}{2 m} + V(q) e^{2 \gamma t}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should include two algebraic results: (1) the equation of motion written in the form m q̈ = ... using only m, γ, q, q̇, q̈, and ∂V/∂q; and (2) the Hamiltonian written in the form H = ... using only p, m, γ, t, and V(q).

subquestions.subproblem: For the generating function $$F_{2}(q,P,t) = e^{\gamma t} q P$$ find the transformed Hamiltonian K(Q,P,t). For an oscillator potential $$V(q) = \frac{1}{2} m \omega^{2} q^{2}$$ show that the transformed Hamiltonian yields a constant of the motion $$K = \frac{P^{2}}{2 m} + \frac{1}{2} m \omega^{2} Q^{2} + \gamma Q P$$
subquestions.solution: For the type-2 generating function we have $$p = \frac{\partial F_{2}}{\partial q}$$ $$Q = \frac{\partial F_{2}}{\partial P}$$ $$K = H + \frac{\partial F_{2}}{\partial t}$$ With $$F_{2}(q,P,t) = e^{\gamma t} q P$$ we obtain $$p = P e^{\gamma t}$$ $$Q = q e^{\gamma t}$$ $$\frac{\partial F_{2}}{\partial t} = \gamma q P e^{\gamma t}$$ Using $$H = \frac{p^{2} e^{-2 \gamma t}}{2 m} + V(q) e^{2 \gamma t}$$ we get $$K = \frac{p^{2} e^{-2 \gamma t}}{2 m} + V(q) e^{2 \gamma t} + \gamma q P e^{\gamma t}$$ For the oscillator potential $$V(q) = \frac{1}{2} m \omega^{2} q^{2}$$ and using $$q = Q e^{- \gamma t}$$ we have $$V(q) e^{2 \gamma t} = \frac{1}{2} m \omega^{2} Q^{2}$$ Also, using $$p = P e^{\gamma t}$$ we find $$\frac{p^{2} e^{-2 \gamma t}}{2 m} = \frac{P^{2}}{2 m}$$ and $$\gamma q P e^{\gamma t} = \gamma Q P$$ Therefore $$K = \frac{P^{2}}{2 m} + \frac{1}{2} m \omega^{2} Q^{2} + \gamma Q P$$ which is time independent and hence a constant of the motion
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should provide: (1) the transformed Hamiltonian in the general case in the form K = ... using only p, q, P, t, V(q), m, and γ; and (2) for V(q) = (1/2) m ω^2 q^2, the simplified time-independent form in the format K = ... using only Q, P, m, ω, and γ.

subquestions.subproblem: Obtain the solution q(t) for the damped oscillator from the constant of the motion
subquestions.solution: Hamilton's canonical equations from $$K = \frac{P^{2}}{2 m} + \frac{1}{2} m \omega^{2} Q^{2} + \gamma Q P$$ are $$\dot{P} = - \frac{\partial K}{\partial Q}$$ $$\dot{Q} = \frac{\partial K}{\partial P}$$ which give $$\dot{P} = - m \omega^{2} Q - \gamma P$$ $$\dot{Q} = \frac{P}{m} + \gamma Q$$ Differentiating \dot{Q} and using the equation for \dot{P} yields $$\ddot{Q} + ( \omega^{2} - \gamma^{2} ) Q = 0$$ In the underdamped case \(\gamma < \omega\), define $$\omega_{1} = \sqrt{ \omega^{2} - \gamma^{2} }$$ The general solution is $$Q(t) = A \sin( \omega_{1} t + \varphi )$$ From $$\dot{Q} = \frac{P}{m} + \gamma Q$$ we have $$P = m ( \dot{Q} - \gamma Q )$$ The constant of motion evaluates to $$K = \frac{1}{2} m ( \dot{Q} - \gamma Q )^{2} + \frac{1}{2} m \omega^{2} Q^{2} + m \gamma Q ( \dot{Q} - \gamma Q )$$ which simplifies to $$K = \frac{1}{2} m \dot{Q}^{2} + \frac{1}{2} m \omega_{1}^{2} Q^{2}$$ For $$Q(t) = A \sin( \omega_{1} t + \varphi )$$ this gives $$K = \frac{1}{2} m \omega_{1}^{2} A^{2}$$ hence $$A = \frac{1}{\omega_{1}} \sqrt{ \frac{2 K}{m} }$$ Finally, using $$q(t) = Q(t) e^{- \gamma t}$$ we obtain $$q(t) = \frac{1}{\omega_{1}} \sqrt{ \frac{2 K}{m} } e^{- \gamma t} \sin( \omega_{1} t + \varphi )$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given as a single explicit expression of the form q(t) = ... for the underdamped case, using only t, K, m, γ, ω1, and varphi, where ω1 = sqrt(ω^2 − γ^2).

subquestions.subproblem: In the underdamped case \(\gamma < \omega\). You may need the integral $$\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}} = \sin^{-1} x$$
subquestions.solution: For the generating function we have $$p = \frac{\partial F_{2}}{\partial q}$$ $$Q = \frac{\partial F_{2}}{\partial P}$$ $$K = H + \frac{\partial F_{2}}{\partial t}$$ With $$F_{2}(q,P,t) = e^{\gamma t} q P$$ we obtain $$p = P e^{\gamma t}$$ $$Q = q e^{\gamma t}$$ $$K = \frac{p^{2} e^{-2 \gamma t}}{2 m} + V(q) e^{2 \gamma t} + \gamma q P e^{\gamma t}$$ For the oscillator potential $$V(q) = \frac{1}{2} m \omega^{2} q^{2}$$ and using $$q = Q e^{- \gamma t}$$ the transformed Hamiltonian is $$K = \frac{P^{2}}{2 m} + \frac{1}{2} m \omega^{2} Q^{2} + \gamma Q P$$ which is independent of t and therefore is a constant of the motion
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should state the transformed Hamiltonian for the oscillator in the format K = ... using only Q, P, m, ω, and γ, and it should not contain t.

grading_standard.formula: $$H = \frac{p^{2} e^{-2 \gamma t}}{2 m} + V(q) e^{2 \gamma t}$$
$$\frac{\partial F_{2}}{\partial t} = \gamma q P e^{\gamma t}$$
$$K = \frac{p^{2} e^{-2 \gamma t}}{2 m} + V(q) e^{2 \gamma t} + \gamma q P e^{\gamma t}$$
$$\gamma q P e^{\gamma t} = \gamma Q P$$
$$K = \frac{1}{2} m ( \dot{Q} - \gamma Q )^{2} + \frac{1}{2} m \omega^{2} Q^{2} + m \gamma Q ( \dot{Q} - \gamma Q )$$

context: We consider a single particle moving in one spatial dimension with canonical coordinate q and canonical momentum p under a Hamiltonian H. We use a type-2 generating function S(q, \alpha, t) to perform a canonical transformation to new variables (\beta, \alpha), where \beta is the transformed coordinate and \alpha is the transformed momentum. The transformed Hamiltonian is denoted by K and is related to H by K = H + \partial S/\partial t evaluated on the transformation. Time is denoted by t, and all time derivatives are written using d/dt. The symbols \alpha_0 and \phi are integration constants determined by initial conditions. When we write q[\beta(t), \alpha(t)] and p[\beta(t), \alpha(t)], we mean the original variables expressed in terms of (\beta, \alpha) and then evaluated on the time-dependent solutions (\beta(t), \alpha(t)). If a symbol \Delta_t appears in any subproblem statement, it should be understood as the time variable t.

subquestions.subproblem: Solve the Hamilton-Jacobi equation for the type-2 generating function S(q, \alpha, t) for a single particle moving under the Hamiltonian H = \frac{1}{2} p^2. Find the canonical transformation q = q(\beta, \alpha) and p = p(\beta, \alpha), where \beta and \alpha are the transformed coordinate and momentum respectively. Interpret your result.
subquestions.solution:
The Hamilton-Jacobi equation is
$$\frac{\partial S}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{2} \Big( \frac{\partial S}{\partial q} \Big)^2 = 0$$
A solution linear in q is
$$S = \alpha q - \frac{1}{2} \alpha^2 t$$
The transformation equations are
$$p = \frac{\partial S}{\partial q}$$
$$\beta = \frac{\partial S}{\partial \alpha}$$
Thus
$$p = \alpha$$
$$\beta = q - \alpha t$$
Solving for q and p as functions of (\beta, \alpha) gives
$$q = \beta + \alpha t$$
$$p = \alpha$$
The transformed Hamiltonian is
$$K = H + \frac{\partial S}{\partial t}$$
For this unperturbed system one finds
$$K = 0$$
Interpretation: The motion is uniform with constant momentum \alpha, and \beta is the initial position q at t = 0.
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of S(q, \alpha, t) = ..., q(\beta, \alpha, t) = ..., and p(\beta, \alpha, t) = .... The right-hand side of S should use only q, \alpha, t; the right-hand sides of q and p should use only \beta, \alpha, t.

subquestions.subproblem: If there is a perturbing Hamiltonian H' = \frac{1}{2} q^2, then \alpha will no longer be constant. Using the same transformation found in part (a), express the transformed Hamiltonian K in terms of \alpha, \beta, and t.
subquestions.solution:
The perturbed Hamiltonian is
$$H = \frac{p^2}{2} + \frac{q^2}{2}$$
The transformed Hamiltonian is
$$K = H + \frac{\partial S}{\partial t}$$
Using S from part (a) yields
$$K = \frac{p^2}{2} + \frac{q^2}{2} - \frac{\alpha^2}{2}$$
Using p = \alpha and q = \beta + \alpha t, we obtain
$$K = \frac{1}{2} (\beta + \alpha t)^2$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of K(\alpha, \beta, t) = ..., written only with \alpha, \beta, t on the right-hand side.

subquestions.subproblem: Continuing part (b), write Hamilton's equations in terms of \alpha, \beta, and t. Solve for \beta(t) and \alpha(t), and show that the perturbed solution q[\beta(t), \alpha(t)] and p[\beta(t), \alpha(t)] is simple harmonic. You may use the integrals \int \frac{dx}{x^2+1} = \tan^{-1} x and - \int \tan x dx = \ln(\cos x) if needed.
subquestions.solution:
Hamilton's equations in the transformed variables are
$$\frac{d\beta}{dt} = \frac{\partial K}{\partial \alpha}$$
$$\frac{d\alpha}{dt} = - \frac{\partial K}{\partial \beta}$$
With K = \frac{1}{2} (\beta + \alpha t)^2, these become
$$\frac{d\beta}{dt} = t (\beta + \alpha t)$$
$$\frac{d\alpha}{dt} = - (\beta + \alpha t)$$
Eliminating \beta gives
$$\frac{d^2 \alpha}{dt^2} + \alpha = 0$$
The general solution is
$$\alpha(t) = \alpha_0 \sin(t + \phi)$$
where \alpha_0 and \phi are constants, and hence
$$\beta(t) = - \frac{d\alpha}{dt} - \alpha t$$
Transforming back to (q, p) using q = \beta + \alpha t and p = \alpha gives
$$p(t) = \alpha(t)$$
$$q(t) = - \frac{d\alpha}{dt}$$
Therefore
$$p(t) = \alpha_0 \sin(t + \phi)$$
$$q(t) = - \alpha_0 \cos(t + \phi)$$
which is simple harmonic motion. For reference, the integrals that may be used are
$$\int \frac{dx}{x^2 + 1} = \tan^{-1} x$$
$$- \int \tan x dx = \ln(\cos x)$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \alpha(t) = ..., \beta(t) = ..., q(t) = ..., and p(t) = ..., written only in terms of t and the integration constants \alpha_0 and \phi.

context: A rectangular solid block of length l along the x-direction and cross-sectional area A on the face parallel to the applied shear force F (see Fig. 2.77) is subjected to a tangential shearing force F. The small transverse displacement field is u(x,t), directed along the y-direction. The shear angle is denoted by phi, the shear modulus by n, and the mass density by rho. Within elastic limits, linear elasticity (Hooke's law for shear) applies. Energies and variational quantities: T is the kinetic energy, V is the potential energy, L is the Lagrangian L = T - V, and V_v denotes the potential energy per unit volume (energy density). The time bounds for Hamilton's principle are t_1 and t_2, and delta u is the variation of u with delta u = 0 at x = 0, x = l, t = t_1, and t = t_2. The wave speed is denoted by v. Units: F in \unit{N}, A in \unit{m^2}, l in \unit{m}, u in \unit{m}, phi dimensionless, n in \unit{Pa}, rho in \unit{kg/m^3}, x in \unit{m}, t in \unit{s}, v in \unit{m/s}.

subquestions.subproblem: Let us apply a shearing force on a rectangular solid block as shown in Fig. 2.77. Find the relation between the displacement u and the applied force within elastic limits. Use F for the shearing force, n for the shear modulus, phi for the shear angle, A for the cross-sectional area parallel to F, l for the length along x, and u for the transverse displacement at the top face.
subquestions.solution:
Hooke's law for shear gives the stress-strain relation
$$
\frac{F}{A} = n \phi
$$
For small shear angles, the transverse displacement at the top face satisfies
$$
 u = l \phi
$$
Eliminating phi gives
$$
 u = \frac{l F}{A n}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of u = ..., and your response should be written with F, n, A, l.

subquestions.subproblem: The elastic properties of a solid support elastic waves. Assume a transverse plane wave which proceeds in the x-direction and whose oscillations are in the y-direction. Derive the equations of motion for the displacement u(x,t).
subquestions.solution:
The potential energy per unit volume due to shear is
$$
 V_v = \frac{1}{l A} \int_0^u F du'
$$
Using F = A n \phi and u = l \phi, this becomes
$$
 V_v = \frac{1}{l A} \int_0^{\phi} A n \phi' l d\phi'
$$
Therefore
$$
 V_v = \frac{1}{2} n \phi^2
$$
The shear angle equals the shear strain
$$
 \phi = \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}
$$
Hence
$$
 V_v = \frac{1}{2} n \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} \right)^2
$$
The kinetic energy is
$$
 T = \int_0^l \frac{1}{2} \rho A \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} \right)^2 dx
$$
Hamilton's principle states
$$
 \delta \int_{t_1}^{t_2} L dt = 0
$$
Equivalently
$$
 \delta \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \int_0^l \left[ \frac{n}{2} \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} \right)^2 - \frac{\rho}{2} \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} \right)^2 \right] A dx dt = 0
$$
Using integration by parts, we have
$$
 \int_0^l \delta \left[ \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} \right)^2 \right] dx = 2 \int_0^l \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} \frac{\partial (\delta u)}{\partial x} dx
$$
and
$$
 \int_0^l \delta \left[ \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} \right)^2 \right] dx = 2 \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} \delta u \bigg|_{0}^{l} - 2 \int_0^l \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} \delta u dx
$$
Similarly
$$
 \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \delta \left[ \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} \right)^2 \right] dt = 2 \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} \delta u \bigg|_{t_1}^{t_2} - 2 \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2} \delta u dt
$$
With delta u = 0 at x = 0, x = l, t = t_1, and t = t_2, we obtain
$$
 - \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \int_0^l \left( n \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} - \rho \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2} \right) \delta u A dx dt = 0
$$
Therefore the equation of motion is
$$
 \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} - \frac{\rho}{n} \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2} = 0
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be a single partial differential equation for u(x,t) written as ... = 0, and your response should be written with u, x, t, n, rho.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the expression for the speed v of the transverse elastic wave.
subquestions.solution:
The displacement u(x,t) satisfies the one-dimensional wave equation with wave speed
$$
 v = \sqrt{\frac{n}{\rho}}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of v = ..., and your response should be written with n, rho.

grading_standard.formula: $$ V_v = \frac{1}{l A} \int_0^{\phi} A n \phi' l d\phi'$$
$$ \delta \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \int_0^l \left[ \frac{n}{2} \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} \right)^2 - \frac{\rho}{2} \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} \right)^2 \right] A dx dt = 0$$
$$ - \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \int_0^l \left( n \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} - \rho \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2} \right) \delta u A dx dt = 0$$

context: A spacecraft moves at constant speed v relative to Earth along the +x direction. Let Σ (Earth frame) and Σ′ (spacecraft frame) be inertial frames. A standard clock at the Earth origin records time t, and a standard clock at the spacecraft origin records time t′. The clocks are synchronized at the event t = 0, t′ = 0, x = 0, x′ = 0. The Earth observer watches his own clock directly and the spacecraft clock through a telescope. Define Δ_t to be the reading of the Earth clock at the instant he visually sees the spacecraft clock’s display. Given β = v/c and γ = 1/√(1 − β^2), and c the speed of light, when the spacecraft clock reads 1 hour, find Δ_t.
solution:
Consider the event on the spacecraft worldline at which the spacecraft clock reads t_2′. This event occurs at x_2′ = 0 in Σ′.

$$
ct_2 = 
\gamma c t_2′
$$

$$
 x_2 = 
\gamma \beta c t_2′
$$

The light-travel time from that event to Earth is

$$
\Delta t = \frac{x_2}{c}
$$

Substituting x_2 gives

$$
\Delta t = \gamma \beta t_2′
$$

The Earth clock reading at the instant of visual observation is

$$
t_{\text{obs}} = t_2 + \Delta t
$$

Using the above relations,

$$
\t_{\text{obs}} = \gamma (1 + \beta) t_2′
$$

Using \gamma (1+\beta) = \sqrt{\frac{1+\beta}{1-\beta}},

$$
\t_{\text{obs}} = \sqrt{\frac{1+\beta}{1-\beta}} t_2′
$$

Equivalently,

$$
\t_{\text{obs}} = \sqrt{\frac{c+v}{c-v}} t_2′
$$

With t_2′ = 1 \unit{h} and defining \Delta_t = t_{\text{obs}},

$$
\Delta_t = \sqrt{\frac{1+\beta}{1-\beta}} \unit{h}
$$

Equivalently,

$$
\Delta_t = \sqrt{\frac{c+v}{c-v}} \unit{h}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form Δ_t = (expression in β) h, and your response should be written solely in terms of β (β = v/c). Do not include any other symbols such as γ, v, c, or t′. The unit should be hours (h).

context: A light source at rest at position x = 0 in inertial frame S emits two light pulses, P_1 at time t = 0 and P_2 at time t = \tau. Another inertial frame S' moves with constant velocity v along the +x direction relative to S. Define c as the speed of light in vacuum, \beta = v/c, and \gamma = 1/\sqrt{1-\beta^2}. An observer in S' located at x' = 0 receives the initial pulse P_1 at time t' = 0. Let \Delta t' denote the light-propagation time from the emission event of P_2 to its reception at x' = 0. In parts (b) and the second (a), \nu and \nu' are the pulse frequencies in S and S', and \lambda and \lambda' are the corresponding vacuum wavelengths. In part (c), consider the hydrogen H_\beta emission line with rest wavelength \lambda = 4861.33 \unit{\AA} produced by neutralization to H atoms of protons accelerated through a potential of 20 \unit{kV}. Assume emission occurs after acceleration while the protons drift with constant velocity, and that the spectrometer optical axis is parallel to the proton motion. Let E be the proton kinetic energy after acceleration, m the proton rest mass, and mc^2 its rest energy. In part (c), let u denote the proton drift speed so that the relevant Doppler parameter is \beta = u/c. The wavelength shift is denoted by \Delta \lambda; the first- and second-order contributions are denoted by \Delta \lambda_1 and \Delta \lambda_2
source: \lambda = 4861.33 \AA from the neutralization to H atoms of protons accelerated through a potential of 20 kV. Assuming that emission occurs after acceleration and while the protons drift with constant velocity. Also, assume that the optical axis of the spectrometer is parallel to the motion of the protons. (Chicago)

subquestions.subproblem: Calculate the time \tau' between the reception of the pulses at x' = 0 as a function of \tau and \beta = v/c.
subquestions.solution: Assume the spatial origins coincide at t = t' = 0 so that the emission of P_1 and its arrival at the observer occur at x = 0, t = 0 and x' = 0, t' = 0. The emission of P_2 is at x = 0 and t = \tau in S. The Lorentz transformation for the emission event gives $$x' = \gamma (x - \beta c t)$$ For x = 0 and t = \tau this becomes $$x' = - \gamma \beta c \tau$$ The Lorentz time transformation gives $$t' = \gamma \left(t - \frac{\beta x}{c}\right)$$ For x = 0 and t = \tau this becomes $$t' = \gamma \tau$$ The light-propagation time from the emission event to the observer at x' = 0 is $$\Delta t' = \frac{|x'|}{c}$$ Using the value of x' above, $$\Delta t' = \gamma \beta \tau$$ Hence the observer records the reception time of P_2 as $$t' + \Delta t' = \gamma (1 + \beta) \tau$$ Therefore the interval between receptions is $$\tau' = \tau \sqrt{\frac{1+\beta}{1-\beta}}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form τ' = ..., and your response should be written with τ and β only.

subquestions.subproblem: Using the result of part (a), express the frequencies and wavelengths in S and S' and relate \lambda' to \lambda and \beta.
